item.title: [Latent Space] The Inference Frontier: from 100 to 10,000 tokens per second — Sean Lie, Cerebras CTO
item.dc:creator: Latent Space
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、"快"的通货膨胀：Overton 窗口的静默漂移

Sean Lie 说了一句被多数人忽略的话："曾经被认为快的 100-200 tokens/秒，正在迅速成为新的 batch mode。"

这句话的杀伤力不在数字，而在心理锚点的位移。它揭示了一个反直觉的规律：速度从不是绝对量，而是一个"应用可能性"的守门人。当 tokens/秒跨越某个阈值，原本"批处理/离线"的东西突然变成"实时/交互"，你之前想都不敢想的产品形态一夜之间出现在白板上。

这与 90 年代"宽带"的定义演化如出一辙——从 56K 到千兆，每次"高速"都被下一次"高速"变成"低速"。但更深的类比在神经科学：人类对"即时反馈"的阈值大约是 100 毫秒，一旦跨过这条线，大脑就把工具视为"自我的延伸"而非"外部工具"。10,000 tps 意味着 LLM 首次真正跨过这条线——LLM 不再是你查询的对象，而是你思考本身的一部分。

二、被"没说的话"出卖的架构缺陷——一场技术侦探剧

访谈中最漂亮的推理，是 Sean 对 Groq/Jalapeno 的解读——他不是从他们展示的东西推理，而是从他们没展示的东西。

一家刚刚被估值几百亿的公司，为什么只在 30B 参数的模型上跑 benchmark？为什么 Jensen 在 GTC 花半小时讲 attention/FFN disaggregation，但 Jalapeno 的 launch 却对此只字不提？Sean 的答案是残酷的物理约束：非 wafer-scale 的 SRAM 架构装不下前沿模型的权重，需要"数千颗芯片"才能存下几万亿参数。

这是一种典型的"沉默即证据"式推理，和苏联学（Kremlinology）里通过主席台上谁站在谁旁边推测权力结构、和刑侦学中"狗为什么没叫"（福尔摩斯《银斑马》）是同一种思维方式。在硬件行业，Roadmap 里的"缺席"往往比"存在"信息量更大——你无法藏住物理定律，你只能选择不去测量它。

三、最出人意料的观察：超快推理的第一杀手级应用不是产品，而是 OpenAI 内部的事故响应

这一段几乎所有人都会漏掉。Sean 提到 OpenAI 用 Cerebras 的很大一部分容量跑内部的 incident response——服务宕机时，每一秒都关键。

这颠覆了整个叙事：我们一直以为"最快的 AI"会先服务于消费者的酷炫体验，实际上它先服务于运维工程师的救火现场。

这是一个递归性的技术寓言——AI 系统足够复杂后，维护 AI 的成本比生产 AI 的成本更高，于是最先进的 AI 反而被拿来维护 AI 本身。类似的模式在历史上反复出现： - 最早的互联网是物理学家分享论文，不是消费者上网； - 最早的 GPS 是给巡航导弹用的，不是给司机导航； - 最早的电力是给电报和照明公司自己发电用的。

"最快的算力最先被内部消化"是一条被严重低估的规律。这暗示着：真正的 AGI 前夜，最强的模型可能根本不会对外发布，因为它们会被用来训练/调试/守护下一代模型。前沿智能会变成一种内向的、自我指涉的资源。

四、隐藏的元洞察：数据中心正在变成一颗芯片

Sean 讲到 "at multi-gigawatt scale, it's as if you're thinking about the entire data center as if it's like one computer, it's like one chip"。

这一句话包含了一个尺度反演：过去 60 年，芯片从"一个电路"扩张成"一整个系统"（SoC）；现在，一整个数据中心正在收缩成"一颗芯片"。中间的所有抽象层（服务器、机架、集群）都在被压扁。这与生物学里多细胞生物涌现的过程完全同构——细胞先专业化，再通过通信协议协作，最终整个身体作为一个"超个体"运作。

Cerebras 的 wafer-scale 不是异端，它是这个尺度演化最诚实的一步。真正异端的是坚持"每颗芯片是独立单元"的传统 GPU 集群——它们只是还没承认自己也在朝同一个方向滑落。

五、被低估的地缘不对称

"开源模型市场 95% 是中国的"——这句话如果是真的（Sean 的原话），那意味着一个从未在主流叙事中被清晰化的图景：

美国生产闭源前沿智能，中国生产开源普及智能。这不是"谁领先"的问题，而是两种截然不同的分发模式的分工。这种分工的地缘政治后果可能比芯片禁令严重得多——因为开源模型一旦下载就无法收回，它们是"分布式的既成事实"，而闭源模型永远受制于 API 的收回权。

十年后回看，历史学家可能会说：芯片战争的赢家是美国，但模型基座层的默认标准之争，可能已经在无人注意时输给了中国。

📝 转录文本

Cold Open: The New Batch Mode

"What used to be considered fast at like 100 or 200 tokens per second is quickly becoming the new batch mode. And so I think that, you know, there's a place for that. It's great for prompt processing. It's great for very very parallel workloads."

— "But my emails take 20 hours. I can hit a button and run it in two hours."

— "Exactly. Exactly. Right. But but quickly, you know, being able to do prompt processing isn't quite enough. That's a big part of the market, but that's not quite enough."

Host's Note to Listeners

Before we get into today's episode, I just have a small message for listeners. Thank you. We would not be able to bring you the AI engineering, science, and entertainment content that you so clearly want if you didn't choose to also click in and tune into our content.

We've been approached by sponsors on an almost daily basis, but fortunately, enough of you actually subscribe to us to keep all this sustainable without ads, and we want to keep it that way. But I just have one favor to ask all of you.

The single most powerful, completely free thing you can do is to click that subscribe button. It's the only thing I'll ever ask of you. And it means absolutely everything to me and my team that works so hard to bring the Inspace to you each and every week. If you do it, I promise you we'll never stop working to make this show even better.

Now, let's get into it.

Welcome — The Day After Hot Chips

Host: Okay, we're here at Cerebras HQ with CTO Sean Lie. Welcome.

Sean: Thank you. Thank you for having us.

Host: Yeah. No, thank you for having me. And it is the day after Hot Chips. Lots of things launching. Even like Apple launched the M6 stuff. But you guys obviously had — we were at Supernova. You talked about CS4. We're going to talk a little bit about CS5. OpenAI talked about Jalapeno. All the hot stuff in Hot Chips. What's your take this year, having been in this industry?

Sean: Well, first of all, thank you for having me. And you're absolutely right — it's a super exciting time right now. Hot Chips is really a good time when the whole community comes together.

You know what — I still remember going to Hot Chips 10, 20 years ago when it's a bunch of like, you know, computer architect geeks geeking out on speeds and feeds. And now it's like this is where industry-changing hardware is being revealed. So it's come a long way. It's a really exciting community.

I think one of the main takeaways that I had after leaving Hot Chips yesterday is: what an exciting time it is for the chip design and the hardware industry. This is really the golden age of hardware right now. And like you said, I've been in this industry for some time. This is a very, very unique time — not just because AI is taking off and obviously a lot of people doing their own hardware, but the amount of innovation that's happening now across multiple fronts we've never seen in the history of the semiconductor industry.

This level of innovation across all the levels — the chip, the interconnect, the system design, the software, the optics, the methodology, the tooling — people are pushing across the board. As a technologist and a computer architecture geek at heart, it's really really fun to see this community and this industry at this stage right now. And when we felt that at Hot Chips, everybody I talked to — that buzz is there. It's amazing.

CS4: Nexus Platform, 2× Everything

Host: We want to go through the chips. Let's talk about your chip first. What's most exciting? CS4 came out. Some crazy numbers here — 30× faster than the GPUs. But you know, walk us through what's new with the new CS4.

Sean: Sure. So we designed our next-generation CS4 architecture — a brand new system platform — with the goal really to make wafer scale mainstream, to bring it to hyperscale, and to solve a lot of the high-density data center problems that we're facing every single day.

We've designed this modular platform that provides:

  • Twice the amount of power to the wafer than we had in our previous generation
  • Twice the amount of interconnect bandwidth
  • Half the latency

And all of it is done at the system architecture level. The result is that by being able to provide significantly more power to the wafers, by packing more density into the rack, we're able to drive up the performance even further.

We like to say that Cerebras with our current product is already the undisputed leader in ultra-fast inference. And what's amazing is this CS4 product will actually push that frontier even further by taking it another 2× faster.

This is a perfect example — right here in this demo that we gave at Hot Chips — we're showing GPT-OSS running at over 4,400 TPS, which is just mind-blowing. It almost feels like it's fake.

We think that this is going to really revolutionize the entire industry. Not only are we able to continue to push the frontier on how fast these models can run, it will enable all sorts of new applications, new user experiences. What used to be batch and offline applications start to become real time.

All of this growth in new agentic flows and agentic frameworks now also mean that you're sitting there waiting for these agents to go over and over and over in their agentic loop. And all of a sudden if you're running your model at over 4,000 tokens per second, you can do more agentic loops, you can do more reasoning — ultimately you get significantly more capable, more intelligent agents.

That's what really excites us about this. Not just the fact that we show these really big numbers — which is also really cool — but the fact that you can really start to do things that you can't really do otherwise and enable brand new capabilities. That's what makes me so excited about this reveal that we had yesterday.

From Tech Demo to Co-Designing With OpenAI

Host: I think it's also very rewarding that you guys started on this journey — the big chip journey, wafer scale, everything that you've always said. People didn't take it that seriously until they had to, and then now they're really really taking it super seriously.

As co-founder, CTO, the architect of this whole thing — how are you guys approaching the new generations post AI boom? I imagine CS1, 2, 3 was a bit more sort of calm. Now literally OpenAI is launching the ultra-fast mode with you guys, and it is a matter of — I don't know — you're co-designing your model with the chip almost.

Sean: Absolutely. The main shift that has happened over the last few years for us is that the first generation chip primarily was a technology demonstration. We had to demonstrate to the world — to ourselves — that you can actually build such a thing. We told a lot of people that this is the future, and most of them were just like, "You guys are insane. This is not possible."

At the beginning it was really about figuring out the foundational technologies to make it possible. What we're now seeing is: now that we have in fact demonstrated that this can be built and it can have the kind of performance that this type of architecture can have, what are all the things that it can enable?

You alluded to our recent ultra-fast launch with OpenAI — that's a perfect example. We're running a frontier-level, one of the most intelligent models — OpenAI's largest, most capable, most intelligent model right now — at 14× faster than their normal GPU speeds. It's becoming this completely transformational thing when you can combine the most intelligent models with the speed that the hardware brings.

This transition from technology demonstration to solving real problems, enabling new real capabilities — that's the transition that we as a company are going through. How we're coping with that right now is we're really shifting our focus to ensuring that we can make this scale. We can bring up the capacity that we need. We can run the models that the users ultimately care about. And then we continue this flywheel by making sure that we continue to put out faster hardware and keep pushing the frontier.

It's unfolding in a way that is almost better than we could have imagined. It's this perfect confluence of having the hardware with the capabilities demonstrated now matching with the capabilities of the models and the applications. So our goal right now is just scale this thing as fast as we can.

Previewing CS5: 10,000 TPS on Medium Models

Host: And so maybe we'll talk about yesterday — previewing CS5. Can you recap for people who are maybe not yet caught up, and maybe are new to the story for the first time as well?

Sean: No problem. So I mentioned that our CS4 system that we just launched is based off of a brand new RAS platform that we call the Nexus platform. What's special about this platform is the modularity. It has a modular power supply in the front. It has a modular server in the back that we call the backpack.

This is a platform that enables that 2× performance that we just all saw the numbers for. But it's also the foundation for multiple generations of products. We've designed it from the ground up to support multiple generations. In particular, we designed it together with our next-generation wafer chip that will be coming next year. With that chip, we'll be pushing the performance even further.

We just saw a 2× improvement this year with CS4. We're going to push it even further with another 2× improvement in performance. And what this ultimately means is:

  • Medium-sized models like GPT-OSS or Gemma at speeds up to 10,000 TPS
  • Frontier-level models like Kimi or DeepSeek and GPT-5/6 Soul up to 5,000 TPS

Completely game-changing. All enabled by this brand new platform that we've designed for multiple generations. This is the trajectory that we're on right now. And now that the world sees the value of ultra-fast inference, our bet is that even this is just the beginning.

Rollout, Capacity, and the OpenAI Partnership

Host: What's the rollout process like? You have a deal with OpenAI over the next few years. When do we get access? Everyone wants ultra fast right now. Sure — there's Gemma OSS. When do we get the big Kimis, the DeepSeeks? When can we start to actually use —

Sean: That's a great question. So right now we are basically sold out of everything that we're building. And we are very strategically making sure that we're deploying every single megawatt in the most strategic way possible. In particular, quite a bit of it is going to OpenAI.

We've been very public about this — they're our biggest partner, not just because of the commercial arrangement, but also because of the fact that we have this co-design spirit, which you guys have heard OpenAI talk about a lot as well. We believe this will basically allow us to continue this flywheel of not just making models faster, but using that speed to make them more intelligent, and so on.

Today a lot of that capacity is going into OpenAI, and within OpenAI they have very strategically decided to use quite a bit of it for themselves.

Host: So they're using it right now?

Sean: That's correct. Right now internally they're using it for a lot of really critical use cases where the speed really really matters. Like:

  • Incident response teams — when there's an outage in their service, every single second, every single minute matters. They're getting a tremendous value out of that.
  • Some of the most critical research applications where the extra reasoning is enabling significantly more intelligent responses.

Right now, quite a bit of the capacity is going there. And then as we mentioned in our launch with OpenAI, we are now also making it open to enterprise customers who are able to use it for some of the most demanding and highest value applications.

Over time, OpenAI and Cerebras — we have committed to bringing enough capacity to make ultra-fast inference available to a much much wider audience. Our CS4 announcement, our CS5 announcement — these are very much part of that commitment to continue to drive more faster tokens, more throughput to satisfy all the various use cases out there.

Host: By the way, the way that you framed it, I realized that they didn't have to expose it to enterprise customers. They could have just kept it for themselves. Nobody knew that. That's an interesting business decision almost.

Sean: Obviously I can't explicitly comment about their thinking — ultimately it's OpenAI's decision how they want to use this. But if you look at it from the outside, it kind of makes sense. Their mission very much is to continue to push what's possible, and by using it internally that helps them do that. But they're also a business now — there's talks about them going IPO and all this. So very much even externally, you can see they're balancing both of these. I think we very much see that playing out.

Jalapeño: The Hot Chips Talk Everyone's Reading Between the Lines

Host: They're balancing a lot. Most recently their hot — we got to talk about this as well. So what are we thinking? Pre-fill Jalapeño, decode Cerebras. What are your takes?

Sean: I think that's a very rational conclusion. Of all of the Hot Chips announcements, probably Jalapeño was the most exciting — to me, but maybe not for the same reason as everyone else.

Host: To double click on that — you're the expert in chips. People see tokens per second. What do you see as interesting?

Sean: They pushed a lot on the performance and the fact that they're significantly better than the GPU, than Nvidia. But what I see is that they've built a significantly better GPU — and that in its own right is a big achievement. Nvidia knows what they're doing. They own the market for a reason. They're not dopes. To be able to come out of the gate and build a significantly better GPU is a big achievement.

But to me, the reason why Jalapeño is so exciting isn't even these Pareto curves. It's really the design methodology behind it. They very clearly took a drastically different approach to building this chip. Having an AI-first methodology enabled them to build the chip faster and achieve some of these very impressive results. That is 100% the future of our industry. It's not surprising to see that OpenAI is leading the way here because this is very much their MO.

Coming back to how we're going to use this — Jalapeño is pushing the boundaries for both throughput as well as latency. Even if I take the Cerebras hat off, I think that's awesome for the industry. This is going to lift all the tides. Everyone is going to benefit. They've also now been able to push the latency into regimes that traditional GPUs can't hit. That's also great because we believe in speed.

What's going to be really interesting — and what I'm super excited about — is: when Jalapeño is available next year, when our next-generation CS5 is available, together we will enable a full fast-inference portfolio that is substantially different and better than what's already available today. And on top of that there's opportunity to integrate even further — like pre-fill and decode disaggregation, for example.

Host: They didn't actually specialize Jalapeño for that, right?

Sean: They did not specialize Jalapeño for that, but they specialized it for throughput. So they get a tremendous amount of throughput. Just as a computer architect, there's so many different things you can start to do with that. Then we have the insane latency — up to 10,000 TPS in CS5. You can start to imagine some really really cool products that we can build together. That's what really excites me about having them as a partner.

We're also excited about collaborations on the AI tooling front. Much of the benefits that they're seeing from the AI tooling infrastructure — everybody probably says this now, but we're obviously doing a lot with AI — but we're also collaborating very closely with OpenAI to use their tools to help us also continue to push what's possible in our chip design, our software, and all that. Both of those together feels like a really unbeatable combination.

Groq, SRAM, and What's Missing From a Product Launch

Host: One thing that people are talking about — I'm trying to get to the disagreements, the hot takes. You haven't really mentioned power, and I do think that something that seems to be a consistent theme is performance per watt rather than tokens per second. Any variation of this theme, or what are people sort of talking about offstage that is more contentious?

Sean: There's a few things. One of the themes that came out quite a bit in my discussions at the conference was around the Groq announcement. Not surprising they have a new chip. In general, I think it's awesome that SRAM designs are becoming more mainstream now.

Host: You've been here the whole time. We've been talking about it for a long time.

Sean: And it's amazing to see the industry starting to embrace it.

Host: Do they feel different post-acquisition? You've been competing with them for a while.

Sean: To first order, no. It's really awesome to see that SRAM architectures are becoming more accessible. Even the biggest of the big guys — Nvidia is embracing SRAM design, acknowledging that traditional GPU designs really can't hit the ultra-fast regimes.

A lot of what was being discussed offstage was: the natural obvious questions like why did they launch on a 30 billion parameter model? And how come when Jensen spent so much time at GTC talking about attention/FFN disaggregation, there was no mention of that? I think that's pretty telling.

Host: I mean, there's a separate Rubin strategy.

Sean: Well, there's Rubin, but the LPX itself — that was supposed to be where it was. It was supposed to be Rubin LPX together. If you guys recall, Jensen spent like half an hour at GTC explaining attention runs here and the MoEs run here and so on.

I don't know if this is like a hot take per se, but it's very suspicious that their product that's in full production — they've only shown performance numbers on a non-disaggregated 31 billion parameter model. To me what this shows is that there's definitely some challenges in running on a non-wafer-scale SRAM design because there's just not enough memory in each of the chips. That's what's happening, and we're seeing the evidence of that. In many ways I think it's very much validating the design choice that we had.

If you think about it, to run a frontier-level model of like, let's say, a few trillion parameters, you need thousands and thousands of Groq LPUs just to hold the weights. So when you start to think about it that way, it's like — well, is it surprising that the only performance numbers they're showing are on 30B?

Host: So they're going to gradient this into this.

Sean: I think it's the other way. I think what's going to end up happening is they're going to end up focusing on significantly smaller models. If you have that limitation in your architecture, then that's what ends up happening.

Whereas in our case, we're running the world's largest models. And in some ways it's kind of simple, because one of our chips has order 100× more memory than one of their chips. So you have two orders of magnitude difference in scale kind of for free.

That's definitely one of the things that was a topic of discussion — again, independent of Cerebras — just kind of odd that you'd launch a brand new product on performance numbers of such a small model. But when you peel it back a little bit, it kind of makes sense. I've been living in this space now for a long time. There's a reason why we needed the wafer-scale integration to be able to aggregate enough SRAM to actually make it useful for large models.

Host: And look, the market's large. You have a different market than them. And you clearly are the longest-running incumbent now in this space.

Sean: Absolutely. The market's large. There's a lot of different opportunities for different hardware to play different roles. In fact, in general at Cerebras, we believe very very strongly in a heterogeneous disaggregated ecosystem — not just pre-fill / decode disaggregation, but I think we're just at the beginning of what's possible in this space.

With the scale of these deployments and of these models, inference is no longer just one workload. There's many many kinds of sub-workloads within it. You really want to use the right tool for the problem. You really want to use the right hardware for the problem. There's a spot for all the different types of architectures out there. And we've chosen to target the frontier.

Host: Frontier ultra-fast.

Sean: Exactly.

Two Views of Workload Classes: Product vs. Computer Architect

Host: I was going to go into some of the other companies that were top of town this year, but it gives me this opportunity — I want to follow up on one thing: how do you think about the classes of workloads? To me, the ultra-fast frontier workload is very clearly one of the fastest-growing segments of the entire inference market. The fact that I want it and I cannot pay enough for it — it might have been a mistake for OpenAI to offer it, even. But it's good, anyway. So just in your experience — you said you're strong believers in a heterogeneous inference solution — what are the buckets, and how do you see it from talking to your customers?

Sean: There's probably two different views here. One is the product view, and the other is the technical computer architect view.

From the product view, it's actually just very simple. Bringing more speed opens up significant opportunities — applications, different use cases, different capabilities, more intelligent models, more intelligent agents. The further you can push that, the more that you can enable. In fact, there's probably all sorts of things that we can't even imagine that you can build when you're even faster than what we are calling ultra-fast today. Which is why we keep pushing that.

Then the other angle really just comes down to capacity. Yes, I want the fastest, but then you need enough to actually be able to serve your use case. So it really just is that simple. Then finding the right architecture and the right mix of architectures to be able to provide that is really the name of the game.

From the computer architect's point of view, in a lot of ways it's even a little bit simpler. I was having a conversation with somebody actually at Hot Chips about this, and they were asking me: well, if you're doing disaggregation, doesn't that mean you have to partition the data center and you have to deploy a certain amount of this kind of hardware and a certain amount of another type of hardware — isn't that restrictive?

And I'm like — when we design a chip, every single day we're deciding: am I going to use the silicon real estate for memory, or if I'm going to use it for compute, or if I'm going to use it for I/O?

From a computer architect standpoint, what I see is: there's significantly different parts of the workload. The simplest ones are: okay, there's prefill, decode. But then you go one level deeper. What's actually happening during these phases? Oh, well, there's loading the actual KV cache. There's doing the actual attention. There's spreading the experts across the various different hardwares and balancing them.

All of these things can now be addressed with more tailor-made hardware solutions and architectures. At small scale, it doesn't really make sense to bring together a bunch of different hardwares just to solve one problem. But at the scale we're all talking about — hundreds of megawatts to gigawatts, the multi-gigawatt scale — it easily pays off.

At that point, it's as if you're thinking about the entire data center as if it's one computer. It's like one chip that you're trying to figure out: okay, well, I want this amount of this capability so I can run attention fast. I want this amount of capability so I can run prefill really really efficiently. Being able to piece all these things together is like the computer architect's dream — to have all of these tools in our toolbox. That's how I think you get the value from this heterogeneous disaggregated ecosystem.

Model / Chip Co-Design: The Biggest Untapped Opportunity

Host: How much of that plays into model design, model architecture? Working with OpenAI, you get to hopefully see what's going on on models. There was the whole reasoning models thing. It's not enough. There's also voice, diffusion. What if there's more interactive models — like the Thinking Machine stuff?

Sean: Absolutely. As we start to get into more interactive use cases that we enable through ultra-fast, we're even seeing a lot of this. If you're trying to interactively, for example, do graphic design — now you mentioned diffusion — image generation or video generation might be inline in your creative flow, interactive use case. There's so many of these different use cases that are coming.

You mentioned about co-design with OpenAI. What I think is the most untapped opportunity right now — frankly for Cerebras, but frankly for the entire non-Nvidia community — is that we're all running models that were designed for Nvidia GPUs. And it's not just Nvidia GPUs — usually they're designed for one particular Nvidia GPU. Like, okay, this thing was designed to run on B200, GB200, NVL72.

As Cerebras, for example, here we were showing that you're running the model like 14× faster already, but it was a model that was designed for a completely different architecture. If you start to open up the possibility of adjusting that model architecture even slightly, you can get massive gains. And if you start to do even more co-design, I think the opportunities are almost limitless. That's really what excites me a lot about working closely with customers and partners like OpenAI.

Host: Yeah. We don't have time for this because we want to move on, but people out there are really sleeping on AI code-gen for kernels — which is very good for you guys.

Sean: Absolutely. I'm a huge believer in that for sure.

Nvidia and AMD: The Better-Rubin Treadmill

Host: Before getting into Etched and super spicy chips — any takes on AMD, Nvidia, what they're doing? Could they be doing anything different? Any hot takes there?

Sean: I think Nvidia is doing exactly what we all expected Nvidia to be doing. Like I said, they're no dopes. They know exactly what they're doing, and they're continuing to push through. In many ways it's absolutely the right thing, because we need more tokens. We need them cheaper. That's a reality.

However, what used to be considered fast at like 100 or 200 tokens per second is quickly becoming the new batch mode. Quickly becoming the new "overnight is true." So I think there's a place for that. It's great for prompt processing. It's great for very very parallel workloads.

Host: But my evals take 20 hours. I can hit a button and run it in 2 hours.

Sean: Exactly. But quickly, being able to do prompt processing isn't quite enough. That's a big part of the market, but that's not quite enough. So all the traditional architectures I feel like are very much all on that treadmill — in a good way, not necessarily a bad way.

AMD, Trainium, in many ways TPU — all of these in my mind are all trying to build a better Rubin. There's a huge amount of value in that. But I think there's also a lot of value in trying to push the boundaries in other vectors as well, which is obviously what we're trying to do here at Cerebras.

Etched: Impressive Graphics, Unclear Differentiation

Host: Okay. Spicy spicy chips. There's this page that you have on your website — that this company Etched just doesn't have. No numbers, no benchmarks. Any takes? That's their one criticism. But that's Etched.

Sean: They have said very little about what they're doing. But what they have said has changed also a lot compared to what they originally said.

Host: Which they acknowledge.

Sean: Which they acknowledge. And the environment is changing a lot, so that makes sense. They're going to pivot, they're going to try to find their space. My reaction when I see pictures like this is that it's very impressive graphics design, but I also don't see them building anything beyond — or trying to build something better than — a traditional GPU.

They've made claims about having a distributed storage that is somehow faster because it's distributed — which I don't quite understand. It'd be very helpful if they can explain those kinds of things. It's hard to see where the differentiation is that they're trying to push. I think they had a rack or something at Hot Chips, so clearly they're building something, but it feels like it's a little bit far off for now.

Host: But at the same time, $20 billion now, it's not a pushover. I think maybe the steel-man for this is: what interesting direction would you want to see them pursue in the best case?

Sean: In the best case, I would love to see them — or others frankly — push the boundaries of more innovative solutions outside of just the chip. I really believe that the next frontier of taking AI compute to the next level is all about better ways to integrate outside the chip — the rack, the node, the package, the interconnect, the factory.

They may be doing something like that — it's hard to tell. But I think this is not just a point about Etched. For the entire industry — even if I take my Cerebras hat off for a second — what excites me the most is our ideas and creative thinking outside of the single chip.

We all know that the applications, the problems, the models are now so large that you can't just do anything on a single chip. So everything comes down to the integration. Everything comes down to: how do you bring together more compute? How do you bring together more memory? How do you bring together more interconnect? Scheduling, pipelining, all those algorithms.

Of the reveals yesterday, probably one of the more interesting ones to me — I mean, it wasn't new news — but was d-Matrix. The fact that they're really leaning into 3D DRAM packaging. This is the kind of stuff that I think we as an industry need to be doing much much more of.

Backpacks, 3D DRAM, and the Real Wafer-Scale Challenges

Host: I was going to say your backpack stuff reminds me of what the memory people are doing. Is that analogy —

Sean: There's a little bit of that. Because what we're doing with our backpack and power delivery is very much a very compact 3D package where we can bring power directly to the face of our chip, of our wafer. In many ways, the DRAM 3D stacking integration is doing something similar — but not with power, but with memory.

Yesterday we also announced that we started two years ago our DRAM stacking program for the very same reason. I think that figuring out ways to do this kind of integration is the key to unlock the next major step forward. I don't know exactly what Groq — sorry, what Etched — is doing underneath the covers. But when you ask what is the stuff that excites me the most about what we're seeing in the industry, it's really more creative integration, more creative packaging, more creative outside-of-the-chip thinking.

Host: Let's leave some hints for people — other than d-Matrix. A couple other names that stood out to you along these lines.

Sean: I think Samsung has some discussions around their ZHBM. All memory guys. Look, in the end there are only three main things to building an AI chip:

  1. Compute
  2. Interconnect
  3. Memory

And more importantly, as we all know, for at least in the low-latency space, memory is the key. The memory bandwidth is the key.

Host: And power and cooling — not as major still? No, absolutely. I mean, you just did a big redesign.

Sean: Those are what's powering all of this.

Host: Yeah — I'm just saying, physical limits.

Sean: That's actually a really really good point. When we originally started with wafer scale, most people thought the biggest challenges were: okay, how do you connect all of these dies together? How are you going to yield this thing? Those were absolutely fundamental challenges that we had to solve.

But what turned out to be the biggest enablers was ultimately: how do you power it? How do you cool it? How do you build it reliably at scale?

I think a lot of the 3D DRAM technologies are going to go through the same thing. It's one thing to draw a PowerPoint slide with a DRAM and logic. It's another to actually make it work, to figure out how you're actually going to power it, how you actually cool it.

That's why a lot of what we've been doing is trying to leverage and use all of the expertise that we've built up there and put it into our DRAM stacking approach. We already have solved yield at scale. We've already solved how you can actually package in a three-dimensional way. Those are problems that Samsung, that d-Matrix, and everybody else are also going to have to solve over this time.

Semiconductor Supply Chain and Chinese Open Source

Host: Thank you for those comments. Last topic because we got to go. US supply chain, semiconductor supply chain stuff. China is slowly becoming completely independent of us. Vision GLM — they're bragging. Huawei and what have you. Hyped outside of knowing what it was on. Just the model is doing good — you know, OpenRouter came out, not even running on US chips. So — are people talking about it? What are we doing?

Sean: Absolutely, of course people are talking about it. We're in a very difficult situation right now. The open-source model market is 100% Chinese.

Host: Not 100%, but —

Sean: Almost. Okay, 95%. Most of the big open models that are high quality are coming from the Chinese labs. In some ways it's great that sharing is happening and the global community is benefiting. But obviously that's a very strategically challenging place to be — to have such dependence on them on the model.

Separately — as is evidenced by this — we have independently all of the infrastructure, the hardware infrastructure, slowly being built up in the background to support all these Chinese models. I think it's absolutely a problem — globally as well as the US, as a national interest — that we have to continue to push the boundaries so that we continue to compete and continue to be ahead.

It's not easy. These guys know what they're doing. But it's something that I believe is not solved by one company or one fab. It needs government-level, national-interest-level kind of initiative to be able to make this happen.

Host: I imagine that should take place at Hot Chips. It's like the secret room of all you guys — you're leaders of our industry. You would be the guys to —

Sean: We have absolutely been pushing for this. We've been very supportive of any initiatives that will continue the US dominance in this space, 100%.

Closing: Congrats on the IPO — and Give Us Ultra-Fast

Host: Okay. You got to go, but you've been very generous with your time. Congrats on all your success. I mean, enormous — you IPO'd.

Sean: Yeah. Yeah. Sometimes I still have to pinch myself to remind me that we IPO'd, and it was the largest semiconductor IPO in history.

Host: Still early.

Sean: That was not bad. That was not bad.

Host: Congrats, and look forward to meeting up with you in the future year. We got to ask — you know, give us ultra fast. Give us bigger, give us more. No, no — I mean, give the people ultra fast too.

Sean: But we can probably get you in line at OpenAI.

Host: Ooo, I hope you didn't bias OpenAI too much to just keep it internally. No — people need it. We need better models.

Sean: It's OpenAI's decisions. We're just providing the infrastructure.

Host: Hey, but give us GLM. Give us DeepSeek. Just give us our own rack and then we'll run it. Okay, thank you again for coming. Really really appreciate it.

Sean: Yeah.

## 一、"快"的通货膨胀：Overton 窗口的静默漂移
Sean Lie 说了一句被多数人忽略的话：**"曾经被认为快的 100-200 tokens/秒，正在迅速成为新的 batch mode。"**
这句话的杀伤力不在数字，而在**心理锚点的位移**。它揭示了一个反直觉的规律：**速度从不是绝对量，而是一个"应用可能性"的守门人**。当 tokens/秒跨越某个阈值，原本"批处理/离线"的东西突然变成"实时/交互"，你之前想都不敢想的产品形态一夜之间出现在白板上。
这与 90 年代"宽带"的定义演化如出一辙——从 56K 到千兆，每次"高速"都被下一次"高速"变成"低速"。但更深的类比在**神经科学**：人类对"即时反馈"的阈值大约是 100 毫秒，一旦跨过这条线，大脑就把工具视为"自我的延伸"而非"外部工具"。10,000 tps 意味着 LLM 首次真正跨过这条线——**LLM 不再是你查询的对象，而是你思考本身的一部分**。
## 二、被"没说的话"出卖的架构缺陷——一场技术侦探剧
访谈中最漂亮的推理，是 Sean 对 Groq/Jalapeno 的解读——**

item.title: [Lex Clips] Vibe Coding vs Agentic Engineering vs Programming | DHH and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的观察：AI 智能体继承了人类被微观管理时的"消极怠工"心理

DHH 提到 Opus 5 的系统提示缩减了 80%——这不是因为模型更聪明了，而是因为过度指令实际上在损害它。他用了一个惊人的类比：pointy-haired boss（尖发老板）走进办公室告诉程序员怎么写代码，程序员会 sulk（生闷气），会故意写出更烂的代码。

这里藏着一个几乎无人指出的诡异事实：大语言模型是在人类文本上训练的，因此它们不仅继承了人类的知识，也继承了人类被微观管理时的心理反应模式。当你在 prompt 里塞满琐碎规定时，模型不是"技术上"变差了，而是在模仿人类在同类情境下的表现——那种敷衍、消极、只做最低要求的响应模式。你以为你在 prompt engineering，其实你在无意中触发了训练数据里数百万篇员工牢骚帖的隐性人格。这是提示词工程从未被公开讨论过的一层：AI 有情绪的镜像，不是因为它有情绪，而是因为你用文本喂了它情绪。

二、专业性的历史性反转——DHH 承认"懂编程"曾经是他的负债

"I actually think, for a while, it was to my deficit to know as much as I know about programming"——这句话若认真对待，是整个软件史上罕见的时刻。

跨领域对照一下：摄影发明后，画家没有变得对绘画更笨；打字机出现后，作家没有因为会写字而变差。技术革命通常让既有专家保留优势并叠加新工具。但 DHH 描述的是一种反向现象：在他自己创造的领域（Rails、Web 开发），他多年积累的"如何做"的直觉，成了阻挡他获得更好结果的滤镜。

这与围棋 AlphaGo 之后职业棋手的处境有一个隐秘的共振——顶尖棋手发现自己被"棋理"束缚，反而是年轻棋手更容易接受 AI 的"不讲道理"的着法。软件领域现在也进入了同一个诡异区间："know-how"（知道怎么做）正在被"know-what"（知道要什么）超越。这也解释了为什么 DHH 写 Am I Right 时刻意选择 C++ 并强制自己不看一行代码——他在做一种自我实验：能否杀死自己的技术自我，让产品直觉独立呼吸。

三、跨领域连接：敏捷宣言的诡异复仇 + 爵士乐 + 认知心理学

DHH 在对话末尾指出：agentic 开发是敏捷运动（Agile）的终极实现——因为它彻底摧毁了"先规范、后实施"的软件思维。这个观察本身很好，但可以再往前推一步：

敏捷方法在人类团队中从未真正成功过。绝大多数所谓"敏捷"的团队最终变成两周一次的假迭代 + 大量前期文档。为什么？因为人类程序员太贵、太慢，你不敢让他们"随便写写看"。经济学决定了敏捷是理想，瀑布是现实。

而 agentic 开发第一次让敏捷的经济学成立了——因为"写一点、试一试、扔掉重写"的边际成本趋近于零。敏捷不是被 AI 实现，而是被 AI 平反。它一直是对的，只是等错了硬件。

再看那个"三选项 vs 22 选项"的悖论（Barry Schwartz 的经典发现），DHH 直觉地用它设计了自己的开发工作流——生成三个方案、投票、迭代。这其实是把认知心理学的实验发现直接嵌入了开发方法论。这与爵士乐即兴演奏的三和弦替代原则、与建筑师 Christopher Alexander 的"模式语言"、与摄影师 Cartier-Bresson 的"决定性瞬间"共享同一个底层结构：人类的高价值判断发生在极短时间窗、极少选项、极低理性介入的条件下。

未来的软件设计师，会更像一个爵士乐手或摄影师——不是构造者，而是从大量瞬时可能性中做直觉选择的品味机器。而"品味"，恰恰是我们最不知道如何教、也最不知道如何自动化的东西。这可能才是 agentic 时代真正稀缺的技能。

📝 转录文本

Omarchy's Plugin Explosion

One of the really neat features about Omarchy is that it has a far more robust plug-in system that allows you to extend your operating system and rewrite it — really in terms of its user interface, its panels, and its features — by creating your own plugins that can be cloned off of tools we ship in the box.

For example, say you want a different calendar. Omarchy ships with a calendar. You click the little clock, it pops up a calendar, and it doesn't have iCal support, for example. It doesn't consume your appointments. There's about 17 implementations of that already.

And in 3 days, we had 330 plugins on the Omarchy plugin marketplace. I have never seen growth like that with any project I've ever been involved in. I've never seen participation that broadly. I've never seen that many people be able to create software that's meaningful for them, also be usable for others, so quickly.

All of it is driven by the fact that Omarchy ships a set of skills that tells any agents you bring to it how to create extensions to the operating system — and therefore affording you the vision of the true malleable... I was about to say "agentic." I hate that [ __ ] word.

The Vocabulary Problem: "Agentic" and "Vibe Coding"

And the reason, in fact, I hate that word is: first of all, it's become marketing slob speak at this point. Like, it's just slapped onto everything. I wish we had a different word that just meant "AI doing stuff."

Lex: Vibe coding feels wrong, too.

It does, because vibe coding to me smells exactly like script kiddies did in the early 2000s. People applying PHP scripts they just downloaded offline — they don't understand anything of.

And while — I mean, that's true in the sense that much of the vibe coding, including my own vibe-coded projects, and as I just mentioned I have several — I've written things in C++, I've written things in Rust.

DHH on Rust: The Ugliest Language, and Yet...

Rust. I hate Rust with a passion. Rust to me is like pouring acid in my eyes when I have to look at the code.

Lex: Wait, wait, wait — why do you hate Rust?

It is, in my opinion, the ugliest programming language that's been invented in probably the last 40 years.

Lex: So it's the opposite of Rails and —

It's the opposite. But —

Lex: You've written it.

I've written applications in Rust because the output of Rust is actually amazing. The memory safety, the fact that it's a system language, the fact that it's highly efficient, and so forth — is incredible.

So Rust to me can both be the most repugnant programming language ever devised for human consumption and a wonderful platform for agentic engineering. These two truths can coexist easily in my head.

Is Agentic Engineering Just... Programming?

Lex: Is there a point at which we can just call agentic engineering "programming"? Can we just change what programming means? Because who's actually going to be programming the old-school way in a few months?

I don't think we should reuse the term. Because for me, programming implies an understanding of certain primitives — loops, conditions, variables — all the constructs of programming languages are what constitutes programming itself, not the creation of programs.

Because you could say in the pre-agentic era, "Well, your CEO is programming. He's hiring a bunch of programmers, he's telling them what to do, and out comes software that he can sell." I don't think most people would call that CEO a programmer. And I don't think we should call the vibe coder a programmer either.

And vibe coding, if we define it here, is: you tell an agent to build software for you, you do not look at the implementation. That to me is what separates vibe coding from programming — or, let's say, agent-accelerated development.

Do Programmers Have an Advantage?

Lex: But don't you think, sir — to push back a little bit — don't you think a programmer, old-school programmer, you, doing agentic engineering is a different kind of agentic engineering than a non-programmer doing agentic engineering? What I mean is: if you know what a for loop is, if you know what functional programming is, if you know some of the basic good principles of software engineering, the way you do natural-language-based agentic engineering will be different and more systematic. And the scale and the variety of things you can actually build is much bigger than a vibe coder. I'm just going to extend the pro case here a little bit, just for the sake of the argument.

I actually think, for a while, it was to my deficit to know as much as I know about programming. Because I was instructing the agents to do things as I prescribed them to do. And they were very good at that.

And in the first agentic moment — let's not call it an era; it was something that lasted 3 months, a moment — in the first agentic moment, that felt very productive. I could get more productivity out of telling the agents what to do in the way I would have done it. And I used all of my experience as a programmer to do just that.

Then I was a little late on the next moment. And the next moment allowed me, allowed anyone, to describe outcomes, to describe problems to the agents, and get better solutions than if you had a programmer prescribe the path.

When Programmers Are Worse Than Non-Programmers

Lex: See, okay, so we're having fun arguing here. Um, so are you suggesting that there's problems for which programmers are worse than non-programmers at agentic programming?

100%. And the reason I say that — let's define it here — the reason I say that is: there's a lot of programmers who are not very good product managers.

Software is product management. What should it do? Who should it do it for? How should it do it? How should it look? What's our priorities? What do we start with first? What does version one include?

All of those skills are not easily or equally distributed across all programmers. And in the agentic era, where you are letting an agent, an AI, do the implementation, these are the skills you need.

And I happen to sit in both camps, and this is why I love this moment. I still get to live a little bit in the old world where I look at the full implementation, because there are domains and areas where I feel that still brings value. And then I also live in the future.

And as I said, when I created "Am I Right," I've not looked at a single line of that C++. I actually made it a point to myself that I was going to treat it as an experiment. This is 100% a black box. I will treat it as though I was any other user who had opinions about how their digital typewriter should work — and therefore felt like it was a fair experiment, as if a writer of any other sort who had opinions about how software should be done and how it should work. As you mentioned, video editors who know exactly where they don't like what Adobe Premiere is doing and how it could be better but don't have the capacities to improve it — how that could be.

The Rigor Question

Lex: The pushback, though — I think what programmers do well, good programmers do well, is systematic design. Like thinking in terms of systems and rigor. And I think still, and probably for a long time to come, even natural-language-based control of agentic systems will require a certain kind of rigor. Not overly structured rigor, but really explain very specifically the goals of the system, how to do the verification, what kind of security testing you want to do — all those kinds of things. Allow them to push back on that; the system should be smart.

I would have said the same thing 6 months ago. And I think the same thing would have been true 6 months ago.

What I have found since — especially even just the last few weeks of the agentically accelerated development of Omarchy — is that more often than not I have the humility to recognize that the agent knows best.

Lex: You can legitimately say "make sure it's secure."

Correct. And it would know more about what that entails. Now, you're laughing —

Lex: [At the] world we're living in.

The Pointy-Haired Boss Effect

A good parallel to this is: there was a hot moment where it was all the rage about micro-optimizing — that "Oh, you tell your agent this, you tell your agent that," and you ended up with this huge file of instructions for your agent.

One of the things that Boris — working on Claude Code — shared in an interview recently about Opus 5, was that the system prompt that they ship for Opus 5 (and presumably also Fable) shrunk by 80%. Because the agent not only needed far less human instruction, it was actually being damaged by overly prescriptive humans.

And any programmer who's had a pointy-haired boss knows exactly what that is like. When the boss walks into the room, doesn't know anything, starts telling you how to program, how to code — what do you do? You sulk. You write shittier code if you're mandated to do things that are against your better judgment.

Why would an agent not be the same?

Lex: Actually, to push back against myself: I do find the actual skill I'm currently developing, which — along those lines is probably what everybody's trying to develop — is not to over-specify things. Just to get out of the system's way. Just specify enough to provide a kind of high-level vision and guidance.

Agile's Ultimate Vindication

It's even better. Because you don't even need that.

The fundamental insight of modern software development came from the Agile software development movement. In the late '90s, early 2000s, a group of smart, honest, and brave people came together and said:

"The way we've been trying to do software development for the last 40 to 50 years has not worked, will not work. We've been trying to specify upfront what software should look like. We thought that we could ask humans what they wanted, write it all down, apply our systems thinking and our rigor to a spec sheet, hand that spec sheet over to a group of programmers who would then implement just that, and everyone would be happy."

Well, guess what? No one was happy. Because no one knows what they want until they receive it. You don't know what a program should do until you play with it.

So, in the agentic age, you should resist the temptation to be overly specific upfront. Be as vague as you can to manifest something, then interact with the something.

The way you arrive at good software is: you write a little bit of software, and then you try to use it. It is in the process of using software that you discover what you really want. It's where you discover what's important and what's not important.

And agents are incredible at allowing you to bumble into this experience of realizing what you want — because you don't know what you want.

Differential Evaluation and the Paradox of Choice

Lex: And I've actually done something similar to what you suggested, which is: implement different designs and totally different implementations, and then I create HTML pages for myself — PHP pages — where I vote on what I like more, and so on. And it does this iterative thing and it's very nice and fun. The interaction with the agentic system, if you create a nice interface for yourself, it can be super fun. And you're focusing on the design part and the most fun parts of the design part.

Correct. And this is what humans are really good at.

Lex: Yeah, taste.

Differential evaluation. You give me three options, I pick one of them.

Now — humans actually fall off a cliff if you give them 22 options. That's the paradox of choice. But you give them three options, they very quickly, within a split second, will tell you what they like.

There are all these ways that exploit the fact that humans will make these snap judgments that are actually pre-intellectual, right? Like, they're coming from the gut, and then they arrive up in the brain, and the brain tries to rationalize why the gut said what it said.

And if you're willing to let go of some of that intellectual pre-processing rationalization, and simply let your gut drive — the agentic age is a revelation.

item.title: [Invest Like The Best] Jensen Huang’s Genius Nvidia Strategy
item.dc:creator: Invest Like The Best
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、"分封制"帝国：Jensen 在硅谷复刻了英国东印度公司的统治术

多数人把 Nvidia 的护城河解读为 CUDA 或制程领先，但转录里那句"如果有一个决定纵向整合，我还有三个饿着肚子的人等着补位"透露的是更古老、更政治化的算计——这不是芯片战略，是分封逻辑。

Jensen 刻意扶植 Neoclouds、推浮多个推理服务商，本质与当年英国借助东印度公司和印度土邦互相制衡是同构的：永远不让任何单个封臣壮大到可以挑战宗主。Apple 走的是相反的路——把价值往自己身上收缩；Jensen 走的是逆向 Apple——把价值往外撒，让下游成为一个互相咬合、但谁都离不开 GPU 供应的生态泥潭。你以为他在"共享繁荣"，其实他在制造依赖的冗余。冗余不是浪费，冗余是权力。

二、意外的观察：他不是芯片商，他是"需求做市商"

这段最反直觉的一点：Nvidia 的真正产品不是 H100，是"买家之间的竞争"本身。

传统硬件公司卖东西给客户，Jensen 却在制造客户——先造出 Neocloud 赛道，再让 CoreWeave、Lambda、Nebius 等互相举牌抢配额。这个结构跟大宗商品交易所比科技公司更像：芝加哥商品交易所不预测猪肉价格，它只需要保证交易发生。Jensen 做的是同一件事——他不预测 AI 需求，他制造揭示需求的机制。每一次 Neocloud 融资、每一次推理创业公司拿单，都是市场在替他做价格发现。

这解释了一个否则很怪的现象：为什么他愿意让别人先赚大钱？因为做市商的收益不来自任何一笔交易，而来自所有交易的抽成。Costco 靠会员费而不是商品毛利赚钱；赌场靠 rake 而不是赌桌胜率赚钱；Jensen 靠"每一次 AI 军备竞赛的通行税"赚钱。让朋友变亿万富翁不是慷慨，是在扩大他自己的赌场。

三、"撕创可贴"是一场精心编排的心理剧——把 75% 降到 73% 竟被包装成利空出尽

最容易被漏掉的一句是那个毛利率宣言。表面上是坦白，实际上是语言艺术的极致操作：

  • 72–73% 依然是荒诞级别的硬件毛利率。整个消费硬件行业能有 30% 就已经在开香槟；他"降下来"的水位，是别人一辈子够不着的天花板。
  • 用"rip the band-aid"（撕创可贴）这种带疼痛感的表达，主动制造了一个假的痛点，好在市场心里植入"最坏也不过如此"的锚。这是行为经济学里的预期管理反向操作：你不是消除焦虑，你是先给对方一份微量的焦虑，让他为你没有给他更大的焦虑而感恩。
  • 更妙的是"we have absorbed the cost increases, we have also repriced our products"——两句话之间藏着一个魔术：成本上升被吸收了，但产品也涨价了。翻译一下就是"我涨价了，但我说得像是我在承担责任"。

跨领域连接：这套话术与央行的前瞻性指引（forward guidance）几乎一模一样——鲍威尔从不"降息"，他"调整政策路径"；Jensen 从不"降毛利"，他"重置预期"。当一家公司开始用中央银行的语言说话时，它的商业模式已经不是竞争，是治理。

📝 转录文本

一、不与客户竞争：善意的战略价值

Jensen is really good at making his friends billionaires, and there's no need for him to kind of destroy that goodwill.

Nvidia is really smart about this: they don't compete with their customers. Nvidia takes the long view on everything.

二、扶植多元买家生态

He wants to create a diverse community of Neoclouds and inference providers who are all jockeying to create demand for Nvidia — such that if any one of them decides to vertically integrate or go with AMD or any other option, he's got three more people hungry to fill that position.

It's great to have competition amongst his buyers.

三、这一季度：主动重置毛利率预期

This quarter, we decided that we would rip the band-aid off, um, reset expectations about our gross margins, and just explain to people that, in fact, we have now absorbed the cost increases.

We have also repriced our products in the marketplace, and based on that, our margins are going to come down from 75%. Um, but it will be between 72 and 73% next year.

And so we've now reset the expectations and, you know, removed this anxiety that everybody had about gross margins.
