item.title: [a16z] Can AI Learn Mathematical Intuition?
item.dc:creator: a16z
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

三个让人意外的观察

一、AI 数学的"负空间悖论"：它的失败比它的成功更能推动数学进步

Daniel 讲了一个精妙的故事：他有一个引理，前沿模型都证明不出来。于是他自己动手研究了大量例子，最终发现——引理本身可以被改写成一个更好的陈述。一旦改写完成，模型立刻秒证。

这里藏着一个反直觉的洞察：AI 的无能反而成了数学发现的催化剂。如果模型一开始就能用 10 页丑陋的暴力计算搞定原始引理，Daniel 永远不会发现那个更本质、更漂亮的表述。换句话说，AI 现阶段"能做暴力活但做不了优雅活"的这个缺陷，恰好构成了一种倒逼人类去寻找概念性理解的压力机制。

这让我想到一个跨领域的类比：GPS 与出租车司机的记忆。伦敦出租车司机因为要背下整座城市的路网，海马体会显著增大；GPS 普及后这种认知能力普遍萎缩。数学的危险不是"AI 能证明我们能证明的东西"，而是AI 恰好能证明"人类必须痛苦才能证明"的那一层，从而剥夺了痛苦带来的洞察。

二、"斯洛特机（slot machine）经济学"正在悄悄重塑数学的科研生态

Daniel 描述的场景细思极恐：一个博士后可以让 Codex "去 arXiv 找五个最近的代数几何猜想并证明它们"，一小时内产出三篇正确但平庸的论文。他说自己已经跑过这个实验，成品正躺在硬盘里等着发邮件。

更惊人的一个观察：模型出现了"模式坍缩（mode collapse）"——不同人独立提交的三五篇论文，居然用完全相同的证明证明了完全相同的定理，几天内密集出现在 arXiv 上。

这不是学术不端的问题，而是一个更深的系统性风险：数学的进步历史上依赖于"千花齐放"——不同人从不同奇怪的直觉出发探索，才形成高维、多样的知识前沿。而当 LLM 成为默认的猜想生成器和证明机时，整个学科的搜索空间会向模型的"心智重心"塌缩。

跨领域连接：这几乎就是生态学中的"单一栽培（monoculture）风险"——爱尔兰马铃薯饥荒不是因为马铃薯不好，而是因为整个岛只种一个品种。数学界现在正在无意识地进入一场"认知单一栽培"。

三、"我们已经赢了"——即使 AI 超人化，Daniel 仍主张保留人类数学家的深层理由

这是访谈里最哲学、最出乎意料的一段。Daniel 假设：即便模型变得稳健超人，人类数学家依然应该存在。理由不是能力，而是"社会设计权（who gets to steer）"。

他的论证链条极其精妙： - 数学的目标不是产出论文，而是产出理解； - 如果理解只驻留在模型权重里，那是"很不令人满意的"； - 一个国家能有少数人做前沿研究，背后靠的是数百万人在学习"数学式思考"的金字塔支撑结构； - 一旦把探索方向的主导权让渡给模型，我们无法保证它优化的是"人类感兴趣的东西"，而只能保证它优化了我们要求它优化的东西——这两者永远有鸿沟。

跨领域的隐藏联系：这几乎是 Elinor Ostrom 关于"公地治理"的论证在认知领域的翻版——共同资源不会因为效率优化而自动被良好治理，必须要有一群"利益相关者"持续在场。数学在这里不是知识体系，而是一片认知的公地。

一个大胆的预测

如果模型继续在"应用已知技巧"这一维度上加速，而"理论构建 / 发现新问题"这一维度进展缓慢，那么未来 5 年数学界会分裂成两个截然不同的物种： - "套利型数学家"：擅长用模型批量产出正确但无洞察的论文，占据低端职位市场； - "品味型数学家"：不再拼输出量，而是竞争"选什么问题、赏什么证明、闻出什么方向有戏"的元能力——数学家的核心竞争力将从"证明力"转向"审美力和嗅觉"。

而这恰好回到 Daniel 一开始那句他自己都不好意思承认的话：他说自己不追求美，但整段访谈他都在用"美"和"概念性解释"筛选证明。美，可能会从一种奢侈品变成数学职业最后的、也是最稀缺的护城河。

📝 转录文本

Can AI Learn Mathematical Intuition?

开场：核心观点预告

The goal of mathematics is not to produce mathematics papers. It's to produce some kind of understanding. Maybe some of that understanding resides in model weights. To me, that's like pretty unsatisfying.

Comparing Anthropic with OpenAI, do you detect any differences in how that is similar to human reasoning?

They definitely are not good at it autonomously, but with some hints, you can kind of get them to do something interesting. A lot of progress in mathematics comes from like letting a thousand different flowers bloom and people pursue their own curiosity and then the boundaries of knowledge expand in some fairly uniform way.

What has been the most impressive result so far?

My favorite fully autonomous result by an AI so far is the solution to the Irish unit distance problem. There was some lemma I wanted to prove — none of the frontier models could do it. So I like worked out a ton of examples on my own and I realized, oh well, maybe like here's some reason why it could be true. Once I had that statement, the models were able to very quickly prove that sort of better statement.

How should like the mathematics community kind of best adapt and benefit from this?

一、嘉宾介绍

I am so excited to have you on, Daniel. And so Daniel is a professor of mathematics at the University of Toronto. Toronto is my hometown, so also very exciting. But the thing that is most special here is Daniel's an actual practicing mathematician, and in addition he's been incredibly vocal about his evolving views of AI in math. So I feel like every — if I just don't check in with you, you know, like in two weeks something different has been revealed, and then you're very kind of like — what do you call it?

I have a lot of opinions.

You have a lot of opinions. Exactly.

So I want to get into that. One of the things I'm most interested in is not just a discussion of how the capabilities advance — I feel like in math that's definitely the headline — but also, you've been very thoughtful about how practicing mathematicians should respond. That gives us a chance to talk about what is actually special about math. Not just, "hey, AI has been really making progress here," but delve into what mathematicians actually do.

So maybe with that arc in line, we can start with: what has been the most impressive result so far, given all the recent progress?

二、最令人印象深刻的 AI 数学成果

Yeah. So okay, there have you know now been a lot of results — some of them produced autonomously, some produced semi-autonomously, some where the AI contribution is just not at all clear. They're in a lot of different areas, so anything I say is kind of — I can only really comment on things that I have some expertise on. So it's quite possible that if you talk to a different mathematician you'll get different answers here.

爱尔兰单位距离问题

My favorite fully autonomous result by an AI so far is the solution to the Irish unit distance problem, which I think was announced in mid-May. At least what I liked about that is it seemed to me that it was in some ways a little bit creative.

Some of the results we've seen have had kind of the flavor of, you know, you kind of take some known techniques and apply them in maybe a clever way. Or — I don't know, they have kind of been results I would characterize as "last mile" — where some recent work was done, quite deep work done by a group of human mathematicians, and then the AI kind of took the final step.

为什么这个结果特别？

But yeah, with the sort of unit distance problem, I think it was something where the result was a little unexpected. First of all, my sense was that people working in the area thought it was true, and then there was a counter-example found. But then also it brought in some techniques from another area.

I think those techniques were not especially deep or new — they were sort of classical ideas from the 60s — but they were new to this area of studying point configurations in the plane. And so that was pretty cool.

事后验证：结果的"富含性"

And then afterwards we got to see it was kind of fruitful. So a bunch of mathematicians took those ideas and used them to find counter-examples to a bunch of other interesting open questions — for example the sum-product conjecture over the real numbers.

That's at least the way I like to think about how cool a result is: you look at it post hoc and you see, oh well, whatever new ideas that were introduced, if any, are kind of useful to do other things. Did they improve our understanding of something? I think that's maybe so far the main example I know of of a result of that form.

三、AI 证明的"人性"与其局限

主持人的追问：解耦"逻辑蛮力"与"创造性"

Yeah, I think it's really meaningful that you're commenting on this. That result came out in May and there's been so many headlines so far, and it's kind of probably hard for somebody who's not a practicing mathematician to appreciate the differences in these headlines.

So you kind of already started laying out sort of a taxonomy of what is different in that proof. It'd be interesting to use that as an excuse to talk about where you sense the model differences are and what mathematicians actually do.

The most naive understanding of what mathematicians do is that we're pushing around symbols in a logical manner. And this is why RL is so successful at this — because you can verify it somewhat cheaply compared to other domains, and also because the rules are quite neat. So if you're superhuman at that, you might be good at math.

But of course that betrays most of what is interesting about mathematics — which is about the understanding, getting at truth, remaining confused, and developing intuitions. Very little — I mean, the tool to do that stuff is having really good, very strong abilities to push out logical implications. But when you say it's most impressive and creative, decoupling the inhumane feats of just logical implication from where is it being creative — what is it helping engender in terms of mathematical activity?

Daniel 的回应：其实证明非常"人性"

Yeah. Okay. So first of all, you kind of characterized it as inhuman in some way. I actually think the argument was very human-like. You know, I'd love to judge — or sorry, OpenAI released some chain of thought — it was very recognizable. It was like, you know, if I tried to imagine my chain of thought in trying to solve a problem, it might look kind of like that.

We haven't seen the raw chain of thoughts — maybe they cleansed it a little bit. Yeah. Or maybe, you know, maybe the model liked to swear a lot in the middle of the chain of thought and they cleaned that up or something. We don't know. But at least the summary seemed pretty readable.

And I would say that's actually kind of typical of most of the results that I've studied. They don't seem inhuman at all. They seem absolutely like something a human mathematician could produce. And they're typically understandable, if not so well written, if you just look at raw model output. It's not like there's some move 37 or whatever. It's like a human mathematician doing math.

哪些方面像人，哪些不像

It's like a human mathematician doing certain types of math. The models are still not very good at some mathematical activities — and here I don't mean by field, but just certain things you do when you try to solve a problem. The models don't seem to be doing those, but certain things they're very good at.

The ways they might be a little bit inhuman: they don't get tired, they know a lot. But if you just have to read the final output, it doesn't seem inhuman.

四、自然语言推理为何有效？Claude vs ChatGPT

训练数据的悖论

It's interesting because obviously we can't get too much information from the labs who are producing these models about what the training recipes are or how they're advancing in reasoning. But at least one of the things we do know — and I think OpenAI spearheaded this — is this reasoning in natural language is actually what they happen to scale up. And it's not actually pushing a lot of Lean-verified proofs as the training corpus. And that's kind of amazing.

On another side, what's interesting is it's not clear that a lot of the mathematical training data, if they use it to a large extent at all, is reflective of how mathematicians think. Because a lot of it is not legible as traces — most of the papers are crisp and polished, the textbooks certainly show very little motivation of how something is developed. Which is why it's usually easier to follow a research direction by actually talking to the researchers.

So kind of curious — comparing Anthropic with OpenAI, do you detect any differences in how that is similar to human reasoning? And if you have any comments on why natural language scales so well?

Daniel：非形式化推理的意义

Okay. So first of all, I really like your point that they're mostly doing natural language reasoning rather than Lean. That suggests to me that these — you know, you hear a lot of people say math is a verifiable domain, that explains the progress, whatever — my sense is that because they're primarily scaling in informal reasoning, probably the techniques are going to generalize to other domains pretty well. That's just my guess.

Claude vs ChatGPT 比较

You asked a little bit about Claude versus ChatGPT. My sense is that they're pretty similar in terms of capabilities. I've played around a lot more with ChatGPT than with Claude Fable, but it seems like there's a lot of cases where OpenAI will drop a solution to some problem and Anthropic will say, "Oh, you know, too." Exactly.

So it actually seems like they're solving a very similar collection of problems, and it's a relatively small portion of what human mathematicians do.

解题的"味道"

One thing that is interesting: we see the solutions have a certain flavor. There'll be things that rely on the models' strengths — their ability to grind out a long computation, or pull together technical ideas from many areas, from many papers that a human mathematician might not have read.

But they seem weaker in things like intuition or having some big-picture point of view. A lot of what I do as a mathematician is: I have some kind of philosophy that's very non-rigorous — maybe I think this thing is analogous to that thing — and then a lot of what I'm working out is figuring out how to make that precise. Trying to measure the extent to which I've succeeded in understanding that by, can I solve a problem? Can I find an interesting phenomenon which I don't understand, and then now I understand it?

So far, even in the best results the models are producing, you don't see that much of this kind of reasoning. It's more like they're very very good at applying some known techniques. Which, to be clear, is a very powerful thing to do — to be very good at applying all known techniques. There are mathematicians who have had great careers doing very high-quality work of that flavor. And a lot of what the models are producing is high quality in that way, but it's some kind of fairly narrow band of what mathematicians care about, so far.

理论构建的初步迹象

I do think there's signs that all the frontier models are starting to be able to do more fuzzy things. I've tried to get both Fable and ChatGPT 5.6 to do some kind of theory building. They're not good — they definitely are not good at it autonomously, at least with whatever scaffolding I've set up. But with some hints, you can kind of get them to do something interesting.

When you give the models hints, it's always a little hard to tell what part is from the model and what part is from you. But my experience is that if they can do it with a hundred bits of hints or whatever, in six months maybe they can do it without hints. I do think there's signs they're also somehow picking up some of this implicit and unwritten mathematical knowledge.

五、日常使用中的偏好与差异

为什么更多用 ChatGPT？

Okay. I would love to go into the intuition part and where it sucks at, to put it in a very basic way. But you actually mentioned a small detail — from the public you've gleaned that Anthropic and OpenAI are probably neck and neck, but you personally are using a lot more ChatGPT. Why is that?

Well, why is — I don't know. I think it's just inertia. One thing is that ChatGPT got better at math earlier. So for a long time the Claude models were just not useful for research math, and then I think maybe around Opus 4.5 or Opus 4.6 they more or less caught up.

But some experimentation suggests to me they're pretty neck-and-neck, and so for my own work, except when I'm just experimenting, I mostly just stick with one at random.

主持人的观察

As people outside of labs, it's really interesting just to compare how they differ on the frontier. And to your point, it might be a little bit of momentum. I do think that at least from my anecdotal experience, 5.6 has been a lot more clear in exposition. It's in the explanations of results — I always find that 5.6 is giving a more accurate theory of mind of what it assumes I know and don't know. Whereas Fable might be explaining something very trivial, but then just jump like, "well, you know, obviously you should know these things."

I find they're both pretty bad at theory of mind.

Okay, great. So then from your eyes, you're probably asking much deeper questions.

六、数学家究竟在做什么？

类型学：解题者 vs 理论建构者

The thread that I really wanted to pull on was when you're talking about the models maybe starting to get better intuitions or even theory building. Before we even dive into that, it would be useful to talk through: what is your primary activity as a mathematician? Especially in your area of algebraic geometry — probably has a very different flavor than a combinatorialist. Can you give a brief lay of the land, and then explain what your mathematical activity was pre-AI and how it's changing with AI?

Yeah. There are a lot of different kinds of mathematicians, a lot of different spectra on which one can put a mathematician. Definitely a lot of mathematicians like solving open problems. I'm one of those — I like to solve an open problem. I think of myself as a problem solver, as opposed to — one taxonomy you could have is a problem solver versus a theory builder.

开放问题作为"理解失败的测度"

At least for me, the point of an open problem is that it's supposed to measure your failure to understand something. So it's kind of like a benchmark. One problem I really like is the Grothendieck-Katz p-curvature conjecture, whatever that is. It measures something about our failure to understand differential equations. So there's some very basic object we would like to understand — if we can't answer this conjecture, we know we don't understand it.

实践中如何攻克

Okay, so in practice, how do you get at a problem which is supposed to be measuring something you don't understand? Well, of course you try to understand the thing better. And in practice what that means is: you try to find the smallest situation where you can't understand something, and fiddle around with it, and then you stare at what you developed to win, and try to turn that into some theory.

So that's one thing you might do — you might try to solve a problem and in so doing develop some new understanding of the situation.

类比与哲学

You might also have some feeling that this thing is related to this other thing. You might start building a table like, "oh, this property A is related to property A-prime, property B is related to property B-prime," and so on.

For example, in my work, a lot of it is motivated by some analogy between homology of algebraic varieties and representations of fundamental groups. That's some fancy stuff — but this analogy is very very fruitful, and really any phenomenon that appears on one side, you can find an analog on the other side. So trying to realize that dream has led to a lot of beautiful mathematics of the last 30 or 40 years, by people like Carlos Simpson and Takuro Mochizuki and others.

Here it's really just like someone noticed here's an analogy, and then that analogy has led to a huge amount of developments. There's not really an open problem at the end — although of course as you develop this you come up with lots of open problems. There's just a philosophy that you're trying to realize. And that philosophy is super non-rigorous, actually. It's not symbol pushing at all.

发现"正确问题"本身就很难

Beyond that, a lot of the activities — you're actually trying to figure out what the right question is. You have some object, you feel like you don't understand it, and figuring out what you don't know is actually a very challenging thing to do. You can go online and list open conjectures, or whatever, and this doesn't really capture in a lot of ways what we don't know. Often finding the conjecture is really really hard.

A good example of this is the Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture, one of the Millennium Problems. It's this beautiful relationship between L-functions of elliptic curves and the set of solutions to the corresponding equations, the rank of the group of solutions.

It was discovered — it was like the first big-data conjecture. Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer had found all these statistics on elliptic curves in the 60s — one of the first ever computer-aided bits of mathematics — and they graphed these statistics and noticed that the slope of some line on a graph was related to some other algebraic invariant they knew. And that was the source of this conjecture.

So a lot of the time you're just working out examples and trying to figure out an explanation — you're doing kind of science: you run an experiment and you try to figure out an explanation for that experiment.

七、AI 在日常研究中的实际用处

老项目 vs 新项目

Going back to AI — these are things where AI seems so far to help a lot more in some things than others. The more vague a phenomenon is, or the less you have a precise question in mind, the less useful it happens to be.

You were asking how I use it in my daily life. Actually what I found is that the projects I have that predate AI — the projects I've been thinking about for three or four or five years — it's just not that useful. It's primarily a substitute for Google or something. I might use it to learn about some related topic, or something where I would have earlier Googled something and read a paper — maybe I'll discuss it with AI instead. So it saves some time for sure. It's not really doing deep intellectual work for me.

新的能力：并行编码与实验

But because I suck at coding, and so now I have my good friend who's really good at coding, and now I have all these coding projects. Because if I had a question where coding would have been really useful, I would have procrastinated on it for six months until —

Tireless PhD student.

Exactly. Now I picked up all these projects where coding is really useful. The models are very good for massively parallel things. If you want to find an example of something, you can just ask it to work through a thousand examples in parallel, or maybe 10 examples at a time, 10 different sub-agents — that's really useful. But these are kind of different activities which are on top of what I was doing before.

八、深度思考、审美与"新想法"的必要性

主持人：为什么长期项目 AI 不适用？

You were mentioning there's projects you've been working on for three, four, five years. I don't know if it's correct to say those are more of the theory-building aspect, because you did characterize yourself as an open-problem solver. What is the thing — for this audience it might be useful to explain — most of pure math is not motivated by, you know, nothing on applied math, but applied math at least has some external motivation for why a certain formal structure might be interesting to study. Whereas this one, it seems almost sociological.

To some extent — I think Thurston made some point about this in the 70s — that it is a sociological phenomenon: more and more mathematicians start examining something, then you'll converge on some interesting structures. But there's some reason why people prefer to study something or think it's beautiful. What is it that drives you in particular, and can you make a more general comment about the profession?

美学 vs 科学的取向

Yeah. Definitely some people are motivated by beauty or aesthetic considerations. I try not to be motivated by that.

I think that's a bad — well, one thing, it sort of limits you. One kind of failure mode I see among young mathematicians sometimes is: you have something and you kind of think you know how to prove it, and then the proof feels really ugly and you decide — but okay, what if you're wrong and it's not ugly? Why limit yourself?

For this audience — what is ugly? Because I have an intuition of what's ugly, but what is that? Kind of spell out —

I don't really know. I don't really have aesthetic feelings, but people sometimes feel this way. Maybe it involves a lot of grinding calculation that's not illuminating.

But you should win by any means necessary, in my opinion. I like to think of what I'm doing as doing kind of physics except with concepts.

追求"基础性"而非美

Instead of beauty, I try to think about what is fundamental, what's going to open up further understanding most. Am I introducing a new idea that will be broadly useful to understand this object?

I guess in some sense there's some aesthetic consideration there, but I try — the orientation of trying to do good science rather than trying to do art is what I prefer. There's a huge variety of opinions here, and lots of mathematicians think of themselves as being closer to poets or something.

好奇心驱动的进步

What I do think is broadly true is that progress in mathematics comes from people pursuing their personal curiosity. And it's been crucial historically that there's a lot of different people with different views of what's interesting, and then the frontier of knowledge expands and expands. And then suddenly you have these opportunistic situations where a new idea has been introduced and you can now cascade through a bunch of other things that we didn't understand before.

九、AI 缺乏什么：新技术、新理论

长期猜想的特殊性

Going back to the three-, four-, five-year problems — where are the models sort of not useful? Is it just that it's not clear you formulate it as a problem, and it's more that you're thinking about the fundamental physics of...

In some cases there is a well-stated problem here. I've been thinking about things for maybe 10 years now at this point for certain problems. Sometimes there is a conjecture that I would like to prove.

One reason the models might not be useful for some of these things is that the conjectures are true. For example, this unit distance conjecture problem — the general belief in the community was that it was true, and then it turned out to be false. What that means is that there's a specific construction you can do to refute it.

为什么"证真"更难

On the other hand, a lot of the things I think about — I know, okay, maybe someone will come up with a counter-example to the p-curvature conjecture hypothesis tomorrow and I'll look like a fool — but in general these conjectures fit into some very broad theoretical framework, which means we actually have a lot of evidence that they're true. So there's not a construction you can do to refute it. You need to somehow — we have this giant framework where certain pieces of it are only conjectural, and you probably need to resolve some of those conjectures to win.

We also have a pretty good sense that very serious new ideas are needed to resolve those conjectures. Of course you can't be sure — maybe there's some very clever construction that will let you avoid having a big new idea. Maybe we'll find this out. But my sense is that for a lot of the things I've been thinking about, they're just not accessible to applying known techniques in a very technically strong way. You need to develop a new technique.

Just to be clear — I'm not saying the models won't be able to do this. It's just that so far they seem not to.

主持人的追问：为什么发展新理论特别难？

That's exactly the point I wanted to delve into. It's true that just providing a construction for a counter-example, they seem to be strong on. If you have to start developing either new theory or new machinery to prove why a conjecture is true, it struggles more — probably because a lot of what it's drawing on is techniques that have happened in other areas and they're porting it over. And that's why maybe the unit distance problem was such a more creative result, because it was doing more of that on its own — it was drawing in something from an unexpected area.

And so — it's not that, because now we're like, okay fine, AI is getting so good so fast we can't count it out — but why? What do you think it has to... you're spelling out what it has to get better at. But some more feelings on why it's particularly hard to develop that new theory and technology?

Daniel：可能只需要不同的 RL 环境

Yeah, it's a good question. I think you just need a different — my guess actually is it's probably totally doable, and it just hasn't been done yet. Maybe you just need a different RL environment. I don't know. At this point my expectation is just that the trajectory will continue upwards. I'm not a skeptic of continued capabilities growth.

What is definitely true is that the skill of developing a theory, or building your understanding of some poorly understood object, is a fuzzier one. So it might be harder — you can tell it, "develop your understanding of zeta functions, then once it proves the Riemann hypothesis you give it a reward" — but it's harder to come up with intermediate things you can reward.

That said, I do think mathematics as a whole provides a lot of conjectures of varying levels of difficulty. So maybe this explains why there seems to be a little bit of progress in these areas — presumably they are trying to get it to solve lots of problems, and some of those problems develop at least some of the skills of theory building. And humans are able to develop these skills. I guess sometimes they get rewards from their PhD advisors — the advisor says "oh that's a good idea" based on some element of human taste. That might be something one can do too. My expectation is that just as part of continued capabilities growth, we'll see growth in these areas too.

十、哲学插曲：压缩、理解与人类的局限

主持人的哲学发散

I like the framing where you're sort of casting these increasingly difficult conjectures as a form of curriculum for both humans and AI. Getting a little bit too philosophical for some people's tastes — it gets at the question of why are we particularly good, or maybe particularly bad, at math. What is it that we're struggling to do, or some people are particularly good at when you develop new theory?

It's related to why can we formulate good structures for physics as well. It's not obvious all parts of the world are understandable and legible, but some parts are, and therefore we try to do it — because there's maybe compressive pressures on our minds because we can't understand anything beyond compressing stuff more finely. I don't know if that's the correct interpretation.

Daniel：无法"硬算"反而是发现的关键

I'm a little bit skeptical as like compression as a metric of interest, but it's definitely a good anthropological reason for why we do a certain theory building. I just think it's true. And in fact I think our inability to just grind is kind of important to our ability to make discoveries.

具体案例：Gemini Deep Think 与引理

Just as an example — I have one paper out so far where the models were kind of useful. They proved a couple of lemmas. This was some situation where we had kind of proven the main result, and then there were some lemmas I was unhappy with — they seemed not to be optimal. I worked with — actually this was with Gemini Deep Think, which at the time was also on the frontier, no longer man.

I kind of worked with it to prove the lemmas. What happened here was there was some lemma I wanted to prove and the models couldn't do it — none of the frontier models could do it. So I worked out a ton of examples on my own, and I realized, "oh well, maybe here's some reason why it could be true." I found a better statement of the lemma. Once I had that statement, okay, probably I could have done it pretty fast, but also the models were able to very quickly prove that better statement.

So our inability to prove it led to an improvement in the result. Now you can take the original lemma I had that the models weren't able to prove, put it into ChatGPT 5.6 Pro, and it will output the worst proof you've ever seen — like 10 pages of just brutal calculation with no insight whatsoever. This would have been a perfectly fine proof, but it would not have led to this discovery of what I think is a beautiful conceptual explanation for why this thing we discovered was true.

So we found a better proof because we couldn't do — I mean, I say we couldn't do the calculation. What actually happened — and here I understand I'm being hypocritical about my complaints about ugly proofs before — is I realized this horrible grind proof would work, and I could not bring myself to do it. So I looked for another argument.

Now the models can do very long technical calculations pretty reliably.

主持人：审美其实还是驱动

To your credit — I don't know — I understand why you're saying, don't shy away from trying to prove something just because it seems ugly, because you have to take the first step and eventually try to work towards insight. So you might be shy about admitting it, but it is still maybe driven by whether it's aesthetics or just pure "I want to understand." And if understanding just means it's a little bit simpler or more compressed, then you've gotten understanding. It's just a deep philosophical question, too — what it is.

Of course, any — there's a reason we do informal mathematics rather than writing out long formal strings of symbols of ZFC or whatever, even though besides length, it's just somehow we're trying to put it in a way where we are actually getting some non-rigorous understanding out.

And even how that relates to why it helps — is it because of our inability to grind, or is it because if we are pushing towards something more compressive, it also hopefully ascends on — does it help understand other fields as well? It's somewhat magical that when we try to optimize for both, it tends to coincide. I don't know if that's a fair, quantitative statement, but why that is kind of magical.

It's at least sometimes true.

We certainly bias towards the cases in which it is — that's why we call it a good theory to build. But it's very much — this is what we can study and understand, and therefore it's also very convenient that it was rich in mathematical results.

十一、数学界应如何适应 AI？

主持人的问题

There's two things we can pull on. Given you've conceded that mathematical ability of AI is going to continue advancing and can do some of the things you're doing nowadays — how should the mathematics community best adapt and benefit from this?

As somebody who doesn't have the time to practice mathematics anymore, this is very great because I can maybe dabble more, there's a lot of results that can come out. But I can also see where you've made the more precise point of, we can not motivate the right kind of behavior of understanding and development.

Daniel：既兴奋又警惕

Okay. So first of all, it is clearly really exciting that there are increasingly capable models that are producing high-quality results — some high-quality results, also a lot of slop.

Some good stuff. As the models get really capable, my hope is that they will answer a lot of the questions I've been kept up at night thinking about, and I'll get to learn the answers. I think that's really exciting. A lot of people got into math largely because they enjoyed learning math. The first thing you do as a math student is learn stuff that other people did, and you do that for like 20 years before you start doing — maybe not quite 20 years, but 15 years — if you're lucky, 20 years.

数学的目标不是产出论文

That said, the goal of mathematics is not to produce mathematics papers. It's to produce some kind of understanding. Maybe some of that understanding resides in model weights or something. To me, that's pretty unsatisfying.

My own motivation for doing mathematics is I would like to satisfy my own personal curiosity. I think people should have the capability to do that. And that requires a pretty substantial apparatus. It's simply not the case that you can study the questions I think are fundamental unless you've invested a huge amount of time and effort getting to the point where you can meaningfully do so.

金字塔式的人才培养

Moreover, even the small group of people doing fancy research math on the frontier relies on a huge apparatus of thousands and millions or billions of people who are trying to learn to think mathematically. You need an entire mathematical community to support a small group of people on the frontier. Without the pipeline, the pipeline doesn't exist.

If you think that's important — development of human capital that can meaningfully engage with frontier mathematics — you still have to incentivize those people to actually invest their time and effort getting to the point where they can engage and then do so in a high-quality meaningful way.

激励机制已经出问题

Right now I think the existing incentive structures for math research do not encourage people to do that. If you're a postdoc on the market — you want to get a job maybe for the next couple years before the community adapts — the best way to do that is you want to produce a lot of papers which prove old conjectures. You can do that by playing the slot machine until the model produces a hopefully correct proof of such a result.

You don't even have to pick the theorem in advance. Here's an experiment you can do: you can take Codex, you can say, "go online, find five recent conjectures in algebraic geometry and prove them." I've run this experiment, and with some back-and-forth, I was able in an hour to get three quite bad but correct papers. Which are now sitting on my hard drive waiting for me to email the relevant people — but this is not a good use of my time to invest results.

arXiv 上的"套利"现象

You definitely see people doing this. There's been a huge uptick in posts to arXiv, mostly not very interesting. Some of it is interesting, but a lot of it is clearly low quality, even insofar as the result is something that would have been highly rewarded a year ago — there's no evidence that a human being is actually engaged with it. There's no development of human capital or understanding.

Sometimes we've seen examples where three or four or five papers with the exact same proof of the exact same theorem have come out within a couple days of each other — clearly some situation where someone's playing the slot machine.

ChatGPT is kind of consistently finding the same —

But that's also interesting. It's kind of mode-collapsed on certain paths of reasoning.

单一栽培的风险

It's not obvious that this problem goes away as the models get better. Maybe it does, but maybe it doesn't. A lot of what I was saying earlier is that progress in mathematics comes from letting a thousand different flowers bloom and people pursue their own curiosity, and then the boundaries of knowledge expand in some fairly uniform way in this really high-dimensional space of mathematics. And then opportunistically you suddenly get some applications or answers to old questions.

It's not clear to me that if we subordinate mathematical exploration to what the model wants to pursue — if what you're getting is one mathematician duplicated a thousand times, or actually a million different mathematicians doing a million different things —

主持人：这也是实验室应关注的

Aside from math having to adapt by changing incentive structures, I think this is actually a maybe dangerous thing that the labs have to pay attention to. On one side, what's been successful for them is that this emergent reasoning capability is incredibly powerful and creating a lot of great PR headlines.

But to your point — human mathematicians are coming from all sorts of weird intuitions. That is why you end up developing the frontier that is so diverse. If it's true that most of these proofs being pushed out by the labs are converging on very similar things because they are technically drawing on the same body of literature — where are they developing their intuitions? It's from practicing mathematicians. It's not clear where that other emergent stronger diverse intuition might be coming from.

It's a huge debate whether you could introduce new capabilities. Precisely, I think it should be studied in the math context, because where it's good at and where it fails — and where human mathematicians are good — is exactly a very precise question to study it on. So it is unclear to me that we'll produce — if we don't incentivize enough people to interact with it, maybe unlike other domains, it might not actually continue producing a superior result without human aid.

十二、"即使 AI 超人化，我们仍然赢了"

Daniel 的反直觉论证

Let me actually push a bit further. Let's suppose the models become really robustly superhuman — like, we're not even adding meaningful cognitive capacity. I claim we still won as human mathematicians.

Great. Why?

It's because there's a question about how we're designing society. Maybe the optimal situation is you have the models doing all sorts of math research, and that leads to — in this highly non-uniform diverse way — maybe you don't need humans to add that kind of diversity. Maybe that's the optimal thing to do, and in the end it leads to lots of applications and improved understanding.

But despite something being optimal doesn't mean you do it. There's no reason to think that if we hand over control of math research to the models and just let them do their own thing, that it will do the optimal thing. In fact, if we instrumentalize what we want them to do — like, "make our life better" or whatever — it might not be the case that what they decide to do is pursue a wide variety of interesting research. They might just try to take the direct path. We don't know what's going to happen.

人类必须留在场上

If you believe there is any value in this broad-based fundamental research — which I do, I think that's one of the most valuable things humans or the models can be doing — the easiest way to guarantee it happens is to keep a community with broad interests who are pushing the models to do it, and helping us design a society where that's what we're pushing for.

At least my hopeful vision for the future is that humans are not totally disempowered — we have some control over where we're going. And if that's the case, what we end up doing is going to be driven by human interests. So you want to have people who have lots of different interests, and also the capabilities to actually pursue them. You want people who are smart and engaged and can do not just mathematical thinking but all sorts of thinking.

主持人：ergonomic 界面很关键

A great fear is as AI advances, we don't develop the right ergonomic interfaces to actually encourage us to continue to be good thinkers. It's so easy to relinquish that because you just off — and the models aren't even good at that level of thinking where it's like the top-level structure — but despite that, it's so easy to.

Especially for math — another selfish reason is if you math-max, I think it's actually a great pedagogical excuse to get really rigorous at thinking about various things. I mean, this is not why mathematicians do it, but as somebody that's part of what we do.

It really helped give me a very good framework to think about many things, not just mathematics. And as somebody who's now a parent of a 2-year-old, I think about this a lot too. It's not about grinding, even though whatever it's still good — but not to un-grind too much. I used to collaborate a bunch with some Hungarian mathematicians, Béla among them, and I heard that in Budapest they would just teach group theory when you're in primary school. And I'm like, well, we should definitely do that.

Now that AI is so good at somewhat good at explaining, but it's far more accessible, we should probably proliferate that even more, so that helps bring more people to the frontier.

十三、数学作为一个"预示性行业"

Daniel：这不是我们独有的挑战

I mean, this is something I'm concerned about, right? Of course I mostly talk about math because that's where I live. But I think one nice thing about thinking about this is that we're one of the first professions to have a significant impact of high-quality models. Although I think maybe we're one of the first professions for it to happen so publicly.

My sense is that there are plenty of other professions —

100%.

Coding. But also just anything you do at a computer — probably a huge amount is being done by the models at this point — and they're not having a public reckoning about it. Because math capabilities are useful for the labs to talk about, I think probably a bit more publicly than everyone else.

One reason to try to maintain human capital in this area is it's a model for all professions. Presumably we still want people who are meaningfully engaging with the world, and experts, and have talents and trained skills. It's actually very convenient that the math profession is so entwined with education here, because we're also seeing some challenges among college and secondary education coming from AI too.

AI 作为学习工具的两极分化

As you said, it's also an amazing tool to learn. People have — I've heard people start talking about a bimodal distribution in their classes, where there's some people who are really figuring out how to take advantage of new tools and other people who are just letting them do their homework and then bombing everything else.

Unfortunately, I don't think that adapts fast enough. But we definitely want to be living in a world where we're producing better thinkers. Even if we talk about just the pure optimization game, I think that's better for us. But as a human being, it would be pretty inconvenient if we became worse thinkers just as AI ascends. It's too easy to let that happen. So we should be thinking hard on how to actually take advantage of this and harness it for our own improvement.

质量 vs 数量

It's sort of interesting to observe. The models at their current level of capabilities let you do a lot more — they let you do a lot of things you wouldn't have done, more cheaply than cheaply enough to do them now. But it's not clear to me that in many cases they're actually improving the quality of outputs.

This is common — you have a new technology that's doing something a little bit worse than was previously done but much cheaper, and so you get a lot of suddenly a lot of low-quality outputs that are displacing previous high-quality outputs. But I think it's possible to use the tools in a way that actually improves the quality along every dimension. It just requires some thoughtfulness and some redesign of institutions to actually incentivize that.

主持人：不能让位于模型

Well, hopefully capitalism works there. I do feel like the most high-value things do require people to use it effectively, and right now the models are not good enough without the human experts to actually participate. But to your point, there's a vast majority of more junior and entry-level roles — it's harder for those roles to adapt as well.

The thing that would be a mistake is to use the AI models in a way that doesn't — basically you need to be ascending and using the models to deepen your understanding. It's so easy for human nature to just be lazy, and you have to resist that. Because that is the moment that you will kind of lose, basically.

Forgive the very competitive language, but it really is that it's so easy to relinquish the thinking to the models. The models can't really think. And so as things are ascending so fast, it's critical that you continue developing those facilities and actually leverage it to improve those facilities rather than relinquish.

十四、"slop 论文"的另一面：兴奋度

意料之外的积极面

One thing I think has been nice about this vast increase in semi-expert attention or model attention on math problems is — okay, I've been complaining about slop papers, people who are not producing really high-quality stuff. Okay, there's a lot of documents on the internet one might have to comb through to figure out if a problem has been solved or not. But to me it seems like just the fact that there's lots of people excited about math is kind of a positive.

I totally agree.

And not even kind of a positive.

Exactly. It's like suddenly there's a spotlight on it and I can nerd out about math more.

That's right.

Have they been mostly more secretive? I think they've released some traces for stuff.

十六、短证明 vs 长证明：一个能力问题

主持人：转述 OpenAI 团队的观察

When you're saying you have to evaluate how the results came — I had Mark Chen and Metab Swani on from OpenAI recently, and they were saying what's been the most charming or delightful is just that the proofs have been relatively short. They're not 200 pages — maybe corresponding to your grinding point as well. But maybe this is optimized for — in retrospect it was picked that it was short. Do you find that on average stuff that you throw at GPT-5 or Fable tends to be shorter and more legible to the human? Or it might just go haywire and just grind it out?

Daniel：短是因为它们做不了长

I think it is nice that they'll sometimes produce short clever proofs. Everyone likes a short clever proof. My sense is that the reason they're not producing long complicated proofs is that they cannot — the ability to check correctness is not yet there.

Even if you ask the models to produce a short proof, you can then often ask them "is that correct?" and they will often say no. They're much more reliable than they were six months ago for sure, but they will still sometimes produce things that are just wrong, and they know they're wrong.

The problem with producing a very long thing is they might not know they're wrong. Presumably internally OpenAI and Anthropic have probably solved a lot more problems than they've released, and I imagine quite a few of them they're just not sure if they're true.

For example, with this recent list of 10 problems released by OpenAI, those were all formalized in Lean, which is very good evidence that they're true. I have no doubt there were a lot more that they could not formalize in Lean — because the prerequisite results have not been put into mathlib yet, for example. There were probably more that were longer, which also makes it challenging to check.

800 页的 AI 生成"证明"

We do actually see very long generated proofs on the arXiv. For example, someone recently posted a claimed proof of resolution of singularities in positive characteristic which was 800 AI-generated pages. I mean, I'm sorry, I haven't read it, I haven't gone in and found an error, but there's no way it's correct — this would be a major result, and it's just not within the capacities of the current models if you're reasonably well calibrated.

Definitely no human has read it. Definitely the models are not able to check this kind of thing. So my expectation is that the reason it's producing short clever things is just that's what we can check. You can get it to produce long things that are grindy or hard to check, but then —

主持人：这更多说明能力边界

We'll have to get there. This is actually more what it says about capabilities — frontier capabilities — rather than in a more negative way, "hey it's just so good at these clever." I think that's totally fair.

Especially if you look at an adjacent domain like code. I remember reading something Cursor put out about testing their long-horizon harness. In this case they're trying to reproduce SQLite in Rust, and it was just so telling how far we are. That seems like a very comparable task of, it's very long, you have to make sure — there's something to verify that it's a correct implementation by testing a suite of cases. But you actually need a harness there. In this case it's not just the raw models, and it takes a while, and you can actually compare with different frontier versus non-frontier models — who's the planner, etc. — differences in their capabilities as well.

十七、Harness、可靠性与"大局校验"

Harness 会降低可靠性

I also think in practice, to elicit a long proof, you kind of need a harness. And when you make a harness whose goal is to elicit a proof, I think it often decreases reliability, because you're just trying to produce output.

ChatGPT 5.6 Pro really tries not to say wrong stuff, for example. Although you know it happens, and then you'll ask it "oh was that correct?" and it'll say no. But when you're trying to get it to ideate — you try to get it to be creative, you try to get it out of this very rigorous rut in order to actually get it somewhere.

If your interest is in — there are a lot of people trying to arbitrage the prestige mechanics of academic mathematics and trying to elicit a lot of proofs which are not necessarily being checked. In order to do that, I think you just decrease the reliability in order to get a lot of stuff. Any harness that can elicit a 250-page paper is probably not being very careful about what it's producing.

And you're saying that it's decreasing or it's not reliable just because the capability isn't there yet, and so it's just kind of forcing a longer-horizon task on it?

Yeah.

人如何检查一篇长论文？

In practice, how does a human checking it — can't check a 250-page paper either, you can't reliably check it line by line. What you try to do to understand it is you try to understand the overall global structure of the argument, and you stress-test it in various ways: would this argument apply to something else that I know to be false? Does it work in this special case, blah blah blah?

And also the models seem not to be able to do that kind of more — I don't know — fuzzy, like unit-testing a proof, very well yet.

一个具体案例：无法定位的错误

Actually, one of my favorite tests for the models, which they haven't succeeded at yet: there's a paper — I won't name it — that came out a couple years ago that was wrong. It was very hard to find — it was in close enough area to myself that I immediately downloaded it and started reading it, because it was claiming some big result. And it was very hard to find the actual specific error, but it was very clear from the structure of the argument that it couldn't work. It was arguing something that was too strong to be true if you kind of took it a little bit further.

Me and a bunch of other experts immediately realized it was wrong. We emailed the author, and we kind of went back and forth until someone figured out what the precise specific error was. So far the models seem not to have been able to do this. The specific error is quite subtle, but they're also not able to do this kind of overall big-picture tax-checking, which is kind of how people in practice check papers.

与代码的类比

Which is kind of — it mirrors why in code it's so clear it's good at the syntax, but higher-level architectural stuff is still very weak. Maybe it'll ascend there, but probably need some harness help. Who knows? People have evolving opinions on how much the harness and the model have to co-evolve and which one is necessary, but the next model requires less. In math, it'd be very interesting to see how you — if you do any experiments with the harness there and how that improves — because it is a mark of general reasoning.

I do have my own sort of bad little harness in Codex. But I personally do not enjoy autonomous mathematics very much, so I mostly do not use the harness. I mostly try to use it to help me understand stuff.

No, it's totally fair. You don't want to automate your job away, because that does involve you being in the loop to understand it, which is necessary to participate.

十八、结尾：教育与下一代

Daniel 的三岁女儿

Maybe to finish off — this could be something you haven't thought about, or actually thought a lot about. I think you also have a toddler, right?

Yeah.

How have you — a three-year-old?

Three-year-old.

Great. Right, so you're one year more advanced and probably have more thoughts on this. How are you thinking about her education in math and — you know, not to grind, but really how to pass on the love of it and how to react to AI?

Yeah. So she's three. She's never used AI. She is starting to add — that's about as far as we are in math.

That's more than she can add — single-digit numbers, by counting on her fingers, and count up to like maybe 30 reliably and 50 semi-reliably. So I'm very proud of that.

That's good.

Yeah, I definitely encourage that. We talk about shapes and stuff. Actually a couple days ago I woke her up and she was hiding under the blankets, and I was like, "Oh, what are you up to under there, Sophia?" And she was like, "Oh, I'm doing some math."

Oh, I think you tweeted about that. That was —

Yeah, it was great. So I think she has some sense that I like math and she's into it because of that.

20 年后的世界

I don't know — I think the world is probably going to look pretty different in 20 years or whenever she's fully adult and doing her own thing. But I think a lot of what we educate people for is like pretty robust changes in the nature of the world.

The reason to learn math has always been to think clearly and better understand the world, and presumably that's something you want to do even if there are extremely capable AIs. And this is also true — I personally like math a lot, but also the reason to like read a lot of books and do the humanities and so on.

The actual values of the math profession, and education more broadly, are things we definitely want to try to preserve. That I hope to instill in my daughter. How much institutions have to change to make sure that happens is maybe an open question I think a lot about. But at a personal level I'm definitely trying to convince my three-year-old that math is super cool.

"icosahedron" 作为第一批词汇

Oh yeah, 100%.

One of her first words was icosahedron.

Was what?

She has a — my parents gave her a little icosahedron toy when she was one. Not literally a first word, but she learned the platonic solids quite early.

Oh, very good. Very fun.

Next up, group theory.

I mean, it's very natural.

That's right. When I teach her about addition and subtraction further, we'll do it in the context of a general group.

Oh, very good. Well, at least you give the motivation. I think a lot of people probably skip that part. And you know, maybe this is how math grad students can also focus — training the next much younger generation to use AI in service of actually getting better at math, rather than just lacking understanding.

告别

Wonderful. Okay. Well, thank you so much, Daniel.

Thank you. It was a lot of fun.

Yeah, it was a lot of fun. And I think there's going to be a lot more progress very soon. I'd love to maybe catch up and chat again.

Sounds great.

观看原视频 →
item.description:
# 三个让人意外的观察
## 一、AI 数学的"负空间悖论"：它的失败比它的成功更能推动数学进步
Daniel 讲了一个精妙的故事：他有一个引理，前沿模型都证明不出来。于是他自己动手研究了大量例子，最终发现——**引理本身可以被改写成一个更好的陈述**。一旦改写完成，模型立刻秒证。
这里藏着一个反直觉的洞察：**AI 的无能反而成了数学发现的催化剂**。如果模型一开始就能用 10 页丑陋的暴力计算搞定原始引理，Daniel 永远不会发现那个更本质、更漂亮的表述。换句话说，AI 现阶段"能做暴力活但做不了优雅活"的这个缺陷，恰好构成了一种**倒逼人类去寻找概念性理解的压力机制**。
这让我想到一个跨领域的类比：**GPS 与出租车司机的记忆**。伦敦出租车司机因为要背下整座城市的路网，海马体会显著增大；GPS 普及后这种认知能力普遍萎缩。数学的危险不是"AI 能证明我们能证明的东西"，而是**AI 恰好能证明"人类必须痛苦才能证明"的那一层，从而剥夺了痛苦带来的洞察**。
## 二、"斯洛特机（slot machine）经济学"正在悄悄重塑数学的科研生态
Daniel 描述的

item.title: [Business of Sport] Rugby 7’s is Great Product BUT can it be Great Business?
item.dc:creator: Business of Sport
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、真正的商业模式不是"卖球赛"，而是"填补空档期"

Ultimate 7s 最颠覆性的洞察其实藏在一个不起眼的时间缝隙里：HSBC 世界系列赛从 12 月打到 6 月，之后就是长达半年的"精英级空档"。Barney 没有去挑战 15 人制的市场，也没有和世界系列赛正面竞争，而是把"日历空缺"本身当成产品定义。

这其实是一个被严重低估的商业逻辑——基础设施套利（infrastructure arbitrage）。世界上最好的 132 名球员，在 6-11 月这段时间基本处于"闲置资产"状态；各国联盟没钱养他们做高强度赛事，球员却仍需保持竞技状态。Ultimate 7s 本质上做的是运动员的"共享经济"——不是拥有球员，而是租用他们的空闲时间。

这跟 Airbnb 早期的逻辑惊人相似：不建酒店，而是唤醒沉睡的房源。差别在于，Ultimate 7s 唤醒的是"沉睡的顶级人力资本"。

二、令人意外的观察：他们赢的不是球迷，而是"迁徙路径"

大多数人以为新联赛的核心挑战是"建立部落归属感"（tribalism），但 Barney 反复强调一个更微妙的问题——奥运后的"迁徙断层"。观众在奥运会被点燃热情之后，找不到"下一次刺激"的落脚点，于是热度自然衰减。

这是一种非常独特的"情绪继承"生意：Ultimate 7s 不是在制造需求，而是在接住奥运会溢出的情感势能。就像流媒体平台不生产明星，而是接住"影院余温"一样。

这里有一个跨领域的类比让人拍案——它更像日本便利店的选址逻辑：不去开辟新客流，而是精准卡在通勤动线的"决策疲劳点"。Ultimate 7s 的赛程刻意压缩在 8 月末到 9 月末，就是要卡在奥运热度衰减前的最后一波势能里。这不是体育赛程，这是注意力经济的漏斗设计。

三、隐藏的悖论：他们用"最不像 7 人制"的方式拯救 7 人制

7 人制橄榄球的传统魅力是"节日化、社交、啤酒 + 朋友"，但 Ultimate 7s 却明确要强化竞技纯粹性——引入战术暂停、10 分钟比赛、教练策略透明化。这看起来是在杀死自己最赚钱的基因。

但真正的洞察是：当娱乐属性成为默认底色时，稀缺的反而是"叙事密度"。7 人制过去输就输在观众"记不住球员、认不出队伍、说不清故事"。Barney 在做的是给这个"啤酒节运动"注入戏剧结构——教练暂停就是电视剧的"广告悬念"，10 分钟就是短视频的"完播率法则"。

这里可以连接到一个反直觉的比较：F1 的引擎降噪争议。当年 F1 把 V12 换成 V6 时，粉丝哗然，觉得"灵魂丢了"。但真正的赢家是那些接受"F1 不是发动机声音、而是叙事密度"的观众。Ultimate 7s 走的是同样的路——不是保留形式，而是保留情绪的可传递性。

四、埋在细节里的天才决策：Draft 工资结构 = 心理定价学

最容易被忽略的一个决定：他们没有像其他联赛那样，让第一轮球员拿走天价合同、后面球员薪水断崖式下降。相反，他们让第 2 轮到第 4 轮球员的差距压缩到 2000-4000 英镑。

这是一个行为经济学的隐蔽应用——它消除了球员心中的"羞辱阈值"。当每一档只差几千镑时，"被选中的荣誉感"永远高于"被低估的失落感"。这跟航空公司刻意压缩经济舱与"高级经济舱"的价差是同一套逻辑——让人愿意升级，而不是让人愤怒地放弃。

这种"心理定价"的智慧，在体育联赛里几乎没人做——他们太迷恋 NBA / NFL 那种"顶薪明星驱动"模式，忘了新联赛真正需要的是中间层的心理稳定性。

📝 转录文本

开场：明星球员与联赛定位

Listen, who wouldn't like to see Pollock and Smith and Aaron play for GB7? Let me stay on the record. Henry Pollock wants to play in this competition to get ready for the Olympics. He's welcome as are the others that we've mentioned. We built the model for the future for crossover athletes, for 15s athletes to come and be part of this, but we built it for rugby sevens players as a foundation.

Ultimate 7s is a brand new global rugby 7s championship launching this September. It will include 132 of the best rugby sevens players in the world. We've got six clubs now. We've got loads of work to do. There may be an immediate interest and intrigued about these teams and who plays in them and so on, but it's not going to create immediate tribalism or connection. We've got to work on that and we've got to build that.

It's amazing to get the sevens into the Olympic program. I think it's had some real challenges over the last few years. What we didn't necessarily have is after the Olympics and you've got that wave of engagement in the sport, where do I go? So, I think how do you take those fans that we know are being introduced to the game and go where do I get my next hit?

I call it cheap shot before again we came on is does this work as a natural business? How are you looking to not just build great product but great business?

欢迎与开场

Yeah. So sport fascinating.

Barney. Good morning. Welcome to the business of sport. It's great to have you in the studio.

Likewise. Thank you for having me.

We've done so much rugby um on the show before, but we've never properly got into sevens. And I guess that is part of the issue that we'll talk about, but it's also now the reason we're doing it today, part of the opportunity. Before I go and ruin um a lot of what you'd say, tell us a little bit about where the sport of sevens is at.

7 人制橄榄球的现状与发展轨迹

Yes. So, I think the sport of sevens is in a really interesting um place. I think it is uh on an upward trajectory. I think it's had some real challenges um over the last um few years over the last decade probably since its inception actually arguably in the Olympics in 2016 which I think on the face of it you might suggest would be the kind of the you know blow the doors off moment and actually Olympic by Olympics you show you you can see and you and it's shown a real increase in interest and intensity around the sport but I think between then it's not quite captured some of that and really kind of invest it back in and I think there are some reasons for that which we I'm sure can go into.

But look in terms of the HSBC 7s World Series um I think there's some amazing work going on there. I think rugby sevens as a true short form short fast format is there. It's snackable, it's sort of made for today's audiences. And you know they're showing that in 550,000 fans attending across 13 events last year, 21% increase year on year. So that's going in the right direction. I think as a digital property it's hit over a billion impressions again two years running. Now these are just sort of I know these are kind of snippets and tidbits from from data but I think they support what sevens is and what it can be for the rugby ecosystem. It's a sport born fast with lots of legacy and lots of heritage and it can be could be really ready and viable for today's audiences in the way that they want to enjoy and consume sport.

娱乐产品 vs. 竞技产品

How much of it is entertainment product versus sporting product? And I asked that question because my engagement historically with Sevens had very much been group of mates on a day on a weekend as an entertainment product with yes of course a nice bit of rugby but I'm a big sports fan so I'm paying a little bit of attention maybe but a little bit of attention. I'm with other people who are not really paying a huge attention amount of attention to it but they're there for the social element the experience element of it. Is that still the case? Has that been the case? Is that a challenge to overcome? Is it an opportunity to leverage?

Yes, I think it is. I think it is still the case. I think it still exists. I think it's an opportunity to leverage, but I think it's also a challenge in terms of the integrity of the sporting product that's on the pitch. And we Ultimate Sevens has been very clear that we want to really lean into that sporting integrity because we believe that the sport itself um is played by some of the best athletes in the world. If you look at what you have to be to be a rugby seven player in terms of your athletic progress, in terms of your ability to execute the sport, you know, it is right up there. I think it's also a really interesting play against other sports, athletics, NFL dare I say, in terms of kind of how you can transition between different audiences and what they and what they like.

You've had that, haven't you? In some of like the I mean, particularly in the US obviously, I mean, there have been a lot of players in US7s have come from those backgrounds.

Yeah, absolutely. Exactly and that's the other thing in terms of kind of if you look at traditional rugby markets versus nontraditional sevens is a sport that is introducing new fans and also indeed um growing uh people engaging and playing the sport. I think it's 11% um in in sort of general terms in uh new new players coming into the sport coming into the ecosystem but that goes up to 20% in places like Spain and other emerging markets. So it's got a real role to play uh in in that sense.

Um, but going back to the piece around the festivalization element to it and the entertainment piece, um, it's got to be something to leverage because I think that's that is people's muscle memory with the sport as well. It's a connection they have. The sevens is where I go with my group of mates. I might have a beer. I want to enjoy the atmosphere. Um, but I think the opportunity there is to is to kind of condense it, bring it all together, bring both elements to the party, so people feeling that they're going to come to something that is really engaging and really energetic and fresh compared to sitting down, dare I say, in the rain or the all the kind of the winter that that the 15s is typically aligned with.

Um, and get that kind of atmosphere. But it's a bit of a running joke, isn't it? That that people, you know, in certain stands, in certain tournaments, you know, who's playing and they don't necessarily know much about the teams. What they will know more about, I think, and I think that's starting in our culture more and more to come to the come to to the frey of the players. So, there'll be one or two that they really interested when they're playing or if they score tries. And I think that's a really interesting play and how we can start to merge those two things. Really focusing on the players, focusing on the personalities, focusing on the rivalries, but making sure people feel that they're coming to that atmosphere um and and that kind of entertainment product. So, it is not one or the other. It is absolutely a merging of those two things. I think the entertainment piece is is one that we can latch on to earlier. I think the sporting piece we've got to build over time in terms of connecting people with a new club identity, a new IP.

奥运会带来的机遇与断层

You know, you have a very exciting sport, right? I mean, to anyone that's seen it, that's the good thing about it. The hardest thing always is you can do all of this, but is your product actually any good? Right. The Sevens product is is really good. It's exciting sport. It's fast sport. You watch amazingly talented people with great speed and power and strength and skill, which if you're a sports fan is is really why you're tuning in. You're also, you know, if you're looking for all the reasons why this is a sport that can and should succeed. 10 to 15 years ago, you were selling out the sport sevens was selling out your Twicken and type stadiums. It was a broadcast product. It was a commercial product. But it just seems in that time and I'm really interested that you said the Olympics was maybe a moment of recognition to to to some of the challenges that may have faced the sport recently because it just seems since the times of them having that level of success, something has happened to just remove some of the attractiveness and the value that Sevens was creating and had created to leave it outside the core sporting attention economy if you wanted. Can you expand on the Olympic point you meant?

I think and I've spoken to a few people about this. I think post 2016 and the and the it was amazing to get the sevens into the Olympic program. I think you you in that you have a uniqueness not completely unique but certainly within the context of sevens exists as part of a massive rugby following ecosystem heritage legacy sport not a new sport that we've come up with in the last 20 30 years it goes back to you know the 1800s and so um and now you've also got it in the Olympic program and and it and it's on its own in that sense so it doesn't share that with 15s that also is in the Olympic program it's on its own so it's a really interesting um play there.

I think what we didn't necessarily have is investment in where after the Olympics and you've got that wave of engagement in the sport where do I go as a as a Joe public as you know as a population because after the Olympics the next piece is going to be up in December in you know in Dubai but as I say going back to this kind of entertainment and festivalization piece that's where what what you what you I think end up with is a localized you know commercial model that in some pockets are really viable like your Dubai or like your Hong Kongs, but in other markets aren't as as easy a hit because they're built on 50 years of legacy and heritage and and expat kind of communities. So, I think it's it was it was how do how do you take those fans that we know are being introduced to the game and go where do I get my next hit? Where's my next sevens thing happening? Who why do I want to follow that person?

And there's also an interesting thing about you know sevens is played at national level with national teams. So they pull on the jerseys. Inevitably I think New Zealand playing England where it's GB now with sevens is is more is is interesting at the 15s level because of all of the legacy and heritage that comes with tours that comes with them coming over here with comes with all of the weight of marketing and everything that goes into the 15's game. So what else could we have given them? Either at the grassroots level, right? This is how you now go and get involved in this amazing sport or this is where you get your next hit, which we hope now will be Ultimate Sevens happening in August, September, you know, moving forward.

Ultimate 7s 详解：赛制、时间、创新

Let's go into that because we can't really talk around all of this without you properly explaining what it is that's bringing all of this right to the four again. Tell us Ultimate Sevens um you know, what it's really all about.

So, Ultimate Sevens is a brand new global rugby 7s championship launching this September, September 2026. It will include 132 of the best rugby sevens players on in the world. Uh those are the players that play regularly in the HSBC 7s World Series that pull on their national jerseys over the over the course of the World Series that as we know goes from December through to through to early June.

Um it will this year um be made up of Cardiff at Cardiff Arms Park on the 12th of September and then Beeritz in the southwest of France on the 18th of September and then we will move to the grand final which will be at the Brenford GT Stadium on the 24th of September.

Couple of really important things to note is that we've taken the game as I say with this legacy and this heritage um and we have reframed it and repackaged it and modernized it. You are still getting a game of rugby sevens the rules and how you how you'll see it being played by the athon same pitches and so on but we've brought in some innovation to really elevate it for these the modern audience. So it's a 3-4 hour window of absolute allout intense rugby breathless rugby as we like to describe it. Um our games will be 10 minutes long. Now, some of that is because we wanted to make sure that we can really maximize that four hours. But there's also a really interesting play here about the fact we're giving each of the coaches a 90-second timeout per game, a tactical timeout. item.description:
## 一、真正的商业模式不是"卖球赛"，而是"填补空档期"
Ultimate 7s 最颠覆性的洞察其实藏在一个不起眼的时间缝隙里：HSBC 世界系列赛从 12 月打到 6 月，之后就是长达半年的"精英级空档"。Barney 没有去挑战 15 人制的市场，也没有和世界系列赛正面竞争，而是**把"日历空缺"本身当成产品定义**。
这其实是一个被严重低估的商业逻辑——**基础设施套利（infrastructure arbitrage）**。世界上最好的 132 名球员，在 6-11 月这段时间基本处于"闲置资产"状态；各国联盟没钱养他们做高强度赛事，球员却仍需保持竞技状态。Ultimate 7s 本质上做的是**运动员的"共享经济"**——不是拥有球员，而是租用他们的空闲时间。
这跟 Airbnb 早期的逻辑惊人相似：不建酒店，而是唤醒沉睡的房源。差别在于，Ultimate 7s 唤醒的是"沉睡的顶级人力资本"。
## 二、令人意外的观察：他们赢的不是球迷，而是"迁徙路径"
大多数人以为新联赛的核心挑战是"建立部落归属感"（tribalism），但 Barney 反复强调一个更微妙

item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一个反直觉的观察：规模正在杀死大实验室的"主体感"

访谈中最令人意外的一段藏在中间——Sarah 指出，OpenAI 从 200 人扩张、Anthropic 迈向数千人、单次训练需要 7500 亿美元资本时，研究员正在集体失去"我在推动历史"的感觉。两种情绪在顶级实验室的走廊里蔓延："反正模型会自己搞定"、"反正只有算力才重要"。

这里有一个诡异的悖论：AI 越强大，实验室越庞大，个体研究者的能动感越低。这不是 Jevons 悖论——这是它的镜像双胞胎。当访谈末尾她乐观地援引 Jensen 的 Jevons 论断（更高效意味着更多就业）时，其实无意间揭示了一个隐藏张力：在应用侧，AI 会创造无限杠杆感；但在前沿侧，AI 正在制造前所未有的"齿轮化"体验。这也解释了为什么她的整个投资策略成立——顶尖研究员流出前沿实验室、加入小团队，恰恰是"规模的诅咒"在为她供货。她的基金不是在与大实验室竞争，而是在收割它们的"心理副产品"。

跨领域连接：她其实在复刻 20 世纪的"哥本哈根学派"模型

Sarah 和 Mike 反复提到的 "250 个人在推动前沿" ——这个数字远小于任何主流社群理论的估算，却几乎精确对应科学史上"革命性时期的核心节点数"。玻尔的哥本哈根研究所鼎盛期的核心圈约 200 人；曼哈顿计划里真正做核心决策的科学家约 150 人；甚至 Xerox PARC 的黄金年代也只有约 100 名主要研究者。

每一次范式革命，都是由一个"超越 Dunbar 数、但小于 500 人的紧密网络"完成的。Conviction 的整个方法论——不追求管理规模、不铺开搜索面（每周只见 4–6 家公司）、痴迷于关系密度而非交易密度——本质上是把 20 世纪科学革命的"小圈子拓扑"移植到风险资本的架构上。这与传统 VC 追求"deal flow 广度"的模式完全相反。她不是在做一家更好的 A16z，她是在做一个"资本化的哥本哈根"。

隐藏的系统性真相：她的"直觉先行、反向补齐"其实是贝叶斯狩猎

她自述的决策模式极具启发：从 8/9 分开始，然后花几周时间搜寻"能把我拉下来的证据"。这看起来像是过度自信，但在信息论意义上，这是一种更高效的搜索策略——它假设你的先验是丰富的（高年龄段的人脉、多年的模式识别），然后主动寻找反证而非累积正证。

这与访谈中另一个隐藏主题共振：她两次强调"我不想告诉别人他们想听的话"（无论对 LP 还是对被投企业）。当你已经在 8 分，你才有资格不粉饰真相——因为你的下行是"降到 3 分放弃"，而不是"从 0 分挤到 8 分"。这解释了为什么大多数机构投资者难以复制她：他们的整个组织结构都是"climb to conviction"型的（层层评审、逐步加码），而她的模型是"start high, hunt for exits"型的。前者产生共识，后者产生 alpha。

一个尚未被讨论的暗线：她所有的判断都在"押注反循环性"

从生物学（"你不能在药厂只卖软件"——她说错了）到半导体（"venture 支持的半导体是烂生意"——她说过时了）到机器人（"数据永远不够"——她说创造性收集就够了）——她每一个具有回报意义的赌注，都是在赌"陈规已死"。

这里有一个跨领域的联想：这与 Renaissance 大奖章基金对"市场教条"的态度完全同构。Simons 团队的核心信念是"任何被普遍接受的市场规律都在被自身的接受度所侵蚀"。Sarah 在做的是同类型的工作——她在寻找"共识信念的半衰期"，并在信念崩塌前 12–24 个月介入。所以她不是"AI 投资者"，她本质上是一个"共识失效检测器"，只不过这个时代最富集失效共识的领域碰巧叫 AI。

开场：一个疾速旋转、无法回测的时代

It is a violently competitive landscape. I think people are very concerned that it is a globally competitive landscape. That there is a really important fundamental thing happening between a couple of labs in AI and kind of everybody else, and that we need to sort of take up arms to make sure we don't end up in a very monolithic outcome. Do you think about it that way?

关于"伟大女性"：她为何选择不做主角

Do you actively want to be a great woman in this sense of the theory?

No. And I I don't mean that from a personal humility perspective. It was just — it's not in my set of goals, right? I want to be the best investor in the things that I try to do. So it's not out of a lack of ambition or even confidence. It's — I think some people are driven by "I want to be the person that made this happen."

And my realization — I thought I was going to be a software entrepreneur for the longest time. My decision that from an identity perspective I was going to be an investor actually had a lot to do with the idea of: I'm deeply curious. I like to understand things. I like to be right. And then I care — I'm very motivated by working with extraordinary people, and if I have a set of skills, using those to make them more successful. That looks like a pretty good fit for early-stage investing.

If I want to work with the very best people, and I want the companies to have impact, the firm can support a movement and support change we want to see — but I don't think it has to be me.

If that's the goal, what does it take, do you think, right now to be the best in a very competitive environment?

And you had this massive technology transition happening. If you took the bet on understanding the technology and the community and approached it from first principles, you might have better access and make better decisions than others who are less focused.

So all you have to do is take the risk and be focused, and then it's an execution play. That's one of those things that I think is pretty simple and it's just hard. It's effort.

250 个人：一张覆盖前沿的关系网

Your partner Mike said something interesting to me a couple weeks ago, which was: there's sort of 250-ish people that he thinks about — some combination of entrepreneurs and researchers doing the most interesting things on the frontier. Just like the people that are actually showing up in the morning and pushing this whole thing forward. And one of your goals as a firm is to be as close to those people, know them all, and support them in as many ways as possible.

I really like that idea. So it just feels like, from the outside looking in, there's more unique stuff going on than just "the competition set was low and we focused more."

To the point of perhaps making a bet that others wouldn't — we thought very carefully about what markets are going to matter, and what might be different about the founders that we look at in this era, if we are right about capability growth and the breadth of impact. If you look at Harvey and the function of the law: rationally, if you think that we can do next-token prediction with language, and you knew that in late 2022 — then law is structured language.
