And everybody, you know, keeps thinking it's going to really standardize. And if you look at the three big, you know, Chinese open source models, Deepseek, Kimmy, Quinn, they're kind of all um evolving in very different ways.

Yeah.

And they can, you know, they can all run on, you know, a more general purpose chip, um, a GPU, but you're going to need, if you want to specialize,

Yeah. You're going to need general purposes at a minimum for the types of evolution you see from that. Yeah.

So, um like I think he's I'm very happy his incentives as a CEO are perfectly aligned with what's good for America.

Yes.

Um so I just make sure your semiconductor guys do [laughter] not talk trash about Michael Jordan.

Be nice to be nice to MJ. Be nice to MJ. Yeah. Exactly.

Yeah. And then it's like, you know, sometimes it's like, you know, you tug on Superman's cape and you get confident.

Yeah.

You know, you get confident and you start to talk a little bit of trash. Well, you know, Superman sometimes he just flies away like that's what happened to the TPU team.

Yeah. You know, and you know, Jalapeno, they're tugging on Superman's cape a little bit.

Yeah. We'll see.

We'll see. And it is kind of amazing that like

Jalapeno did something that none of the big

like I this is as competitive of a chip as I have seen. Yeah.

But again, it's just competitive with one of his eight or nine chips.

Yeah. One of his nine. Yeah, of course.

They'll continue to work closely together. Yes.

Yeah. They'll continue to work closely together. So, it's like, hey, that's great. You did the one thing. Well, to actually be competitive with him at the system level, you need another eight chips.

Yeah. Exactly.

二十五、Jensen 是 "AI 的中央银行"：三种客户偏好信号

Yeah.

Um and he is at and you know, Dylan at some analysis talks about how he's the bank of AI. He's like he's the central bank of AI. He's the Federal Reserve of AI. Yeah.

And so I actually think it was really smart for Elon instead of like

competing, you know, with somebody who is

fully aligned.

Yeah. Fully aligned.

Mhm.

And I think that history is going to judge that to be a wise decision.

In a world that is so supply chain constrained, it's actually really hard to tell what true customer preferences are right?

Because like you come out,

Yeah. they'll take anything. Yeah. This is this is how you know that like very old whatever the price is held up of H100 is very high.

Yeah. Yeah. And if you have a TSM allocation, you're going to be sold out. Yes.

Particularly if you can get the DRAM to pair with it. You're going to be sold out.

So, it's actually kind of hard to infer true customer preferences.

And I actually think one of the best ways you can like see true customer preferences is the kind of deals they cut with chip companies. So, broadly speaking, you know, the first deal is where the chip company invests

Yep.

in a customer. And you saw TPU and Tranium, Amazon and Google do that with Anthropic. Yep. And that was to their im immense advantage because it really helped their businesses, I think, helped those chips really level up because you kind of need to use a chip. There's a cold start problem.

And [clears throat] um and in that scenario, as long as the dollars you invest are less than the gross profit, you can't lose money.

And then there's a scenario where you do the RVG, Blackstone finances it or whoever, Blackstone, Apollo, KKR, Goldman Sachs finances it. Um, and as long as that RVG is actually less than your gross profit, you can't lose money and you have upside probably through a revenue share on top of it,

then there are deals where you give warrants away, but they're tied to um like a fixed price per million tokens. And as long as the performance of your chip kind of outruns the performance of your stock,

you're going to do good in that situation. If you just give warrants away, it could be negative NPV because the better the does the more value that's captured by the person. Yeah.

Yeah. And so you can kind of look at that hierarchy of deals and like infer something about true customer preferences.

Yes. That's interesting.

Yeah.

So Nvidia does pretty good deals.

Uh like Yeah. I mean there's a reason that people I consider smart are investing in their deals.

结束

Yeah, I see it. Gavin, thank you. Fun. Always fun to hang with you.

Thanks, David. This was great, man.

item.description:
## 一、被忽视的"债务结构逆转"：AI 正在把资本主义的杠杆逻辑倒转过来
大多数人看到 Blackstone、KKR、Apollo 在给数据中心做债务融资，第一反应是"这像不像 2008 年的次贷"。但真正令人意外的观察是：**在 AI 领域，债务的时间价值方向被反转了**。
传统债务融资建立在一个假设上——资产会折旧、贬值、变旧。但 Gavin 提到了一个被忽视的数据点：**GPU 的"有效使用寿命在延长"**。因为模型每变强一代，同一块 GPU 上跑出的 token 变现率就同步上升。这意味着这些"抵押物"在被使用的过程中不是变旧，而是**升值**。
这是人类金融史上罕见的一种资产类别：一台机器，越用越值钱，越旧越赚钱。它更像一座随人流增加而升值的商业地产——但速度快了 100 倍。你在给一个通缩型硬件（Starship 让发射成本崩塌）加杠杆去承载一个通胀型现金流（token 单价可能涨 10 倍）。**这是巴菲特意义上的完美生意结构，只是它披着"资本密集重工业"的外皮，让所有人都误读了它。**
## 二、跨领域连接：AI 基建的政治叙事失败，本质是"零售业教科书问题"

item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一个反直觉的观察：这场"AI 牛市"的本质是"防御板块的隐性转型"

最让我意外的是——市场表面上被 AI 叙事主导，但真正被 AI 悄悄重构的，恰恰是被贴上"超卖/防御"标签的板块。小陶提到 XLU 公共事业和 XLI 工业已经"不再是传统意义上的公共事业和工业"，Caterpillar、GE Vernova 都在享受 AI 上涨。这意味着一个隐藏事实：如果你现在买入"最悲观的防御板块"，你实际上在通过折扣价买入 AI 敞口。市场情绪把它们打到低位，是因为投资者的心理标签还停留在旧分类学里——这是分类惰性造成的定价错误。VST（他自己的持仓）就是最典型的例子：核电公司挂在"公共事业"标签下，估值锚被拴在防御属性上，但它的现金流已经开始由 AI 数据中心的电力需求驱动。

一个跨领域的连接：1.3 万亿美元 CapEx = 2008 年中国的"四万亿"翻版

小陶把英伟达老黄的 1.3 万亿资本开支和 2008-2009 年中国四万亿基建做类比，这个类比比他自己讲得还要深刻。共同结构是：一个中心化的"确定性需求"，被强行注入一个原本供给端已经紧张的系统，最终溢出为通胀。 中国四万亿溢出到大宗商品和房价；美国 1.3 万亿正在溢出到——注意这个惊人的传导链——苹果手机的涨价。因为数据中心抢占了 memory 产能。这意味着我们正在见证一个前所未有的现象：AI 基建的通胀不是通过工资传导，而是通过"物理硅片挤占"传导。传统菲利普斯曲线在这里失灵，通胀的锚从劳动力市场转移到了"晶圆产能"。美联储的思考框架如果还停留在就业-通胀的老范式，就会持续错判。

隐藏的系统性真相：三个"平衡"信号在讲同一个故事

把小陶散落的几个数据点拼起来，会浮现一个惊人的整体图景： - JOLTS 空缺回到 2018 年水平 = 劳动力市场"表面回到疫情前" - ECI 工资增速 3.4% = 但成本结构"永久性抬高了 0.7 个百分点" - 退休率从 15.5% → 20% = 供给端结构性收缩

这三个数据合起来讲的不是"经济正常化"，而是"劳动力市场用更少的人达到了旧的平衡，但价格更贵了"。这是一个"缩水但更贵"的经济体——就像疫情后餐厅份量变小但价格更高。通胀 2% 的时代已经结构性死亡了，但市场和美联储还在用旧目标做锚。这也解释了为什么小陶说"加一次息、加两次息都合理"——因为真正的问题不是要不要降息，而是2%这个数字本身已经过时。

一个出人意料的悖论：特斯拉 160 辆无人车的"分子级现实"

在所有宏大叙事里，最扎心的是小陶提到的这个数字：特斯拉全美所有城市加起来只有 160 辆完全无人驾驶的车在跑。这个数字与市值、与 Cyber Cab Day 的期待、与马斯克的宏大叙事之间形成了荒诞的落差。这揭示了一个更普遍的系统性真相：在 AI 时代，叙事的估值和物理部署的规模，其解耦程度达到了历史新高。市场为一个"未来的可能性曲线"定价，而实际部署曲线的斜率还处于早期。这也是为什么小陶宁愿"观察"——他在等待叙事和物理现实收敛的那个拐点，而不是在纯叙事阶段买单。这种耐心，恰恰是这个时代最稀缺的能力。

📝 转录文本

开场：本周关注焦点

上周五的 Jackson Hole 会议让市场上调了 9 月份加息的这个预期。那本周其实还会有非常重要的大非农数据公布。所以今天这期内容我主要就和大家分享一下：

一、现在还有哪些板块相对是便宜的。那么如果要加仓的话，哪些板块可以去考虑，包括里边的一些标的等等。

第二点，我们对于本周将要发布财报的公司去做一个展望，包括宏观数据一起做一个展望，好吗？

欢迎大家来到一个不单只聊新闻的专业美股频道，我是市场分析师小陶。我就废话不多说，大家记得留言点赞加转发。

一、市场参与度：三大指数高位，但情绪并不高

我们先来看一下市场的参与度。即使现在三大指数都是接近于高位，但市场的参与度其实并不高。

  • 纳指这边：20 日均线和 50 日均线分别在 39% 和 44%，是处在一个中性偏悲观的位置。
  • 罗素：20 和 38 和 49，也在一个中性偏悲观的位置。
  • 标普：54 和 2 和 53，处在一个中性的位置。

板块参与度：谁最超卖？

同样还是参与度，如果我们把这个指标延伸到各个板块里边，我按照 20 日均线，最高到最低进行了一个排序。排在最低就代表这个板块相对来说比较悲观。那 again，从 20 均线和 50 均线的这一个指标去出发，指数越低就代表越悲观。

第一名超卖：XLU 公共事业板块

排名所有板块标普 500 里面，排名最后的是 Utility 公共基建板块。那这一个板块，20 均线和 50 均线分别在 10%，也就是仅仅只有 10% 的公司在这个板块里边是在 20 均线和 50 均线以上。所以从参与度这个角度去看，现在 Utility 公共事业板块是在一个非常超卖的位置。10% 其实已经相当低了。

那里边我拿了五个权重股：NEE、SO、DUK、CEG、AEP，这类标题都在里面。那我自己的持仓 VST 也在公共事业板块里面。

第二名超卖：XLP 必需品消费

然后排名倒数第二的，就是相对第二个悲观的，就是必需品消费 XLP。那里边那些权重股是按权重股是最高的，这个占比比重给排序的：沃尔玛、Costco、KO 可口可乐，然后 PG 保洁，还有 PM。那这五家公司是在 XLP 里边排名前五家的。那 Nike 并不在这一个板块里边，但是我知道我自己的持仓 Nike 也是在必需品消费里边。

第三名超卖：XLI 工业板块

然后第三个板块是工业板块 XLY（编者注：应为 XLI）。理论上来说，现在的工业板块，包括 XLU 必需品消费，还是非 AI 板块。但是 XLU 公共事业包括工业板块，其实已经不再是传统的公共事业或者工业板块，都是里边很多的标题都是和 AI 相关的。工业板块就尤为明显。

那 CAT Caterpillar 它是非常明显享受到这一波 AI 的一个上涨；GE 算是和 AI 没有太大的一些关系；RTX、GEV，那 GEV 也是受到了 AI 的这个影响。排名前五的：CAT、GE、RTX、GEV、UNP。

布局建议

所以这三个板块现在仍然是在一个超卖的位置。而且 XLU 是公共事业板块现在是非常的超卖。我在一周前吧，我说公共事业板块可以去进行布局了，那过去这段时间似乎没有上涨，也没有下跌。但是 Again，现在这个位置，你从参与度去看的话，还是在一个非常超卖的一个位置。

所以你如果说你一定要去配置一些仓位去加仓的话，那 XLU 可以是一个考虑的一个标的本身。当然，XLU 的波动不会非常大，你不用期望你今天买入 XLU，在接下去的未来的一年，未来的半年或者一年左右，给你上涨个百分之四十五十——这个概率几乎为零。因为这个板块本身就是偏防守属性的板块，第二点波动非常的小。

然后现在所有板块里面最超买的一个板块就是能源板块。那 20 日均线能源板块在 71%，五日均线能源板块在 90%。

二、半导体板块：投机仓位已大幅离场

在周五的那期视频里面，我和大家分享了 SOX 现在半导体板块的一个估值。那我们来看一下，其实整个 7 月份的一个下跌，多数是杠杆的一个平仓。

韩国指数波动率信号

我们来看一下韩国指数的一个 Volatility Index 它的一个波动率。这条线显示，其实即使在 8 月份的时候，整个指数是出现了反弹，但如果我们把整个 8 月份全放在一起的话，Volatility 波动率仍然在下降。

就代表什么？代表背后投机仓，韩国指数这边，基于韩国指数上的一些投机仓位仍然在离场。截止到上周五的收盘，现在的波动率指数接近于今年三月底当时的一个位置。那也就是告诉我们当下的一个市场，在韩国市场里面一个投机仓位和情绪面现在已经相当低了。

个股杠杆 ETF 换手率断崖式下降

另外一个衡量的指标叫做 leverage ETF，个股的一个杠杆 ETF。其实现在美股里面几乎每一个标的都有杠杆的这个选择在背后，所以个股就会发现它的一个波动会非常的大。然后在这个基础上，个股的杠杆 ETF，然后还有华尔街的一些量化的一些基金，一些机器人的交易，就使得短期市场的波动会非常的大。

那从个股的杠杆 ETF 成交量或者换手率吧，turnover 换手率这一个角度去看，其实在过去四周，这每一根柱状体代表是过去一周的一个走势，可以看到过去四周 Single Stock 个股的杠杆 ETF 的一个换手率断崖式下降。

所以这两张图告诉我们呢：虽然 8 月份半导体板块是出现了反弹然后又下跌，但是从投机仓位这个角度去看，情绪面其实已经相当低了。

三、本周财报展望

然后我们就一起来对本周将要发布财报的公司来做一个展望。周一还好，周二的盘后就会有非常重要的一些公司发布财报：

周二盘后：CRDO、Dell、Palo Alto、Palantir、MongoDB

Palo Alto，Palantir 是在我上一个季度财报我去听了，听完之后他们的管理层有聊到，现在 Enterprise Commerce AI Agent 这一块其实根本就还没有起来。企业对于 AI 这一块 B 端这一块，B 端对于 AI 的一个接受程度其实刚刚才开始起来。那所以这个季度财报我们可以有一个更新。

从软件板块，软件公司的一个财报里面，我们已经看到软件公司已经开始 monetize，已经开始去变现了。所以我希望从 Palantir 的一个财报里边，也可以听到一部分 AI 落地在 B 端这一块落地的一些进程。

MongoDB 也是一家软件公司，那过去几周发布财报的软件公司涨幅都非常的好。我们可以看一下 MongoDB 是不是对他们也是一个利好。GitHub（编者注：应为其他公司）也是在周外的盘后发布财报。

周三盘后：Broadcom、HPE、Snowflake

周三的盘后又是一个重点：Broadcom。那博通我在上一周无论是直播的时候，还是上周五的视频里面，我已经聊过博通的估值。我认为博通的估值现在是在一个低位，且我并不认为短时间之内——起码一年半的时间之内——我并不认为 Marvell 可以对于博通造成任何的这个影响。

那么从谷歌这个角度，他们去分散未来的供应链，那这个供应链是我们要讨论这一年半两年之后的这个供应链。短期之内 Marvell 对于博通是不会造成任何的影响。而且博通自己本身也在分散他们客户过于集中的这个风险。

然后周三的盘后还有 HPE、Snowflake。

周四盘后：UiPath、DocuSign、ZS、Lululemon

周四的盘后：UiPath、DocuSign、ZS、露露柠檬。不同的行业的公司都有。虽然第二季度的财报解读基本已经结束了，但这一周发布财报的一些公司还是非常值得我们去关注，有和 AI 相关的，有和软件相关的，有一些传统的一些公司像露露柠檬。

四、特斯拉：9 月 3 日 Cybertruck Cap Day 前瞻

那除了发布财报的公司以外，9 月 3 日特斯拉还会有一个 Cybertruck Cap Day。其实特斯拉的基本面我还是有一些追踪，但是没有那么的紧。

因为很多人一直问我：你年初减仓特斯拉，这个仓位什么时候会加回来？暂时我还没有找到这个机会。当然交易的话也许会有机会。

无人驾驶的物理现实

今天我特地去更新了一下，现在因为网上是有追踪的，特斯拉现在到底有多少辆完全无人驾驶的车在路上去跑。在过去这段时间，我们可以看到这条曲线上升的速率还是非常的快，但是到现在为止，就根据人们的追踪，差不多现在特斯拉也仅仅——所有的城市全部加在一起——仅仅只有 160 辆车是在运营的。

技术面 vs 基本面

如果说从技术面然后结合本周的一个消息面这个角度去看，那特斯拉是有可能会去补掉前段时间下跌的这个缺口，是在 370 左右。周五的一个收盘价格是在 350。所以从瑞思罗（编者注：Risk-Reward）这个角度，如果你要去读比如说本周的这个事件的话，也可以。那么下面做好一个止损，然后上面是有可能会突破。

但是从基本面这个角度去看，或者从投资从长期投资这个角度去看，暂时我还没有非常舒适的可以说：噢，我现在这个位置就可以把年初减仓特斯拉这个仓位给捡回来。除非我看到有非常明显基本面的这个改善。那即使在这种情况下，即使在右侧，我是愿意去接回来，但是暂时到现在我还没有想，或者还没有非常的舒适说可以把特斯拉仓位给加回来。

如果我有找到这个……所以我现在没有一个非常明确的点位，你现在问我我不知道这个点位，但是我会根据一些事件出来，包括一些情绪面出来之后，会去做出一些调整。

在 7 月底那一波下跌的时候，我和大家分享过我的一个期待：是从技术面这个角度，RSI 不破新低，然后价格去破一个新低，但是最终却没有看到。那没有看到就算了，那么这一类的机会，而且也就是从底部反弹多少百分之十左右，那么所以其实并没有差太多。

但是如果技术面上没有这个机会，然后基本面我也没有看到一个非常明显的一个入场点，情绪面我也没有看到非常的悲观，反而大家其实对于 Cyber Cap Day 非常的期待。这时候的话，我个人愿意做的就是去观察。如果交易层面有些机会的话，我也会给大家分享。

五、宏观展望：非农 vs CPI，美联储更看重哪个？

最后我们回到宏观这边。那本周其实有两组比较重要的数据：一组是求职 index，就业上的空缺职位；另外一组就是在本周五将要公布的大非农数据和失业率。

非农预期与美联储的思考框架

市场预期是在 5.5 万，彭博他们的预期是在 1.2 万。说实话，即使是 0 增速也好，5 万也好，1 万也好，即使负增速也好，对于市场暂时的影响，其实我认为没有那么的大。

那 Nick 有说到，包括彭博他们的这个团队也有说到，他说这一次大非农有可能会低于市场的预期，所以会影响到美联储在 9 月份是不是加息这个决定。但是明显现在美联储的这个——他们背后的一个思考框架里面，一定是放更多的重点在通胀上面。

那所以如果出现这种情况：如果比如说大非农数据比市场预期要低，甚至于是负的，但是 CPI 数据比市场预期要高，那这两者之间你觉得能不能抵消呢？我觉得是不能抵消的。因为美联储更加担心通胀的这个反弹，比起一个有可能会进入衰退的一个劳动力市场。

所以现在在美联储的视角里面：劳动力市场是平衡的，一组数据出来是 0 增长也好、负增长也好，不会影响到他们的决定。但是通胀数据如果比市场预期要高的话，他们可能就会比较的警觉和有些紧张。所以这两者之间对于美联储最终做决定的这个影响，现在这个占比是不一样的，美联储更加倾向于关注通胀这一块。

失业率这一块市场预期是在 4.1%，彭博 Anandone 的这个团队预期是在 4.2%。

JOLTS：劳动力市场已回到疫情前

然后我们来看这张图。这张图是 JOLTS index。那我其实拿这张图并不是我们要去预测本周的 JOLTS index 到底在什么样的一个位置，而是我们其实看一个趋势。我这边是过去 11 年的一个走势，你可以看到现在求职 index 就业场的空缺职位，基本上回到了疫情之前的这个水平，在 2018 年的一个高位。

所以从这个角度去看，就整个劳动力市场，从 JOLTS Index 这个角度去看，基本上已经达到了一个平衡的阶段，回到了疫情之前。

工资增速 ECI：仍高于疫情前

然后另外一个角度，一，我们看了座位上的空缺职位，然后我们来看一下工资增速。我和大家分享过工资增速里面最重要的一组数据，或者最好的一组衡量数据是什么？ECI，那么 Employment Cost Index，每一个季度公布一次，然后一个季度环比增速把它年化。

最新公布的这一组数据，一季度的数据是在同比增速年化之后的一个同比增速是在 3.4%。你可以看到从最高点的 5% 的确出现了下降——工资增速。但是比疫情之前的 3% 不到，接近 2.8%、2.7%，还是高出了 0.7 至 0.8 左右。

如果说工资增速平衡在一个百分之三点三、三点四这个位置的话，且我们前面看到劳动力市场已经趋近于平衡了，那在这种情况下，我认为接下去 GDP，你说 GDP 要进入一个负增长，或者消费者的消费能力不行，我觉得得不出这个结论。反而是通胀可能回不到 2%，因为工资增速比疫情之前要高。

即使我们可能从各个渠道 anecdotal 的，对吧，听到一些可能经济要进入衰退，劳动力市场不行，消费者不行。但是最好的一个最大范围的衡量劳动力市场的一个指标，真的是没有之一啊，就是 ECI（Employment Cost Index），工资增速现在还比疫情之前要高。如果劳动力市场真的非常的差，工资增速绝对要比疫情之前要低的，你不会看到比疫情之前还要高的工资增速——百分之三点四。

那工资增速如果长期可以保持在百分之三点四、三点五、三点三的话，那就告诉我们通胀很难会回到疫情之前的百分之二。

长周期视角：美国人口老龄化与退休率

最后我们来看一组相对比较长周期的一组数据。我们不要拿这组数据去做任何的一个短期判断，它是一个非常长的一个周期，从一个退后一步去看，起码是未来的 5~10 年这个角度了。

这组数据是什么？这组数据是美国劳动力人口的一个退休率，退休的一个比率。可以看到从 2009 年之后，这一个退休的比率一直在上升。疫情这段时间，图里蓝色这条线，然后橘色这条线是一个趋势。蓝色这条线可以看到疫情之后突然退休率——就退休的这个人数的一个占比出现了上升——但是经过一段时间的一个修正之后，再次回到了这条橘色的一条趋势上面。

而且你如果看左边那样 Y 轴的话，你可以看到退休的比率从 16% 疫情之前的，呃，09 年的 16%，15.5/16，一直上升到现在的 20%。

这张图说明了什么问题？其实说明了整个美国人口结构的一个老龄化。当然其他国家、其他发达国家也可以看到同样的一个趋势。但是我要提醒一下大家，就这个人口的一个老龄化，其实告诉我们在劳动力上的一个供给端可能没有那么的足。那供给端如果没有那么的足，就这张图里可以引出的一个结论是通常有可能持续保持在高位。它其实是这样的一个结论，因为劳动力上的一个供给端受到退休率的这个影响。

那但是我们这边要注意到，它从什么时候开始上升？从 09 年就开始上升。但是在 09 年至 19 年这十年期间，那即使退休率出现上升，从 15.5% 上升到了 18%，但是在这段时间里边，我们并没有看到通胀。

六、通胀的三重推力：AI、工资、CapEx

那我个人对于通胀的这个判断：

下行推力：AI 对劳动力的替代

首先通胀下行的这个因素可以是——因为未来如果企业，广泛的这个企业，他们对于 AI 有这个接受在那边，AI adoption 在企业之间如果上升的话，是有可能会对于劳动力上的下行形成一个推力。那么企业通过增加他们的 IT 这一块的花费，去取代一部分的人工。

因为现在 AI 的一个扩散程度还非常的小，非常的局限。这是有可能会对于……会使得失业率会开始出现上升，然后劳动力上出现下行。这是一点。

上行推力一：工资增速仍偏高

但是同时另外一点我们看到的是，当下劳动力市场的一个工资增速仍然还是保持在高于疫情之前的这个水平。

上行推力二：1.3 万亿资本开支

第二点，明年所有的公司，包括科技公司，包括大科技加在一起资本开支，英伟达上次给了老黄说 1.3 万亿。我在上一年我就有在思考这个问题，对于——诶，整个这一次 AI capex 对于通胀的这个影响。

1.3 万亿可以理解为是美国政府或者美国财政部的一个撒钱，或者大范围的造基建；也可以理解为是 08、09 年之后中国政府的一个 4 万亿的一个基建。那在那段时间之后，也无非就是政府花钱，然后现在是企业花——美国这边是企业花钱嘛。那政府花钱 4 万亿的基建之后，那后面那一段时间，我们看到中国出现了非常大的一个通胀。

当然从体量这个角度，1.3 万亿的一个资本花费已经是非常高的这个体量。当然了，就这个资本花费也不是全部花在美国的企业身上，所以对于美国的企业的通胀影响不能说是 1.3 万亿全部是造成这个影响。但是势必美国这边的数据中心建造完之后，你会发现数据中心对于很多其他的一些 3C 产品也造成了挤压，特别是 memory 这一块，比如说苹果产品的这个涨价等等。

我认为或多或少对于美国这边的通胀一定是一个向上的一个推力。所以我认为接下去的通胀很难会回到以前的一个 2%。

总结判断

美联储你说你加一次息、加两次息，我认为都是合理的，那只要不打开加息周期，都是 OK 的。那主要向上的这个推力：一，来自于资本开支；第二点，来自于劳动力市场现在的工资增速仍然是保持在高于疫情之前的这个水平。

当然接下去我们看要看 AI 的这个落地。如果 AI 落地落得非常的好，是有可能会出现企业增加了 AI 这一块的花费，然后去取代一部分的人工，导致劳动力市场出现一个下行。

所以整个市场是在一个变动，是在一个是 dynamic，那它是变化非常的快。所以我们还是需要时刻去关注这个市场，包括 AI 这一块的一个落地，对于劳动力市场的影响，对于股市这边，对于不同行业之间的这个影响。

结语与活动

最后，今天要带给大家的活动是 Vivo 微牛证券。温友证券在美国其实做的很好，大家如果有了解的话应该并不陌生。

  • 美国市场这边现在通过开户且入金，只要入金 100 美金啊，就可以获得 12 股免费的股票，抽取的这个金额最低是 36 美金，最高可以达到 3600 美金。那同时还可以获得一个月免费的 Vivo Premium 订阅。
  • 加拿大这边通过开户且入金，最高可以获得 250 加币的这个返现，入金 500 就可以获得 50 加币的这个返现。

大家如果感兴趣的话，可以在置顶的留言里边找到开户的链接。那今天这期内容就到这边，下期见。

item.description:
## 一个反直觉的观察：这场"AI 牛市"的本质是"防御板块的隐性转型"
最让我意外的是——市场表面上被 AI 叙事主导，但**真正被 AI 悄悄重构的，恰恰是被贴上"超卖/防御"标签的板块**。小陶提到 XLU 公共事业和 XLI 工业已经"不再是传统意义上的公共事业和工业"，Caterpillar、GE Vernova 都在享受 AI 上涨。这意味着一个隐藏事实：**如果你现在买入"最悲观的防御板块"，你实际上在通过折扣价买入 AI 敞口**。市场情绪把它们打到低位，是因为投资者的心理标签还停留在旧分类学里——这是分类惰性造成的定价错误。VST（他自己的持仓）就是最典型的例子：核电公司挂在"公共事业"标签下，估值锚被拴在防御属性上，但它的现金流已经开始由 AI 数据中心的电力需求驱动。
## 一个跨领域的连接：1.3 万亿美元 CapEx = 2008 年中国的"四万亿"翻版
小陶把英伟达老黄的 1.3 万亿资本开支和 2008-2009 年中国四万亿基建做类比，这个类比比他自己讲得还要深刻。**共同结构是：一个中心化的"确定性需求"，被强行注入一个原本供给端已经紧张的系统，

item.title: [Dwarkesh Clips] Who Captures the Value Created by AI? - Dylan Patel
item.dc:creator: Dwarkesh Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被忽视的"价值捕获波"：AI栈里的孤立波现象

Dylan 描述的"价值捕获在栈里到处漂移"其实有个更深刻的比喻——它像流体力学里的孤立波（soliton）：一个能量包在介质中传播，永远跑在观察者预期的前面。

2023年价值在HBM内存；2024年跑到台积电又跑到英伟达；2025年到了模型层；现在Dylan告诉你，波峰其实早已越过模型层，冲到了Jane Street 和 Meta 的广告算法里。

让人不安的洞见：如果这个波真的存在，那么现在所有押注"OpenAI/Anthropic 会成为下一个Google"的人，等于是在波峰已经过去后才冲进海里。真正的巨额价值捕获永远发生在栈的下一层——一个还没被市场命名的层。这可能是"AI原生金融套利者"，也可能是"注意力操纵者"，甚至是"AI能耗套利者"（下一段会讲）。

二、马斯克的算力操作：这不是AI故事，是1999年的暗光纤重演

Dylan 讲 SpaceX 把算力以 $40M/MW 卖给 Google/Anthropic，市场价却只有 $20M——这不是AI叙事，这是电信业2000年前后暗光纤（dark fiber）套利的原样复刻。

当年 Global Crossing 和 Level 3 疯狂铺光纤没有客户，破产。但活下来的、能囤积光纤的玩家（Google 早期就是靠白菜价扫的暗光纤搭起全球骨干网）——他们捕获了下一个二十年的互联网价值。

跨领域连接的惊人之处：Meta 和 SpaceX 现在扮演的角色不是AI公司，是"AI时代的Google暗光纤交易者"。他们用资产负债表囤积算力，然后在别人的融资周期被卡住时，以3倍价格出货。这意味着——AI最赚钱的玩家可能既不做模型，也不做芯片，而是做算力做市商。这个角色在传统金融里叫"prime broker"，在AI栈里目前还没有名字。

三、"百万AI工程师=1000亿美元"的荒诞算术：GDP会说谎

Dylan 那段被Dwarkesh笑着接过去的计算——"一个吉瓦养一百万白领 × 10万美元 = 1000亿"——其实藏着一个AI经济学界都在回避的哲学问题：

当边际认知劳动力的供给趋近于无限时，"工资"这个价格信号就会崩溃。

想象一下：一百万个软件工程师同时上线，他们生产的软件价值不是一百万个人类工程师工资的加总。因为软件工程师的工资本来就是人类稀缺性溢价——不是他们创造的价值，是他们的不可替代性。

让你意外的观察：如果AI真的能替代白领，那么测量AI价值的正确单位不是"节省的工资"，而是"被解锁的、之前因为人力成本而不做的事情"。Jane Street 用 Claude 赚的钱 >> 他们付给 Anthropic 的钱，这不是"AI效率高"，而是Jane Street 之前根本不做的策略，现在因为边际认知成本崩塌而变得可行。

这直接指向一个悖论：AI越强大，模型层越难捕获价值。因为强AI创造的价值大多来自"以前不可能做的新事情"，而这些新事情的收益天然属于发起这些新事情的实体（用户），而不是提供认知的实体（模型）。这就是为什么Dylan说"目前大部分价值给了用户"——这不是暂时现象，这是智能商品化的结构性宿命。

📝 转录文本

如果AI真能取代白领：一个惊人保守的估算

What if the AI models were literally as good as a fully automated software engineer? They're not currently there yet, right? Like I think they're far from just being able to fully automate the job of like a full white-collar worker. But white-collar workers earn, you know, six figures or north of that a year.

Um, and if you have a gigawatt that can sustain a population of like, say, a million uh white-collar workers. It just — let's, let's say roughly, right? Um, that's like — you could then off the back of that — that would be 100 billion. That's actually surprisingly low.

[laughter] Yeah, 100k per person, million population yeah. Yeah, yeah, yeah.

Um — I don't know. But it'd be many hundreds of billions of dollars if you get like full AGI uh per per gigawatt.

价值都跑去哪了：不是OpenAI，是用户

Other aspect of this is, and we've continued to see this, that most of the value capture is not happening, right? Like most of the value that these models generate does not get given to OpenAI and Anthropic. Um, thankfully so far, it is mostly just being given to the users.

Yeah, yeah.

Right? Jane Street with their exclusive contract with OpenAI for GPT-5.6 ultra-fast mode, or Jane Street where they're like one of Anthropic's biggest customers — is generating way, way, way, way more value out of the [snorts] tokens they're paying for than Anthropic is uh generating in terms of profit, right? Cuz they get to, you know, make money off of the market.

Um, or Meta, who at one point was, you know, rumored to be, you know, as much as 10% of Anthropic's business — um, you know, they're generating way more efficiencies by optimizing their ad algorithms or what have you, and getting engagement time 5% longer, and you know, all these things. They're making way more money off of using these models than than Anthropic. And so, ultimately, you know — and that's what's required. So, sure, if you had a million new software engineers, the cost for software engineer would also fall.

市场会均衡吗？算力与模型收益的诡异裂口

One thing I'm confused about is — does the market come into equilibrium? And if it comes into equilibrium, would you just expect the price of compute to equal whatever Anthropic and OpenAI can generate from it, or be very close to it with like a small amount of markup for Anthropic and OpenAI?

Like right now it's really weird that there is a 4x or more difference between what compute sells for and how much money Anthropic can make from it. And in the world where the revenue per gigawatt continues to increase, if Anthropic's ability to monetize a gigawatt doubles or triples or something, it'd be weird if then the gap continued to increase. And so Anthropic just by like having some software, having some weights, can take something that cost them $10 and then turn it into $100.

价值捕获在AI栈里到处漂移

Yeah, so there's a bit of um — this is always a fun question, right? Which is: where does the value go in AI?

AI is generating all this value. You've got, you know, the end user, which I think we all agree is generating more value than anyone else, hence they're paying a lot for these models. But then you have, you know, the app layer. Well, so far the app layer has generated very little value.

Um, then you've got the model layer, which again up until a year ago was generating negative gross margins and is now generating massive positive gross margins. Um, and looks like it's on the path to generating, you know, $100 million per megawatt. Um, so turning, you know, $10-$15 into $100 as you said.

Um, but if we go back again a year ago, the hardware supply chain was generating all this gross margin while literally everyone else was losing money on it. Um, OpenAI and Anthropic were just plowing VC money in. Um, and as were many other startups and many of these hyperscalers — building infrastructure without knowing if there was going to be a payoff.

Um, so ultimately you had this like, you know, negative value being created on the model layer almost, if you will — um, because they were selling the tokens for less than it cost them on the infra side. And all the value was being created — used at the chip, the fab. Initially in 2023, the memory guys were making no money off of, you know, HBM or memory for AI, even though theoretically the value they were delivering was humongous.

Now you've got — well, actually TSMC makes way less value than the memory guys. Um, is that actually how much you know, they're capturing less value even though — So, the value capture has shifted around a lot, which is very fun for um, people tracking the market or participating in the market like Jane Street as an example.

[laughter] There's no need — there's no need to plug them that hard. Um [laughter]

Elon 的算力套利：40M/MW 卖给对手，一年回本

So, you know, what happens going forward? Does Anthropic and OpenAI, you know, they've slowly started to balloon in value capture. Do they balloon and take all the value capture?

Well, that was a thought — and then Elon showed actually no, I can sell my compute for $25 million a megawatt or $40 a megawatt to Anthropic and Google. Even if it's a short-term thing, I've sold it for this price and I'll recoup my entire capex in a year.

So, what's your prediction of how much the relevant Toronto compute, like B300s or whatever, that sold for 40B a gigawatt, that SpaceX sold for 40B a gigawatt to Google — what does that sell for at the end of next year?

I think most compute will still continue to transact at sub $20 a gigawatt.

Even at the end of next year?

Because all of it has to be financed. For compute that you can build without financing, right? If Meta can build compute, Microsoft, Amazon, SpaceX can build compute without finding a customer — just saying [ __ ] it, I'm going to build this compute and then turn around and wait till it's already built — they now control what's going on. So most compute is contracted well before it's built.

Yeah, yeah.

And so this is sort of what Elon took advantage of in the market. He actually had all this compute and he was like, "Hey Anthropic, I know you're making like 60 plus billion dollars per gigawatt. Why don't you just buy my stuff for a crazy amount of money?"

And obviously, you know, it's not like Elon decided this or Anthropic decided this — it's sort of the market figured itself out.

融资结构决定权力结构：为什么 Meta 和 SpaceX 是隐藏第三极

Other people, you know, you go to a random cloud, they're like, "Okay, I'm going to build a gigawatt of compute or 100 megawatts of compute. I'm going to spend the capex. I need to turn around and find a customer. If I want to find a customer, I need to find the capital. Who's going to give me the capital and the customer? The customer has to sign a deal, and then I take the customer's commitment to the credit markets, and I raise the capital."

And so, there's this sort of like completely different power structure where Meta, who is effectively hoarding compute — them and SpaceX — are plausibly the like number three. And the only plausible number three is because they're hoarding all this compute. They're using their balance sheets and capabilities to build compute — to build compute without end customer — that's monetizing at a huge degree.

And they have an actual balance sheet, so they can go to the credit market and being like, "Hey guys, I have, you know — you build a megawatt, you can make, you know, your margin, not a crazy margin, but you can make a good margin, and I now have all this compute."

And now Meta and SpaceX have this optionality of looking around and being like, "Is my internal use case going to make me more money, or should I go out there and sell it to Anthropic / OpenAI at crazy margins?"

Yeah. So, now we've sort of entered a regime where um SpaceX and Meta are saying, "Actually, I'm going to build the compute, and I can start to rent it out for not 13, I can sell it for 25, 50, and more."

If you enjoyed this clip, you can watch the full episode here and subscribe for more clips. Thanks.

item.description:
## 一、被忽视的"价值捕获波"：AI栈里的孤立波现象
Dylan 描述的"价值捕获在栈里到处漂移"其实有个更深刻的比喻——它像流体力学里的**孤立波（soliton）**：一个能量包在介质中传播，永远跑在观察者预期的前面。
2023年价值在HBM内存；2024年跑到台积电又跑到英伟达；2025年到了模型层；现在Dylan告诉你，波峰其实早已越过模型层，冲到了**Jane Street 和 Meta 的广告算法**里。
**让人不安的洞见**：如果这个波真的存在，那么现在所有押注"OpenAI/Anthropic 会成为下一个Google"的人，等于是在波峰已经过去后才冲进海里。真正的巨额价值捕获永远发生在栈的**下一层**——一个还没被市场命名的层。这可能是"AI原生金融套利者"，也可能是"注意力操纵者"，甚至是"AI能耗套利者"（下一段会讲）。
## 二、马斯克的算力操作：这不是AI故事，是1999年的暗光纤重演
Dylan 讲 SpaceX 把算力以 $40M/MW 卖给 Google/Anthropic，市场价却只有 $20M——这不是AI叙事，这是**电信业2000

item.title: [a16z] $1,1,00,000,000. The Machine Age Fund | a16z
item.dc:creator: a16z
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一个被藏起来的隐喻：他们不叫"AI 时代"，而叫"Machine Age"

最让人意外的，不是这支 11 亿美元的基金规模，而是它的名字——Machine Age。这个词组来自 1920—1940 年代，是对钢铁、电力、流水线的礼赞，而不是对"信息"或"智能"的致敬。a16z 有意绕开了"AI Fund"、"Intelligence Fund"这类命名，选择了一个带着重金属味道的旧词。这暴露了他们真正押注的东西：这轮机会的本质不是软件，而是一次物理世界的重工业化。当所有人还在讨论 GPT 会不会取代白领时，a16z 已经在讲电网、变压器、冷却塔、砂子。这是把 AI 从"云"里拽回"地"上的一次估值重构。

牛顿隐喻的黑色反讽：他们在完成一个被历史判定为失败的项目

发言人用牛顿花 20 年寻找"贤者之石"来类比 AI，这句话表面是浪漫化，实际上是一次极其精妙的风险叙事重写。要知道，牛顿的炼金术研究在他死后被视为职业污点，凯恩斯买下那批手稿后曾说"牛顿不是理性时代的第一人，而是最后一位魔法师"。而 a16z 现在说：炼金术不是错，是时候没到。把沙子变成思想——SiO₂ → 晶圆 → 算力 → 认知——这条链条在物理上完全成立。这就把 AI 投资的合法性锚定到了一个跨越 350 年的哲学冒险上，而不是季度回报上。跨领域连接：这与 mRNA 疫苗的发展轨迹惊人相似——Katalin Karikó 被大学扫地出门几十年，直到 2020 年 mRNA 突然从"民间科学"变成"改变世界的技术"。被主流判死刑的探索路径，往往才是复利最深的埋伏点。

真正的稀缺不是芯片，是"瓶颈本身的所有权"

发言人说"almost everything is the bottleneck"——电、算力、芯片、数据中心、供应链，样样短缺。这里藏着一个被忽视的经济学转折：当一切都稀缺时，稀缺性本身就成了一种可被资产化的物品。SaaS 时代的数据中心是为"高并发低功耗"设计的，AI 数据中心却要为"高功耗低延迟"重构——这意味着老的基础设施不是简单升级，而是要报废重建。这种"存量作废"的规模，历史上只在两次转变里出现过：马车厂到福特流水线，以及交流电取代直流电。跨领域连接：这跟明治维新时期日本的"殖产兴业"逻辑一模一样——不是投资单个工厂，而是投资"建工厂的能力"。a16z 这支基金真正买的不是 AI 公司，是"制造 AI 所需一切的产能"。当每个环节都短缺，谁掌握了瓶颈的调度权，谁就实质上收了整个未来的"过路费"。这也是为什么名字里没有"AI"——他们卖的是收费站，不是车。

📝 转录文本

The Alchemist's Dream, Rediscovered

Isaac Newton spent 20 years looking for this key to what he called alchemy. The idea of alchemy was to transmute something that was very common into something that was very rare. There was this thing called the philosopher's stone that he kept trying to discover.

Imagine a form of alchemy that turns sand into thought. And so AI quite literally is that. It's thought at scale, for everybody, in perpetuity.

Everything Is the Bottleneck

So now almost everything is the bottleneck. Look, America's got to rebuild its entire infrastructure. Like, right now the whole supply chain is just feeling immense pressure.

The bottom line is this is a very unique moment in time. The entire compute ecosystem is being rebooted for AI. You know, these data centers were built for SaaS — and so you really have to restore.

Short on Everything

The United States is short power, short compute, short chips. There are going to be shortages in all three.

We don't have enough anything to be in this future world — and somebody's got to fund it.

观看原视频 →

item.title: [GoldRepublic Global] Michael Every: The Global System Is Coming Apart
item.dc:creator: GoldRepublic Global
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的观察：金融市场的"和平红利"时代已终结，我们正在回到"作物歉收—自然灾害—战争"的古典定价范式

Michael 埋在长篇论述中的一句话，其实是整场对话最锋利的匕首："markets always used to move primarily with war, crop failures, natural disasters..."

这不是怀旧，而是一个隐藏的范式回归诊断。过去 40 年，我们把"央行会议纪要 > 一切"当成宇宙常数，其实那是冷战末期到后冷战短短一代人的历史反常态——一个由西方绝对军事优势 + 低债务 + 职业化远征军所"补贴"出来的金融幻象。当这三根支柱同时松动，市场自然会重新拥抱它的历史均值：物理世界的冲击才是定价的第一驱动力。

意外之处在于：这意味着未来 10 年，最优秀的宏观分析师可能不是经济学 PhD，而是气象学家、军工工程师、能源物流专家。华尔街正在经历一次悄无声息的"技能贬值"——擅长解读点阵图的交易员，正在被擅长解读乌克兰无人机产量数据的分析师超越。

二、跨领域连接："3D 打印无人机拦截器"预示着 AI 时代的"军事—工业—货币三位一体"重构

Michael 提到的那个细节看似技术八卦，实则是整场对话的罗塞塔石：阿联酋一家小公司用 3D 打印零件造出 5000 美元一枚的反无人机拦截器，比伊朗神风无人机还便宜。

把它和另外三条线索并置——你会看到一个惊人的图案：

  1. 稳定币立法（Clarity Act）→ 创造"离岸美元"的双利率结构；
  2. 军工再工业化 → 需要天量廉价融资；
  3. AI 驱动的 7×24 无人工厂 → 让"低毛利、大批量"第一次在西方经济体成为可能。

跨领域的意外洞察：西方过去 40 年之所以选择"金融化 + 高毛利"，本质是因为人力成本使得"中国式低毛利大批量"在西方不可行。而 AI + 3D 打印正在第一次给美国提供一条"绕过人口结构、绕过工会、绕过工资黏性"的去人力化再工业化路径。

换句话说：Trump 关税、稳定币立法、AI 资本开支狂潮、无人机革命——它们不是四件事，它们是同一件事。它们共同构成了一个赌注：美国能否在中国之前，率先建成"AI 原生的军工—工业—货币复合体"。谁先做到，谁就重新定义 21 世纪的美元。

三、隐藏的系统性真相："经济胁迫"和"物理胁迫"正在合流为一种全新的国家艺术——"仓鼠轮政治经济学"

Michael 用了一个极其精妙的比喻却几乎没人注意到：市场就是仓鼠，跑得越拼命越好，但笼子的门始终掌握在国家手里。

这不是简单的"国家干预市场"的老话题。它揭示的是一个更深层的结构性变化：

  • 旧范式：国家设定规则 → 市场在规则内自由跑动 → 结果是"涌现的"。
  • 新范式：国家设定结果 → 市场被诱导、恐吓、被"喂食"以精确达成该结果 → 市场依然在跑，但方向已被预设。

最反直觉的推论：这意味着未来的黄金、稀土、铀矿、造船产能，将出现一种"薛定谔的市场"——名义上有价格发现，实际上有价格上限（防止国防成本失控）和价格下限（防止战略产能死亡）。你可以买入这些资产，但你永远不会被允许获得 10x 收益，因为那意味着国家安全成本的爆炸。

跨领域的镜像：这与晚期罗马帝国的"戴克里先最高限价令"惊人相似——每当一个帝国从"扩张—财政丰裕"阶段进入"防御—财政紧缩"阶段，市场的"自由度"就会被系统性削减。我们可能正处在一个"戴克里先时刻"，只不过工具从铜板价格表变成了稳定币算法。

四、给读者的"啊哈时刻"

Michael 通篇没有明说、但反复围绕的核心洞见是：

"国家力量塑造市场"这句话，过去 40 年被降级为一句陈词滥调；未来 10 年，它会重新升级为唯一值得认真对待的宏观命题。

而这个命题的残酷推论是：如果你的投资框架里没有"letters of marque（私掠许可证）复活"、"NATO 第五条被试探"、"稳定币双利率套利"这类词汇——你不是在做宏观投资，你是在做冷战后短暂太平世界的怀旧考古。

📝 转录文本

Michael Every: The Global System Is Coming Apart

GoldRepublic Global 访谈 · 主持人 Alex Adronov · 2026 年 8 月 27 日

开场：全球系统正在崩解

Everything pretty much in terms of how we understand the global system — whether it be the security architecture, the geopolitical architecture, the geoeconomic architecture or the geo‑financial architecture — is coming apart at the seams. And to some extent it's unplanned and unforced, and in other areas it's very deliberate and being either ripped or snipped. But it's happening. We have to deal with it. There's not a lot as individuals we can do about it.

That's the western disease. That's what we've been through for 40 odd years. It's all about the quick buck, financialization, and the massive margin. And that doesn't work against a system that we are now rubbing up against.

If it comes down to one kind of war where it's purely military, it's going to be the one that's got the best, cheapest technology that can produce it at the highest volume. But I'm not for a second saying that the East goes to war with the West. I'm saying that we are preparing for a world in which there is much more confrontation, resilience — quote unquote — you know, the need for self‑reliance and preparedness, which of course looks like…

主持人开场

Alex: Welcome to the Microscopic Podcast. My name is Alex Adronov, I'm your host, and today I have the pleasure of welcoming back Michael Every. Welcome back, Michael.

Michael: Thank you very much, and it's nice to be here without any stomach trouble this time.

Alex: [laughter] Yes, that's true. So I had a conversation with John also a week ago, and we were just saying that obviously this conversation hits a bit different. I mean, it's great to see you virtually, but it was obviously a different format in South Africa — with a bit more backdrop and sunburn, I could say. But we'll do with this.

Today is Thursday, 27th of August. I always like to give the date in my interviews, because things happen at a very fast pace — especially when we talk about geopolitics, financial markets — things change on an hourly basis.

So today's conversation is obviously a follow‑up based on a lot of what we've talked about already in March. That was a few months ago, and I would like to pick your brain on: what do you think were the most notable developments that happened since then?

一、自 3 月以来的关键发展：级联式危机

Michael: Well, where do we start? [laughter]

When we were talking last in person, the war against Iran had only really just got started. I remember I was flying out to South Africa to meet you on the day it began, which was an interesting time to be in the airport.

Obviously that has dominated headlines all around the world since then. But so has, to a greater or lesser degree, a cascading — logically cascading — series of related and/or conflating stories which all point to the same underlying dynamic which we did discuss in March, but which is now accelerating like a snowball, becoming larger and larger as it comes down a mountain:

Everything pretty much in terms of how we understand the global system — whether it be the security architecture, the geopolitical architecture, the geoeconomic architecture or the geo‑financial architecture — is coming apart at the seams. To some extent it's unplanned and unforced, and in other areas it's very deliberate and being either ripped or snipped. But it's happening. We have to deal with it. There's not a lot as individuals we can do about it.

二、多线压力：美国是否已经过度延伸？

Alex: There's obviously a lot of fires as well that we can see — places of confrontation in one level or another, whether military or financial‑economic.

The US has simultaneously been trying to deal with the Iran war. Since then, it has had repercussions on the bond market. We've had the debt situation and the fiscal strain in Japan, which was maybe triggering what we've seen now and accelerating the distress in the bond market in the US.

Then we still have the Russia and Ukraine war ongoing. We have talks about NATO security. Taiwan is also on the table — it's something that has not been getting a lot of spotlight lately, but it's still ongoing, in a more hidden way. And there's obviously the economic confrontation with China.

So if we tie this all together and we look at it now from a US perspective: has the US overstretched on multiple fronts without being able to handle them accordingly? Or how is your view about that?

两条被忽视的新闻线

Michael: Well, before I answer that — and I will in full — we've also had two other headlines. One last week (not a new one, but getting attention), and the other one today as we're speaking.

The one last week was that there were very serious conversations being had in the Middle East about the potential for genuine military clashes between Turkey and Israel — something that not a lot of people who don't know the region would have had on their cards. But that was something really worth paying attention to.

The other one today is that even the likes of Bloomberg — the go‑to source for financial news — is talking about the fact that there is more and more fear both within Russia and without it, that you are going to see an escalation from Putin on multiple different fronts, which could potentially even include the use of a tactical nuclear weapon. I'm not saying if he will or he won't, but the fact that that's in the press is pretty scary.

Letters of Marque:私掠许可证复活

Additionally, Bloomberg is also saying today that something I flagged years ago — which directly relates to what I'm about to say — is coming to pass: the US looks like it's going to bring back letters of marque.

Letters of marque are a hundreds‑of‑years‑old legal device by which, if the state isn't capable of doing something, you effectively legalize piracy to allow you to do it. In this case, it would be: if you can seize Iranian oil anywhere, you get to keep it as a prize — including the ship and all the oil in it. So, effectively legalizing piracy because the navy can't be everywhere doing it.

结论：巨人被无数小对手咬住

That leads me to the longer answer. When you look at the panoply of different pressure points building up, the different crises where the US would traditionally get much more involved but now can't or is struggling to maintain balance between two other forces — and the fact that they're now having to lean on letters of marque — then yes, the US is very, very clearly overstretched.

It's still a giant compared to anyone else, but it's surrounded by a very large number of ever‑larger opponents who can hold it around the ankles and the knees and bite his legs and bite his fingers and jump around his neck and his shoulders. And collectively they can really hold it down — short of really extreme measures, which I wouldn't rule out, by the way, but which again take us further and further away from any kind of norms of behavior or of action.

三、CIA 局长秘访莫斯科:意味着什么？

Alex: I would like to add to that what we've also seen recently — something that was a bit of a surprise: Ratcliffe's visit to Moscow. So the head of the CIA, the number one spy, is going to Russia. And Peskov, the spokesperson of the Kremlin, was officially also not really notified or had any information about that.

There's obviously a lot of speculation about what exactly the content of the talks was. But it's very unusual, because the last time this happened was when Burns, the former head of the CIA, came in on the eve of the Russian invasion of Ukraine.

What analysis do you have on that, and how does this tie in with what we just talked about — US overstretching and trying to handle all those crisis points?

慢速拆解:三重国家艺术

Michael: Sure. Well, there's a lot that I threw in there. So let me now try and slow it down and address your point and link it up and unpack it.

Obviously, the US is in a conflict with Iran and it's saying publicly that it doesn't intend to attack them physically at the moment because it's overstretched in terms of missile interceptors and precision ammunition. It doesn't need the precision ammunition — it can take a risk and use less precision ammunition — but it means you have to be closer and you can take casualties. And the US is showing it doesn't want to do that. So it's overstretched in that respect.

It's implementing an economic war against Iran, which I think is actually going to be effective. But to do that, you have to get everyone to comply. They're now talking about therefore literally ripping up the global system — or "blowing it up," as Bessent said — to those who don't want to help, and saying: "Well, we'll kick you off the US dollar," which would completely fracture the world system. That's their words. That's their threat.

目标一个,敌人一堆

So obviously that means you have to look at countries as various as Turkey — who I just spoke about, who is still clearly trading with Iran — Qatar, various other countries in the Middle East, Russia, Pakistan (who's acting as a mediator), Central Asia, and China. And China has already come out and said that they won't help. So again, you go for one target, you end up with several.

伊朗可能先下手

Iran, as it's being throttled, could easily see that the US still doesn't have missile interceptors in the right numbers yet and say: "Well, you're not going to attack us — we're not going to wait around until you're rearmed to do so in another couple of months after the midterms," which is still something I think could happen. "We'll attack you now while you're not ready."

And if Iran is going to do that, even if it's on a limited scale, it can do a lot of damage within the Middle East — to desalination plants, LNG plants, oil fields, etc.

俄罗斯的完美时机

What a perfect time for Russia — which has backed Iran as much as it can, just as Iran has backed Russia — to then escalate against Ukraine, because Ukraine's also out of missile interceptors and is carrying out very effective attacks on the Russian energy complex, which is having a global impact.

Putin's increasingly frustrated, and we've had rumors for weeks now that he would mobilize after the September 19th and 20th elections for the Duma. So from the 21st onwards, he could mobilize and bring in another half a million men. We've had rumors that North Korea might send 50,000 men to fight on the front, which Ukraine can't match.

And at the same time, now that CIA visit is probably — and you have to look at the spectrum related to the US spotting signals — that that could be about to happen. The US also spotting that the EU, when they visited Ukraine for its Independence Day just a few days ago, pledged significantly more military aid, including helping them build more and more weapons with European technology in Ukraine — and the UK saying: "We will hand over the blueprints for advanced long‑range missiles which will allow you to strike Russia much harder than you already are."

Russia might be saying: "Well, you know what? Maybe we have to escalate here to try and worry the Europeans, who seem to be thinking they can do more and more but tend to back off when we bite back."

最坏情境:战术核武 + 试探 NATO 第五条

So the worst‑case scenario — as I've already alluded to, and this is on Bloomberg, not me just speculating — is that Russia can say: "Right, we'll move beyond ballistic missile attacks on Kyiv. We'll actually set off a tactical nuke somewhere as a warning, just to prove how far we're prepared to go." Which I don't think China would be in favor of, by the way, and would open a Pandora's box.

But if they don't do that, the other risk — and I think serious people are taking this seriously — is that they make a token strike against NATO. So the Russians could say: "Right, we'll seize a tiny amount of territory from one of the Baltic states — just a little cut — or we'll strike across the border deliberately." So it's fairly unambiguous that we did that.

Is NATO going to go to war with Russia over that? If the answer is yes, then whatever you're pricing in markets, you're wrong right now unless you're pricing for that. And if you think, "No, everyone will say that's ridiculous, of course they won't" — well, then Russia has already established that NATO Article 5 doesn't hold up, that there is a level that you have to cross for them to actually do something, and everything below that they can get away with. Which is problematic, as you can imagine.

And it wouldn't be illogical — it'd be very high risk, but wouldn't be illogical — for Russia to say: "Well, let's hope NATO retaliates to some degree or rattles its sabers, because then we will roll out the tactical nuclear weapons, etc., just to show them on the ground, and then we'll see if that gets us to the dialogue that we want to have."

Because what they want is a conversation with America over the heads of Europe about a new European strategic architecture, where effectively they get most of Ukraine back and Europe understands that Russia gets a seat at the table and a veto over everything. And they're not achieving that on the battlefield — maybe they can achieve it with a massive escalation here.

That's all within the realm of possibility. I'm not giving a forecast probability on any of it. But after the ride we have had since 2022, anybody who wants to dismiss this and purely think that the monthly inflation data or payrolls numbers coming out of the US are the single most important thing you can be looking at right now, I'm afraid, is in the wrong job.

四、经济国家艺术是否有效?

Alex: I mean, those are definitely greater forces than financial markets. And as we talked about, they're intertwined.

Your thesis is that the geopolitical factor — the factor of power, brute force, sheer force — is actually dwarfing the financial and economic dimension.

三种国家艺术:军事、经济、政治

Michael: Well, let me rewind just for a moment. There are three different kinds of statecraft: military, economic, and political. And I've always argued that you need to use all of them. So I'm not saying one's superior or inferior to the other.

Clearly, the US is pivoting back to economic statecraft right now because the military avenue is not working. They couldn't topple Iran as easily as they thought they could, like Venezuela. So they miscalculated on that front — because, as you rightly say (and as has been known for a long time to many people except, apparently, those making decisions at a higher level in the US), they don't have the stocks and the supply chains and the flow of weapons and defensive goods to maintain a long war. They thought they did, or some people deluded themselves they did. They simply don't.

So they were always going to try and reshape their economy to a more military‑industrial footing. That's something I've been saying for a long time; many people agree about.

经济战能否成功?

Will it work to pivot back to economic warfare for now? I think it can have an extremely important effect on the Iranian economy. I think it really can make an impact.

The problem is, as we've already alluded to, you have to get everyone to go along with you — because it isn't only the US versus Iran. If you have smuggling through the Middle East, smuggling through Central Asia, if Chinese planes hypothetically continue to land in Tehran full of dual‑use goods, etc. — if things can carry on as normal, then you have to extend those measures to others.

So we will see whether the US is or isn't prepared to take on what is effectively a bloc. And there's been a slow realization for far too many parties: this isn't about the US versus any one country.

Now, if they could have managed to topple Iran quickly — which is what I think they aimed to do — that would have reshuffled the pack and given them a stronger hand versus China in the constellation of countries in their group versus America's. Because that hasn't worked, I think for now it's economic warfare. I think they will go back to physical warfare.

范式在动态转变:5000 美元的反无人机

Importantly, the paradigm continues to shift very dynamically. For example, the Wall Street Journal — I'm using this as a benchmark of information, of course others may have far better insider sources — has a story that there's a US startup operating in the UAE which is now producing anti‑drone drones (drone‑defense interceptors) for $5,000 a pop using 3D‑printed parts, which are even cheaper than the Iranian kamikaze drones, which are themselves vastly cheaper than the interceptors that the US has been using up until now.

So the US was caught flat‑footed. Its industrial network was caught flat‑footed, as we knew would be the case. That doesn't mean it can't pivot and adapt. Now, it's hard to do everything everywhere all at once — otherwise history would just change in a weekend, which is what financial markets like to price for because they can. The physical world takes longer to react.

But I think it's an effective tactic against Iran to a large degree. It won't be, given that the bloc will stand up to it. Russia clearly looks like it's indicating it's going to try and escalate. If China were to escalate above and beyond just saying "we won't help," things get infinitely worse again. So the US itself will then have to pivot.

If they can start pumping out — what the report said in the WSJ — 15,000 drone interceptors a month from a small shop in the UAE using 3D‑printed parts, well, that can easily be 150,000 or 1.5 million if you scale up the same technology. So things will move rapidly.

But what that means for those of us who are looking at markets is that above and beyond having to accept this thesis about the world now running by statecraft — political, military, or economic — the ways in which they conflate and then change because of a technological breakthrough or a political argument or a political agreement (for example, the one between the US and Canada, which suddenly went from being handshake to daggers drawn) makes everything pivot. Everything can change really dramatically.

So it's an exhausting job trying to look at it, because you're looking at so many things at once, everywhere, and all of them are important in different ways.

五、Trump 的 "D‑Day" 与债券市场

Alex: True. And apologies for the lack of distinction I made in the question — it's absolutely a mix of all those factors.

We see this now as well with Scott Bessent, who announced this "D‑Day." Prior to that, Trump said they would have ways to use the military — he said "military" — to get this Treasury market crisis under control, with the higher long end of the yield curve going higher and higher, and Scott Bessent at the Treasury trying to get control over it by selling the short end.

What do you think Trump meant by that?

"认真对待,但不要字面理解"

Michael: Well, as is so often the case with Trump: take him seriously, but not literally. I keep repeating that, and too many people fail to heed it.

He's not talking — amusing as it is in theory — about bombing bondholders. He's not going to bomb Wall Street. He's not going to bomb Asian pension funds. Clearly, no.

What he is alluding to, however, is the fact that the entire construct that financial markets sit on — believing that they are masters of the universe, that where they want to go they can go, they can trade 24/7 on their phone using 5G, high‑speed internet, etc. — is a world that was created by American physical power in winning World War II, defeating fascism, winning the Cold War and defeating communism, and then saying, "Okay, let's have globalism," and rolling it out to everybody. Which didn't work out well for America — which was predictable to some of us — and is now being reversed.

If that's reversed, the reverse policy is to explain to people: "Look, we can change the world at the drop of a bomb, the push of a button, and markets won't like it." Now, obviously that doesn't mean you bomb individual people — although that's certainly happening around the margin, and it even did under previous US presidents and even during globalism. But it's making clear that the paradigm you operate within can and will be changed.

If you think that we are going to let the long end of the bond market tell us we can no longer get involved in a war in the Middle East, ergo we're no longer a world power — you're wrong. That happened to France and the UK in the Suez Crisis, which I drew a parallel to when this war started (I think we said that to each other when we met). The US is not going to let that happen.

用哪些手段?各类国家艺术的组合拳

So what tricks will they use to get around it? Lots. Many, various — all forms of statecraft, all mixed as one. But they're making it clear to anyone who understands — and some of us do, and many in markets who come from nice peaceful pacifist countries who put war behind them a long time ago in their minds do not understand this — that it will involve physical pressure. Absolutely.

One very simple way to explain that: you can use traditional market tricks — which Bessent clearly will — such as more T‑bill issuance, taking maturity from far down the curve where yields are rising, moving it to short‑dated maturity.

You can then take that and say: "Right, we're going to create an extra bid for T‑bills by shifting people to using stablecoins," which is something I think will happen soon. They're just pending one or two little changes to legislation, then that can happen. That gives you lower interest rates at the short end of the curve, which buys you fiscal space.

With that fiscal space, you incentivize this new military‑industrial economy to make sure you can pump out masses of drone interceptors and new weapon systems at much lower cost — rather than seeing nice padding of invoices, which is what so many contractors have been doing on a cost‑plus basis for decades.

And with that — to use a crude term — you go and explain to people in regions like the Middle East that key commodities and commodity inputs upstream (which ultimately flow downstream and either create inflation waves or deflation waves) are going to remain priced in US dollars at attractive prices for America and its group of friends.

That's a very, very old game.

市场回到"战争—歉收—灾难"的古典范式

And in fact, just one more thing, then I'll shut up. At the very beginning you said that markets are now being buffeted by all this. They absolutely are. But if you look at the history of markets — hundreds of years of history, which we have in printed form if not on your screen — markets always used to move primarily with war, crop failures, natural disasters. That was what it was nearly always about, in its totality.

It's only in the later years of the Cold War, and then the post‑Cold War period, when the West was so much more powerful than everybody else, and our debt levels were so much lower than everybody else's (which they're not now), and we're not that powerful anymore relatively, and wars used to happen with professional armies rather than conscript armies far away on the other side of the world, and we could forget about them after a weekend — that the market was able to say: "Where's more? Where's my tax cut? Where's my rate cut? Where's my buyback?" All the things.

Well, that world has now gone, and we are back to what it always used to be: crop failures, natural disasters, war. So we've come full circle in that regard.

六、这是"管道问题"还是"资金问题"?

Alex: Just to close off the US funding question — in your eyes, if I understood correctly, you think that the US and its administration at the moment will find creative ways to always prop up the funding? So it's more of a plumbing problem rather than a funding problem — that the global architecture doesn't just suddenly break and everyone walks away from the US?

Michael: Which is extremely unlikely, because they have no one to export to, and nobody wants mass unemployment overnight. Longer term, maybe — but not in the short term the way that markets think it could happen.

I think this is going to be a plumbing issue. We have seen an enormous number of episodes in the recent past — before "geopolitics" became a word that everyone was mentioning over and over again — in which we would have a crisis in a pocket or pockets of the financial market, and frankly it was a very predictable drama. You'd have meeting after meeting, worried note after worried note, and then a central banker somewhere would create a new acronym, and everything went back to normal. Because it was always just a plumbing problem, and you could always print money one way or another, or just create liquidity.

Why can't that happen again now, in different ways? The answer is: of course it can, if it has to.

但你无法印刷原子

But the important caveat here is that it's now about physical supply chains. You can print dollars, you can create liquidity, but you can't create diesel, you can't print atoms.

So the plumbing can still be re‑plumbed, but it needs to be linked to the physical plumbing, not just the financial plumbing. They can do that, but then you are really getting involved in the physical economy too. And as a result, I think they will.

七、"炸掉全球金融系统"?

Alex: Now I'm pedaling back to what I mentioned about Scott Bessent, who said in a press conference — and a journalist was asking him about the D‑Day question analogy and the fact that in that sense we didn't give a heads‑up to the Germans — why they haven't done it yet. And he said, "Why would I want to blow up the global financial system?"

Do you think this is something that would really be a possibility, if they really go for it?

全面制裁 = 撞墙

Michael: Well, if you think of it in principle: if the US were to turn around and say — not just to Russia, which it has done to a degree already, but to China, Pakistan, Turkey, and even India, all really large countries with nuclear weapons — "All of you are off the dollar tomorrow. All your FX reserves are gone. Finished for NATO. Everyone's sanctioned. You can't import anything from anyone else anymore in dollars…" — I think we can comfortably say that the global economy and financial system would hit the wall. I think we can comfortably say that.

Is that going to happen? I think that's extremely unlikely.

疯子理论的悖论

On one level, saying it but then not doing it does look weak. Undeniably so. So does putting a nuclear weapon on display physically — does that look weak or strong? Well, it looks weak: "Why haven't you blown the world up yet?"

Equally, you're hoping you don't have to, but you are testing madman theory to a degree.

黑手党式的定向打击

I would say the more logical threat from the US is that someone is going to get blown up. Some people are going to be nailed to the wall. Not everybody, but some countries, some key firms, some wealthy individuals are going to suffer. And that's a more targeted and more effective way to do it. It's mafia style: "One of you will disappear over the weekend, but I'm not going to tell you which — up to you collectively whether you're going to change your behavior or not, but one of you might disappear if you don't."

So I think that's the underlying way to see it. But again, there are a lot of people with a very financial‑market framework who don't understand realpolitik, who think it's bluff — because they've never been in that kind of situation where things really are physically threatening to them. And that voice will be prevalent in the market too, genuinely.

So then that does unfortunately lean towards the likelihood that the US will have to nail someone to the wall somewhere at some point to try and get that impact.

反向情境

And if we flip it around the other way — because I'm doing this from the standpoint that the US achieves its goal — if it doesn't, and everyone else says, "Well, we are going to act so outrageously we're going to force you to do this or back down," then either the US is forced into torpedoing the entire global system ahead of its plans to alter it to its own benefit (it wants to blow up some bridges but to keep a lot of the infrastructure the way it is now — either it'll be forced to blow all the bridges up), or it'll be forced to just retreat entirely and to give up lots and lots of geostrategic, geoeconomic and geo‑financial territory that it currently holds.

It's a really, really great game being played out, with very, very, very high stakes.

I'm kind of doing your job for you here a little bit, Alex — but if that isn't an environment in which people who like assets like gold aren't rubbing their hands, I don't know what is. I'm not advocating for anything — you know that I don't give financial advice, and I certainly don't do that about buying or selling gold. But this is certainly the kind of topic of conversation that whenever in the past I've brought up, I've always generated a flood of interest from people who do talk about nothing but gold.

Alex: Well, thanks for the promo. I appreciate it.

Michael: I didn't give any advice. I'm really recognizing who I'm talking to, that's all.

Alex: You're just talking facts. I get it. [laughter]

八、霍尔木兹的"暗中交易"?黄金与中国

Alex: Talking about gold, that's a good segue. Now I'm entering really speculation territory — tell me if it gets a bit too wild for your taste.

There have been some theories floating that for the Strait of Hormuz — the fact that China had a bit of an agreement with the US in terms of importing less oil during that time (40% less demand has been recorded in China) — and this theory floated by Chris Martenson: that on the contrary, China would also get more imports of gold to prop up their gold reserves.

Now, obviously we need to differentiate facts from speculation here. It's something I've never come across before, I just saw it through an interview recently. Do you think that in the end there might be those kinds of incentives from global powers that in the headlines are all having confrontation, but in the background are trying to actually stabilize the system by reaching such kinds of agreements? Do you think it's plausible?

分阶段回答

Michael: Okay, let me answer that in stages.

First of all, nobody knows what happened vis‑à‑vis China and the US on Hormuz — you'd have to be an ultimate insider to know. I think it's entirely plausible that some sidebar agreement was struck, and that of course would have generated a lot of goodwill towards China from the US.

If that's the case, I think it's just as plausible that China flexed versus the US and said: "Hey, look, we've got a year's worth of reserves, and at the same time we can get everyone using EVs. If you're going to try and play the Venezuela card against us via the Middle East too — because that's the US plan, get the whole Middle East on their side — we can ride that out for a year, which is a lot longer than you can survive without X, Y, Z, A, B, C, which we still produce and you rely on for now."

I lean more towards the latter. And I'll tell you why.

与"金本位派"分道扬镳

I want to be completely clear here — as I said, I'm not taking a stance on gold per se either way, that's not what I'm doing. But when I look at things as a global strategist in terms of the architecture, and I talk to people who are big gold bugs, we get along — as we say in English — "like a house on fire" for the first couple of miles of the long walk we're on together, and then we take sharply divergent paths.

Because if you're presuming that the deal was "China gets more gold because of Hormuz" — what's the endgame? That only makes sense to me (and everyone's entitled to have their own opinion) if the US believes, as some friends of mine do, that a shift back to a global gold standard solves all the problems we have.

And this is where — I didn't think we were going to get to this point at all, or certainly not this early, but if we did — this is where there's just a big ideological, conceptual difference between myself and gold as an entity or a thing. While I think it makes a lot of sense for individuals to look at all the historical reasons, etc., where we are right now from a global architectural perspective, I don't think that any asset or anything "neutral" brings back what the US needs to get back from China in terms of supply chains.

没有一个价格能让中国交出供应链

Say for example the price of gold goes through the roof, which is entirely possible — I'm not making a call on it either way. I don't believe that there is a price for gold or any asset at which China turns around and says: "Wow, we played a great game. The gig's up. You can have all your supply chains back. We're going to let you have all rare‑earth mineral processing again. Market forces rule. We're going to let you have it all back. We're not going to be in a closed loop in terms of intellectual property anymore. We're going to share everything equally. We're going to change the entire structure of our industrial policy. We're not going to try and export — we're going to import much, much more, because that's what we've always wanted to do, etc." — and "fair do you, you re‑industrialize, and we'll all live together in peace."

Now, I think everyone wants to live together in peace. I'm not trying to talk about the war part. But I don't see there's any market mechanism, whatever the market is, to get us out of what we're in now.

仓鼠轮:市场是一种被利用的能量

That's why I have been advocating and predicting and explaining what economic statecraft is — and statecraft in general, whether political, military, or economic — and how it isn't market‑based. How you use parts of markets like a hamster in a wheel. They know the hamster is running and running, there's all the market energy, the poor little thing isn't getting anywhere — it's actually doing what you want it to do. It doesn't get to run free across the grass and enjoy itself nibbling whatever it finds. That's how I think economic statecraft works.

So if you've got that view (I do — I'm not saying you have to at all), then I lean towards the "flex" argument on Hormuz rather than the cooperation one.

But I will say that those who know, know that within every major country there are always parts of the body of state which are looking to collaborate with others, and there are always parts which are looking to nick at the others. That's just the way politics works. So both could be true at the same time, but I think one is more significant than the other.

九、中国的通缩与购金

Alex: If we look at the situation in China itself, the bond market is actually doing the opposite of what we're seeing in other G7 countries, where bond yields are rising — not just in the US but across the board. China is also entering a bit of what we call a deflationary period, where the 10‑year for example is approaching 1%.

In the meantime, they're also importing a lot of gold — not just the PBoC, but the country as a whole. This is a bit of a classic relationship. Do you see this as China overusing its deflationary weapon, in a way of being driven by deflationary forces for all those years and now having to deal with it in a more severe way? Or how's your analysis about their situation right now?

结构性通缩 + 购金作为应急机制

Michael: Well, again, this depends where you start from, because it does become partly ideological — you have a stance on how you think the world works, whether something is a solution or it isn't, and then you work back to there.

Now, I'm really cynical: I don't think anything works in the long run, as I've made clear. Different things can work in different ways in different countries for a while, but there's no one rule for everyone that works everywhere all the time.

I would say this: if China is importing a lot of gold, traditionally countries do that when they're worried about inflation, and it can be an excellent inflation hedge. Okay, there's no denying that at all. I don't see the argument to say: "If we're deep in deflation, which they are, because structurally we've pushed this net exporting model to an extreme never seen before in a major economy, but we're stuck and we can't get out of it — therefore we're going to bring in gold, which is deflationary, to compensate for the deflation that we already have." That makes very little sense to me.

I also don't think it makes sense to presume they're bringing it in ready to inflate their way out of it. I don't think that's going to work either — because if there's one thing that those who know China know, is that China is terrified of inflation. They absolutely don't want inflation, and I think they're right not to want it. Some deflation can actually be pretty healthy. I think a lot of people would like lower prices for things right now, if you look around you, and demand on the street in the West.

So their bond yields are going down because of this deflation. Whether they are or aren't bringing in gold, I think, is unrelated to that.

应急:非美元数字货币的替代方案

I think it comes again to this "flex" attitude — which is: "Look, if we're seriously hearing the US threaten what we kind of always knew they were going to say, which is that at some point you might be kicked off the US dollar bloc as it were, we need to have something ready as an emergency mechanism. And it's going to be very difficult to get this fully functioning global non‑US digital currency up and running." (You know, they're trying to patch one together with others; some people have a higher opinion of it than I do — I question its long‑run validity for a number of different reasons.)

No one's going to question gold as a stop‑gap within a cluster of countries for a certain degree of trade for certain things. So I can certainly see the logical answer for it being at the back of mind for some countries as a fallback. But that's a very different prospect from saying "there's the cure — rule for all countries for all international transactions," which is what the dollar is doing now. And I don't see it filling that.

Do you see the continuity between the points I'm making?

十、美元武器化 vs 人民币的定位

Alex: I do. And it also brings up the question: if we tie this all together with, on the one hand, the weaponization of the dollar — which is what set gold to be one of the biggest factors that gold‑price appreciation has benefited from — and on the other, pushing it too much where it becomes a trap for the US by overusing it, with Scott Bessent reiterating "if you do not comply, we'll just take all the chairs off"…

That is a bit of a fine line, and obviously it's a signal that most countries — especially China, Russia, and the opposing blocs to the US bloc — are taking notes. For years already, China has been dumping US Treasuries for the last 10 years, and is preparing alternative payment systems like CIPS, but also now setting up SGE vaults for convertibility of yuan gold exchanges and so on and so forth.

We talked about this also in our very heated discussions — not just heated intellectually but also literally — in South Africa, which I recommend everyone to watch again. Even though sometimes some people talk over each other, it was very insightful.

Thereby then the question is: China's ambition — some say, yeah, it will not be able to replace the US dollar. But the question is, does it need to replace the US?

中国并不想成为下一个美元

Michael: I don't think it wants to, whether it needs to or not. It doesn't have any intention of allowing a global renminbi to replicate the function that the US dollar has — the financialized function which undermines industrial production.

Given that China wants to maintain as much industry as possible, the only way in which it would be using the renminbi internationally more would be for clearing trade payments for certain strategic interactions and deals with certain countries. They don't want two completely unrelated parties — Party A and Party B on the other side of the world — speculating on it and bidding up asset prices with it, to effectively inflate it and undermine China's real economy.

So it's not just of whether they need it or not — they don't want it. They're aiming for something very different.

美国也想要一个"工业化的美元"

Now to be fair, one aspect of this which I alluded to just a little bit and I have to come back to: I don't think the US wants to keep the dollar the way it is either. I think they absolutely want to keep as much of the global reach of the dollar as possible. But at least what my understanding is, is that they know that a financialized dollar is not good for them. They want an industrialized dollar.

Again, they want a dollar that people demand because the US makes things and is the center of a real‑economy nexus — not a consumer nexus where everyone looks to America because you're going to buy stuff from them that you've made, rather than buying stuff from them and paying for it in dollars.

To get there is, I think, going to require a lot more financialization first. There will be a lot more bank loans needing to be made, a lot more borrowing that needs to be done — as we see, for example, in AI, which is part of that race for dominance. Because AI can be used for really frivolous purposes (I've been making some wonderfully silly pictures with it today to use in a report — talking about this subject, by the way), but equally it can run a factory for you. It can be running factories 24/7 and innovating on an iterative cycle to push productivity frontiers further and further forward and creating new technologies.

So all of that's going to take an awful lot of borrowing and lending, which is inflationary and liquidity‑creating. And I fully expect to see a lot more of the old mechanisms in play for one last burst to try and shift the American economy from one state to another.

If they fall short — wow, that's going to be interesting with a capital I. If they succeed — just as interesting in a very different way. But that's what a lot of all of this comes back to: the attempt to try and lock in all the supply chains, all the coalition of countries that will work with you even when it hurts in the near term, to achieve something very different. And, to be honest, a lot more Chinese in some respects on the other side of it, versus those who like the way everything was done up until now — even though it didn't work — and want to do a lot more of it.

十一、稳定币:双利率与国际采纳

Alex: I would like to also tie in with what you said — the prioritization of statecraft. The fact that a state with lack of funds is taking recourse to private entities to do the job for them, right? 未必是零收益:双利率美元

Michael: Well, first of all, it remains to be seen if they will be zero‑yielding. They're not allowed to pay interest. But if the Clarity Act — one of the pieces of legislation I was referring to earlier — goes through in the form that it seems to be in now, you will get paid rewards or incentives.
