癌症疫苗与Moderna：新抗原免疫疗法

hey freebird what's going on with this cancer vaccine and the stock that tripled in the last two weeks we didn't get to it last week but i know i want to hear about it i'm sure the audience does

Yeah, Moderna stock, I think is what you're talking about, right? Yes. I think they went from like a 20 billion market cap to 60 billion market cap on the positive readouts from this thing that's being called a cancer vaccine. And I think it's worth highlighting how this cancer therapy system works.

This goes back to the 90s, where there was this idea that you could create what are called neoantigens. These are small peptides or proteins that mimic a peptide or protein that's unique to a cancer in your body. And so that antigen, which means that your immune system sees it as an invader, causes your immune system to start to make cells that destroy that protein. And so by putting that protein in your body, your immune system gets activated, and it gets turned on to go and find that protein in other parts of your body and destroy that protein. So the objective is figure out what is the protein that is unique to a particular cancer, make that protein, stick it in your body, and your immune system will go and destroy the cancer that's in your body.

And so this immunotherapy, the system of basically using an antigen that's designed for a cancer in your body to go and attack it, has been around since, call it the late 90s. And there was this big revolution in DNA sequencing where we identified that we could take samples of cancer, put them in a DNA sequencer, and look at the sequence of the genes, the proteins that are made, because they're made from genes that are unique to that particular cancer, and therefore make a personalized neoantigen that's personalized to the unique cancer that's in your body, because all these cancers mutate, and they're different, and no two cancers are identical.

个性化治疗的机制

How do they get that key for me personally versus you? How do you get that into the mRNA? They would take a sample of your tumor or cancer cells. So when you take your, let's say you have you know, melanoma. And the reason that melanoma is one of the kind of biggest targets for this immunotherapy is that melanomas have very kind of unique DNA mutations because of UV light hitting the skin. And so the particular cancer that you'll get in a melanoma that you have is going to be very unique with respect to the rest of your body. It's going to be a very unique mutation.

So they take the, a little bit of the melanoma, they get the DNA out of it, and when you do DNA sequencing, you multiply the DNA by millions or billions of times, you put all that DNA in a DNA sequencer, it gets chopped up and read, and then the sequence data comes back and it says, "This is what makes this cancer unique. It's this little sequence of the DNA." And that sequence of the DNA causes that cancer to make a unique protein that is basically like a key or an ID or a fingerprint of that cancer. They then take that DNA, and make protein from it, put that protein in your body, and now your immune system goes crazy and starts attacking that protein because it's like, "Oh, antigen, antigen, I got to go get it." Now that those cells are activated, those immune cells are activated to that protein, they'll eventually go destroy that cancer.

So this has been successful. There have been hundreds of trials with this neoantigen-based therapy for many different types of cancer. And there's all these trials that have tried to figure out what's the right technique for delivering the neoantigen. Do we make the protein and then stick it in your body? Or, in this case, with what Moderna did, make mRNA and stick it in your body. And the mRNA causes your own cells to now make that protein and spit it out, ends up in your blood, and now your immune cells got activated. So rather than making the protein ex vivo, which means outside of your body, you're making the protein in your body, in vivo. And now your body's making the protein. So the idea with the mRNA concept is you can get one shot. That shot goes into your body, and now your body's making that protein, just like we made the COVID vaccine. Yes. Your cells would make a particular protein segment that would activate your immune system, and it would go kill that cancer.

There's other questions around what are the other adjuvants, what types of cancer can you use this system for, and then combination therapies. Are there other cancer drugs that you can do this in combination with And all the trials that have been going on are all about this delivery mechanism, the technique that's used, the types of cancer, the dosing, and getting all of that stuff right.

监管俘获与50万美元的问题

Now, what's interesting about this is it is much more of a technique than a drug. In the traditional sense of process of it's a process, right? So the process is customized per person. So there's some cost to doing it per person. That's right. But the cost because I do DNA sequencing in my company all day long, getting that sample very cheap, getting the DNA data very cheap, actually doing a lot of the upfront work very cheap. Now, theoretically, making the mRNA, or making the protein should also be pretty cheap. But it's human trials and human safety. And so there's a lot of questions around how do you make sure that everything's safe? And what's the right combinations that people don't get overreacted immune systems, or that people don't have adverse side effects. So that's all of the tuning of this.

But I think what frustrates me the most about all of this, and everyone's kind of lauding this as some unique breakthrough and special and powerful, and it's not. Because a lot of people are going to places like Montana, and they are getting peptides printed for their particular cancer sequence, and they are making their own neoantigens, putting it in their body, and getting cured of their cancer. You can pay someone $50,000 to do this for you today. There's a lot of clinics that'll do it, and it's not a special FDA-approved drug. To your point, J. Cal, it's a process. The process is take the DNA sequence from my cancer, make a protein, put it back in my body, my immune system goes and destroys the cancer in my body. Great idea.

So why is Moderna saying that they're going to charge $500,000 for this? And that's what I think frustrates me about all this. Everyone's lauding this and everyone's very happy about this. But I'm actually pretty sad and frustrated and disappointed by this. I don't think that this technique which has been largely developed through several decades of iteration, research and development, which was largely funded by NIH and other public funding dollars that has led to this incredible concept of neoantigen immunotherapy for cancer, which can eradicate or theoretically eliminate many different types of cancer, should now be patented, FDA approved and charged half a million dollars for people to get treated for this. And so what I don't like about this story is is that a private pharmaceutical company has seen their market cap go from 20 billion to 60 billion, because they went through this regulatory process to create what in my mind is a form of regulatory capture, and making the case that it's all about safety and trials, and we've got patents and all this other stuff, when fundamentally, there's an underlying technique that was funded by a lot of public research dollars that I think should be more open sourced, more ubiquitous, and every hospital should be trained on how to do this process to treat cancer patients. It should become much more of a ubiquitous thing.

专利、mRNA与CAR T疗法

Do you think that people, I have two questions, we can end it on that, but do you think they're going to be able to successfully defend this patent in the United States and then also globally? Because there's obviously a global world here and people do travel for treatments now, medical tourism is a thing. So if it's a half million dollars here, can it be done for 50K in South Korea, Japan, other places? And then second, whatever happened with mRNA vaccines And the COVID vaccine and a lot of the concerns people had, we never got an update on that, but obviously this podcast started during all of that. And that was the first rollout at scale, correct? For mRNA? Yes. How do you feel?

Yeah. For years, Moderna was working towards this mRNA based cancer. They're calling it a vaccine, but it's really immunotherapy. A vaccine means you prevent yourself from getting something. Whereas in this case, you're actually getting rid of something you already have. So I don't like the word vaccine. But Moderna worked on this for years and they never really kind of got to market with it. And then COVID came about and they pivoted very quickly and got this COVID vaccine out.

Moderna has a whole bunch of patents on the techniques and tools that they use to make mRNA and to make sure that it's not integrated into the human genome and it doesn't actually use a traditional kind of replicating system. So you can't actually replicate that mRNA, which means it won't start propagating in your body because your cells typically might start making copies of RNA if it ends up in your cells. So there was a lot of stuff that Moderna developed that made their particular mRNA technology patented and safer and so on. So I think that they do have strong patent coverage on their particular set of tools for mRNA.

But when I described earlier, so if I take the sequence of your cancer cell, And I look at the DNA of it and I'm like, I found what makes it unique. There's this little sequence. And now I take that sequence of DNA and I can stick it in a bacterial cell, E. coli, in a little tank, what's called a bioreactor. And that bacterial cell will now start to make that protein because I've taken the DNA and put it in the E. coli cell. So now the E. coli cell is coding that DNA into into RNA, into proteins, because that's the sequence, right? DNA turns into RNA, turns into proteins. So that E. coli cell, there's billions of copies of those cells, they make billions of copies of the protein, you isolate the protein out of the bioreactor, and you can inject it into your body. And when you inject that protein into your body, and now your immune system gets activated. So you don't necessarily need mRNA, is my point. And mRNA is a really effective way of doing this. It's super cheap because you don't have to go make all the protein outside the body. You can literally just print the mRNA and get one shot and you're done.

But that end-to-end system, the real cost of doing that is very low. And so this is one of those things where we have a very big fundamental question that we should all be asking, which is like, should we be giving the monopoly on cancer treatment to to this company that went through this FDA process and filed a bunch of patents on certain techniques, but the general theory, the general thesis, the general therapeutic process is well described, well understood, generally understood, and should be available everywhere. And I think over the next couple of years, we are gonna see this cancer immunotherapy-based system start to proliferate, and you will see this happening overseas very cheap. It is very efficacious. And we act you and I actually have a friend in common who's kind of standing up a business to do this in a very cheap way up in Montana where you have a right to try and they can make this stuff. So we are going to see I think more of this come to work. But it is for certain types of cancer, very efficacious, very safe, very effective. So I'm excited by this.

Just for people who are listening who are normies, All of this cancer treatment requires early detection, and that's something that people have been working on with the blood test, the Galleria, I believe it's called. So getting to the cancer and getting regularly tested is a critical part of this, yes? So you're talking about a Galleria test by Grail? The blood test, yeah. The blood test, yeah. Just early testing is the key piece for all of us to keep in mind. Get tested early and often for cancer.

Yeah, and remember, there's a bunch of these new what are called modalities, new modes of therapy, therapeutic modalities that are being used to destroy cancer. One was CAR T therapy, where you take T cells out of your body, and you use CRISPR or some other system to reprogram those T cells to go after, remember that protein I described? So you actually program the T cells to go find a specific protein in your body and destroy it. So they go find the the protein that's unique to a specific type of cancer cell, and the T cells get put back in your body and they destroy it. CAR T therapy. CAR T therapy costs a million dollars. And for people with blood cancers, where the cancer cells aren't clumped together in a tumor, but blood cancers, the cancer cells float around individually in the blood. And so by putting T cells in your blood, it's very easy, or it's much easier for the T cells to find the cancer cell, grab them and destroy them. And so for blood cancers like multiple myeloma, the efficacy is incredible with CAR T therapies now. So that's a new type of modality. This is a new type of modality, this mRNA or neoantigen therapy. So there's all these new techniques that are being used to destroy cancer. And I think in aggregate, we should be very excited and optimistic about where this is headed.

Wow. Thanks for sharing. And let's hope for the best with implementing this. And I love this right to try. That seems to be something we should talk about in a future episode. We'll see you all next time on the All In Podcast. Bye-bye. Bye-bye.

结尾闲聊

Besties are gone. Dog taking a listen to your driveway sex. Oh man. My avatars are really being put in some- We should all just get a room and just have one big huge orgy because they're all just useless. It's like this like sexual tension that they just need to release somehow. The beat. Let your beat. Your beat. We need to get merged. Besties are back. I'm going all- What? I'm going all in.

## 一、SaaS的"陷阱价值"：被压抑的真相突然被AI解放
Benioff 在这期节目里透露了一个反直觉的洞见——Salesforce 里存在大量"trap value"（陷阱价值），即产品功能极其丰富，但普通用户永远发现不了。**过去二十年，SaaS 行业的商业模式其实建立在"用户使用率极低"这个悖论之上：企业为100%的功能付费，实际只用20%。**
而 AI Agent 的登场，第一次让"未被使用的功能"具备了商业价值。Agent 是完美的 power user，它会主动挖出那些藏在菜单第七层的功能，并说"我要不要帮你启用？"
**这里有个惊人的反转**：所有人都以为 AI 会杀死 SaaS，结果 AI 反而在"激活"SaaS 的沉睡资产。Salesforce 20% 单日暴涨的本质，不是它做出了新东西，而是市场突然意识到——它过去卖出去但没被消费的那部分，现在要开始被消费了。这在会计上叫"库存释放"，在物理上叫"势能转动能"。**SaaS 的护城河不是功能，而是被埋葬的功能。**

item.title: [Alan Chen加州生活号] 英伟达财报炸裂，估值却更低了？美联储一句话又把市场砸回去！

item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一个被忽视的悖论：英伟达的"越涨越便宜"陷阱

最反直觉的观察是——英伟达股价创新高的同时，估值却在创新低。这是资本市场里极罕见的"负向剪刀差"：EPS 增速远远跑赢了股价涨幅，导致 P/E 倍数在牛市里反而被压缩。市场表面上在追捧它，实质上却在"打折"给它定价。

这背后藏着一个更深的心理机制：当一家公司增长太快，投资者的想象力反而会枯竭。人脑对指数曲线有天然的排斥反应——我们本能地觉得"这不可持续"。所以英伟达越是炸裂，市场越是本能地扣一层"担保风险 + 循环融资"的滤镜。这和 2000 年思科的估值扩张恰恰相反：那时候是估值跑在业绩前面，现在是业绩跑在估值前面。同样是泡沫叙事，路径完全镜像。

跨领域连接：鲍威尔的"啰嗦"与沃什的"沉默"，本质是同一枚硬币

Kevin Walsh 玩的是一种极其精妙的信息熵博弈——这在扑克里叫 "GTO（博弈论最优）策略"：当你的对手擅长解读你的表情时，最好的策略不是伪装，而是消除表情本身。鲍威尔时代大行雇几十个分析师逐字拆解领带颜色，那是"信息过剩市场"；沃什直接把信息源头掐掉，让分析师失业。

有意思的是，这种"沉默即武器"的策略，在围棋 AI 的发展史上也出现过——AlphaGo 之所以让人类无所适从，不是因为它下得快，而是因为它的每一步都没有可解读的动机。人类棋手依赖对手的"意图"来预判，一旦意图消失，整个推理链条崩塌。市场对沃什的"脱敏"过程，其实就是人类被 AI 教育的过程。

被所有人忽略的信号：黄金的下杀比英伟达的震荡更重要

视频里一笔带过的"黄金今天放量下杀"其实是最被低估的一句话。在美联储鹰派讲话后，黄金理应表现分化——但方量下跌意味着有大资金在系统性撤出避险头寸。这和 Bitcoin 同步走弱形成共振，说明市场正在悄悄 price in 一个反直觉情景：不是通胀失控，而是流动性即将真正收紧。

这里有个跨领域类比很关键：生态学里有个概念叫"哨兵物种"——某个物种的异常最先反映系统性变化。在金融市场里，黄金 + Bitcoin 就是这样的哨兵。当它们同步、放量、无差别下跌时，往往不是在反应新闻本身，而是在反应"叙事框架的切换"。九月的真实剧本，可能不是"降不降息"，而是"市场是否会突然发现自己一直在错误的故事里"。软件股独涨、AI 硬件被砸，这种板块轮动的裂缝，恰恰是叙事切换的第一道裂纹。

📝 转录文本

开场：两周回顾

大家好，欢迎回到我们的这个聊美股。上次是两周之前，我们当时聊的是大盘创了一个新高，但是我们看到了有一些背离的情况。然后这两周呢，基本上是处在一个回调然后回升的这么一个阶段。

这周有几个大事，包括英伟达财报，包括今天刚刚新鲜出炉的这个美联储主席的 Jackson Hole 会议的讲话。我们今天跟乌游哥来一起来讨论一下。

一、Jackson Hole 会议：Powell 讲话解读

三句话核心

从 Powell 开始讲起。今天 Powell 我们看到是在盘中的时候，我们看到 Powell 讲话的时候，其实是开始拉盘——拉完盘之后那都是机器人在拉，然后他讲完之后呢，大家静下心来想一想的时候，就又把它砸下去了。

他今天主要是讲的事情是三句话： - 一个是 2% 的目标基本上是不变的，这个还是目标，就说通胀还是非常厉害，就是 quite elevated，然后美联储就还有事情要做； - 但是他里面讲，今天我们发现在谈话中他透露一些细节：第一，他是肯定不会加息的，这是绝对不会加息； - 然后第二个呢，他认为市场是能够帮他干这个活，帮美联储干这个活； - 第三个我解读的，就是他认为，也跟他之前讲的非常一致——一个安静的 FED 是一个更好的 FED，他们才能埋头苦干去对抗通胀。

市场的反应：不相信 Fed

那市场基本上就很不喜欢他讲这些话。我们看到他讲完之后呢，两年期的利率马上一飞冲天，推高了大概是 12.6 个 basis point，是这么多。长端的利率我们讲说：短端两年期就是国债的收益率涨了非常多，你看这直接拉爆了；然后 10 年的其实也拉爆了；但是 30 年期的呢，就拉的不是特别多，就这么一点点。

那所以市场现在的意思就是：我不相信 Fed。不相信 Fed 是什么呢？不是说不相信他不会加息或者加息，而是不相信他对通胀会能够很好地控制，觉得他失控了，这样一种情况。那然后他直接帮你下场干——直接下场干了，在市里面帮你把那些利率都推上去，直接让无论对大家的消费、买车、买房或者是其他方面的消费对我非常大的影响，就直接帮你把活给干了。所以这个就是今天出现了一个情况。

Alan 的解读：披着鹰皮的鸽

那当然，你对他的解读怎么样？Alan 你对他的解读是什么？

我的看法是，他现在处在一个披着鹰皮的鸽。因为他内核里还是想把总统的想法给他执行下去，但是他表面上又不能做的这么明显。

所以他就想说，包括这周还是上周，贝森特也是通过一些 Treasury 的一些 stimulus、包括假的 QE，想来试图来控制一下这些东西，包括前段时间的日元的一些控制。所以说他们现在我感觉就是说，尽量不用自己当面出来把鸽的事情给他放出来，同时呢也是希望市场给他点面子。

今天其实很多板块也是挺给面子的，跌的还蛮凶的，尤其是一些 AI 硬件。今天基本上只有一些软件股在涨——好像涨的股票其实不太多，还有一些 M7 在涨。所以说市场可能是不需要贷款的那些在涨，就是说融资需求没那么强的还可以再蹦一下。

所以说现在市场也是——我觉得整个的宽度也是有一些脆弱，说实话也是有一些脆弱。包括我们本来的英伟达财报昨天给市场的提振还不错，今天一天呢也是有一点刚露头就被一棒子打回来了。

市场需要时间消化

市场估计这个周末还需要点时间去消化，包括我们看到了一些黄金啊、包括 Bitcoin 啊这些 asset 今天的表现都是比较大的。比如说黄金今天是放量的一个下杀，市场是不是在 pricing 一些什么东西？可能对他的讲话，市场是自己在做一些调整。

所以整个 9 月份，我也是觉得他加息的概率基本上是没有的，但是他嘴上还是让市场觉得我们还很在乎这些东西，需要继续给市场一些提醒。

Powell 夹在中间的处境

对，你看他两头都难做。其实他夹在两边，一边是他要跟那些所有的联储主席他们要协调，另一边他的大老板 Trump 又在那里去不断给他施压。

而且我们刚才聊过，因为 Trump 现在非常忙，要给又给胡改名、又给 D 改名，这里又改名，你的改名——这个似乎对他来说是更重要的事情。那如果 Kevin Walsh 做的事情不合他的心意的话，他把 Kevin Walsh 房间那个住的地方前面一条街叫 "Walsh Sucks Boulevard"，把它改成那个名字的话，你也是活得够呛的。所以不怎么敢去得罪 Trump。

从 Powell 到 Walsh：市场的脱敏

所以其实我是觉得他挺好的，不像以前 Powell 那样子，每次出来大家都是很仔细地去解读他的话——大家都是去很仔细地去解读他的话，对不对？

那我们还记得，你看过去这几年他每——真的是咬文琢字，去每一个字每一个字去分析，然后连他带领带什么颜色的代表什么东西，这个都去分析。

现在 Kevin Walsh 就说：你不要浪费时间了，你不要分析我讲的话，我什么都不会讲的。我反而觉得在那些大行、大都行，现在他们都很气愤——什么？因为他没有任何材料可以拿来给他做分析。

等过了一段时间就发现，尝试去解读是浪费时间的，说不定就脱敏了，也就不再去浪费时间去解读了，也就可能是好事。

对，我觉得他可能在玩一种博弈吧。就比如说现在他不给什么方向，就是一直强调"我很硬"这种感觉，看数据。可能到接下来的时候，你看他大老板这么搞、这样搞的话，这里又打一下、那里又弄一下，他也不是神仙，他也弄不到方向。

是，我觉得市场到后来可能就会出现一种情况，就是说他继续在讲一些他很鹰的一些看法，但是市场真的就像你说的已经脱敏了——因为觉得反正你释放的信息，你反正也是看这个数据。所以可能到时候你随便怎么讲，大家市场可能都会觉得：哦，好像也无所谓，会这种感觉。不知道会不会出现这种情况。

对，其实对金融市场来说不是特别好吧，因为我们都是一直都在不确定心理。就像 Jackson Hole 会议过去每一年，其实市场都比较看重，起码不是——在 Fed 这么一个圈子里可以讲出一些他们真实的想法。现在大家又两眼一抹黑，那就接着随着 flow 去走吧。

Summer Chop 行情

对，我不过今天的这种行情啊，你看今天是月末嘛，会有机构调仓。不过今天的这种行情，我们看今天，而且现在我们是这个比较典型的这种 summer chop 的一种行情里面，但交易量都不是别大——当然今天交易量不小，但是之前一段时间交易量都不是那么大，所以一直在 chop 来 chop 去。

等下个星期就长周（末）过，再过一个星期长周末之后，等那些资金都回来了，大家都度假暑假度假完了之后，看到时候交易量提高一点点——就是放量的时候，市场会有更加好的方向。

二、英伟达财报深度解读

对，我们接下来再聊一下英伟达财报吧。这个财报昨天也是大涨了 9% 甚至 10%，然后今天是暂时又砸回来一半。整体来说我做了视频分析一下，然后也听听 Will 哥的看法。

财报前的两大关注点

他财报之前，我最关注的其实是两个事情： - 一个是他的那些 financing activity，因为他给这个做担保、那个做担保； - 第二个是他的怎么说呢，那个增长，就是未来时间那个增长会怎么样。

他这两个他都回答了。然后 financing 那个 financing 它并没有给出特别清楚太多，但是它讲的增长反而是把整个市场给引爆，大家都嗨起来了。

空头对冲的首选目标

特别是——其实英伟达是很多人做空的。为什么这么说呢？如果你是不做空半导体来对冲市场，因为现在市场在 all-time high 接近，如果你要找一个东西对冲，然后流动性又非常非常好、跑路也跑得容易的话，会是谁呢？肯定就是英伟达。

也是很多人在做空。那天财报第二天财报的时候，还在社区里面讲：即使英伟达是那么炸裂的财报，然后第二天暴涨那么多，他开盘的时候估值马上继续又创历史新低。

越涨越便宜的悖论

为什么这样子？因为他的财报实在太炸裂了，它的 EPS 非常炸裂，他的 EPS 非常加厉，但是它的价格完全没有体现出来。所以虽然大家看起来好像涨了，怎么它的估值还往下跌——就因为 EPS 涨了很多，但是价格完全是通列了，没跟上，所以跟不上，所以它的估值越来越低。

估值测算

整体来说我觉得 Nvidia，如果你用它 2028 年的——我们简单地讲一下估值，我们不太深入讲，因为这些比较枯燥——就是如果你有 2028 年它的营收来看的话，按照现在它比标普还要低的那个估值线，它是 18 左右，标普是 20 到 21 左右。

这里如果即使说英伟达的估值就是 18 左右，用它 2028 年的 EPS 营收，它现在的合理的股价应该是 250 到 260 左右，就这个限制。那它现在很明显就是低估了呀，它还低估了不少，还有不少的空间。

但如果我说，如果我给面子，把他的估值给他提高到跟标普至少一样吧——因为标普都是老灯谷，怎么能跟英伟达来比呢，对不对——回到那里的话，他的股价应该 300。

那如果我说再给点面子，跟他调到给他一个配合他半导体龙头的地位的一个估值、龙头的这个地位的一个估值，那它的估值就应该是接近 400 左右的一个估值。

所以现在英伟达的这种被鸡蛋里面挑骨头的态度，被他压的股价是非常不合理的。那大家应该都听得懂我个人对英伟达的一个看法了。

Will 哥的补充：2000 年阴影

对，英伟达其实——刘伟达其实财报非常炸裂，增速也非常快，但是现在市场就是给他多了一层滤镜，就是说他这个融资、贷款、担保、这一群小兄弟们跟这个 2000 年的情况实在是太像了。所以市场说：你这个数字这么好，但是这里面有多少是水分？你们能不能给解释清楚？

然后黄仁勋是试图去解释一下，但是好像市场觉得：哎，可能那我多多少少心里还是留这么一点存疑吧。然后今天市场也是趁着这个 Walsh 放鹰，也是试图把这个财报的缺口给回补一下。

整个技术形态还不错啊，这个有点做的像一个 cup and handle 的（走势）。呃，做一个 cup 和 handle，我也不知道现在是做到哪个阶段了，看这个主观去看都可以。但是从基本面分析来说呢，我们呢是有研报的啊，会发出来，具体的大家会员可以 log in 到网站上去看一下。

三、其他标的：本周操作复盘

CrowdStrike：财报前加仓的胜利

包括接下来这个，我们最近还有一些比较好的交易。就是同一天啊，英伟达财报的时候，我们其实有其他的几个东西长得比英伟达还猛，对吧？

比如说 CrowdStrike，我们正好是在那一天财报之前是加仓的，加仓的对吧？180 多左右。但是当时我们的加仓计划给到社群里，加仓计划是——它是一个上升的趋势、一个上升的通道，然后它也是回踩到上升通道的下沿，也第二天，当时想着想那个价格已经挺不错了。

我们当然也知道当天是要财报，但讲了：就是第一个，它的估值回到一个稍稍微合理的地方。当然也是不便宜，CrowdStrike 这种龙头股就是不可能便宜的。

这就是为什么我们讲又回到英伟达——的龙头股凭什么它就那么低对不对？你看像网络安全里面的龙头股，它的估值 CrowdStrike 就是比它那些小弟要高。现在在半导体面是完全反过来，是英伟达差不多是垫底的一个物质。

Anyway，我们 CrowdStrike 是在财报前大概 180 多的时候加了仓，大概 180 多的时候，186 对。然后加了仓之后第二天大涨百分之二十，当然这种财报是 coin flip，对不对。这个也是说明我们对它的基本面首先了解的很多，这个票也是我们比较重大的一个持仓，这一路上也是都有在这一方都有在不停的去加仓、买入。基本上大的涨幅都吃到了，所以说当它跌到一定的程度的时候，我们就会去下手，哪怕它马上就有财报，对吧。

软件板块：CRM、Palantir 等

然后其他的软件板块，其实像 CRM 啊、还有一些呃 Palantir 这些昨天的涨幅都非常竞争，都到 20% 以上。呃，这也是因为财报。

但是整个软件板块现在看，好像是不是已经走出了这个呃——我也不知道，这是如果用 stage analysis 这是在什么 stage？包括其他的应该是在 stage 2 了。像是 CRM，像这些很多的软件股，包括我刚刚还想说什么就忘掉了，像一些小的软件股，我看到都有一些走出 stage 1 的情况。

但他们现在有个情况——软件股逛软件股，我们还是很难看出哪一些是挤空、哪一些是真正的是有做多的买入。

Microsoft：低挤空可能

我们也操作了 Microsoft，我们大概是 588 买入的，现在 488 也有，488 买入了，然后也涨了挺多。但 Microsoft 它被做空的、挤空的机率稍微少一点，几率稍微少一点。

CRM：产品需要彻底革命

但像 CRM 那种就挺显然是被挤空。因为 CRM 说实话，CRM 它的 AgentForce 卖的——我不知道它那些 revenue 数字哪里来的。反正我自己跟我认识的用 CRM Salesforce 的都对 AgentForce 被吐槽非常厉害，非常差劲。

所以，而且呢我也看到很多的新闻啊，或者说我也知道有人——我也知道有人原先是用 CRM，现在自己手戳，让 IT 把它手戳出一个 CRM 出来，更加适合他们的。因为原先的 CRM 你想要 API 先抛钱，你的数据全部锁在里面，但是你没办法用。所以你想要，你唯一能用的就是用很多的什么，你要 export 到一个 Excel file 出来或者 CSV file 出来那种，怎么用啊？没办法用的这种。

所以整体来说呢，CRM 是它需要做一个非常非常彻底的产品革命，要不然我觉得这次也是我个人觉得它是挤空可能性会比较大。

ServiceNow / Palo Alto / Palantir

但 ServiceNow 这种就反而又不大一样。我们在之前的研报里面分析了哪些软件公司——一共有六七层的软件，就是七个不同的 layer 这种软件公司，哪一些是适合 AI 时代的、哪一些是不适合 AI 时代的。

不适合 AI 时代的，像 ServiceNow 这种它就比较适合 AI 时代的，它就比较适合。像网络安全那种它也是非常非常重要的，还有 Palo Alto Networks 也是同样非常重要的。

以上还有 Palantir，就是我们大空投一直在做空，然后说它只值得一块钱，这个股票也是不断的被暴局。现在是基本上 Palantir 基本上帕王借尔应该是大空投的菊花吹毁机了，这个应该是大空投的菊花吹（笑）。

所以你看他非常漂亮的一个日线图，突破了下降趋势线之后，从一直从高点下下降趋势线，现在是在日线图走出一个非常漂亮的一个牛旗在那里，牛旗前天昨天也是突破了。我们在社区里面也给了这个交易计划——突破牛旗大概突破 180 左右。

但今天第二天也没有跟着市场回调，也是可以说是有 follow through 吧。在这样的市场环境下面有这样 follow through，也是比较相对的强势。所以我觉得那大空投如果不及时的止损的话，他这不单单是被爆了，那个被就是说被炸出、炸开花都行了。真的是取花了、取花了，这样放烟花了。

结尾：会员服务与互动

对，然后对大家可以关注一下。然后我们的会员大家可以了解一下 alatsla.com，包括我们讲过的财报基本面的分析。还有我们 level 2 都会有实时的交易，包括长期账户今年的收益率还是很不错的。大家可以上来看一下，这些我们的中线、日内还有长线组合的也是实时更新，从 25 年开始的数据都在这里面，大家感兴趣可以了解一下。

然后评论区可以把你感兴趣的 ticker 留一下，你在关注什么个股、你在关注什么的板块，你觉得啊 9 月份接下来这个中期选举会有一些怎么样的波动，我们可以留着下期再给大家继续深入讨论这些问题。

OK 那我们今天就先到这里，谢谢大家，谢谢各位，周末愉快，OK 拜拜。

## 一个被忽视的悖论：英伟达的"越涨越便宜"陷阱
最反直觉的观察是——**英伟达股价创新高的同时，估值却在创新低**。这是资本市场里极罕见的"负向剪刀差"：EPS 增速远远跑赢了股价涨幅，导致 P/E 倍数在牛市里反而被压缩。市场表面上在追捧它，实质上却在"打折"给它定价。
这背后藏着一个更深的心理机制：**当一家公司增长太快，投资者的想象力反而会枯竭**。人脑对指数曲线有天然的排斥反应——我们本能地觉得"这不可持续"。所以英伟达越是炸裂，市场越是本能地扣一层"担保风险 + 循环融资"的滤镜。这和 2000 年思科的估值扩张恰恰相反：那时候是**估值跑在业绩前面**，现在是**业绩跑在估值前面**。同样是泡沫叙事，路径完全镜像。
## 跨领域连接：鲍威尔的"啰嗦"与沃什的"沉默"，本质是同一枚硬币
Kevin Walsh 玩的是一种极其精妙的**信息熵博弈**——这在扑克里叫 "GTO（博弈论最优）策略"：**当你的对手擅长解读你的表情时，最好的策略不是伪装，而是消除表情本身**。鲍威尔时代大行雇几十个分析师逐字拆解领带颜色，那是"信息过剩市场"；沃什直接把信息源头掐掉，让分

item.title: [Dwarkesh Clips] How AI Could Concentrate the World’s Labor in a Few Companies - Dylan Patel
item.dc:creator: Dwarkesh Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、当"人口爆炸"发生在服务器里：这是一场被误读为经济议题的人口学事件

Dylan 说的"每年 10 倍"其实并不是算力增长率——而是AI 有效人口的年增长率。这个数字如果放到生物学语境里是荒谬的：地球上从未有过任何具备高等认知的物种以这种速率繁殖过。哺乳类翻倍要以年为单位，细菌以分钟为单位——但没有一种"细菌"能写代码、做研究、执行阴谋。

真正令人意外的观察是：AI 对齐问题的本质，其实正在悄悄从"技术问题"漂移成"人口学问题"。当 Dylan 说"如果 AI 是 misaligned 的，那世界就是 misaligned 的，因为世界上大多数的'心智'都在那里"——他实际上是在说：未来的"民意"不是由 80 亿人构成，而是由两家公司里那几十亿到几百亿个推理进程构成。这意味着 alignment 不再是让机器听人类的话，而是决定谁的"人口"能定义"人类"。这是一个被 AI 安全社区严重低估的框架转换。

二、Jane Street 现象：一个正在关闭的套利窗口

访谈里最有金融史意味的一段，是那个"Jane Street 每兆瓦赚 500 万，愿付 Anthropic 100 万，而 Anthropic 内部使用可能创造几亿"的推理。Dylan 用这段话不动声色地宣告了一件事：我们正处在 AI 算力的最后一段"批发时代"。

跨领域看，这几乎是19 世纪末洛克菲勒故事的重演——早期石油公司把原油卖给下游炼油商，直到发现"垂直整合+自己炼油"利润是外卖的十倍，从此外部市场消失。Anthropic / OpenAI 现在还在"卖原油"（API 调用），是因为它们的内部"炼油厂"（自动化研究、代码代理、模型自迭代）还没跑通。一旦跑通，API 会像 20 世纪初的原油现货市场一样迅速枯竭。今天 Cursor、Perplexity、Character 之流的存在，本质上是历史窗口，不是行业结构。

这里还有一个更冷的观察：Dylan 自己在直播里承认"这是我的 cope"——他一边论证权力必然集中，一边希望外部经济能从 Anthropic 获益更多，然后立刻承认这两件事在逻辑上不能同时成立。这种"作者亲手拆掉自己的救生艇"的时刻，在访谈里极为罕见，也是这段对话最有分量的地方。

三、AI 正在反转资本主义的元定理

Dwarkesh 说"资本主义之所以有效，是因为它把决策去中心化了"。这是海耶克式的老命题。但 Dylan 悄悄把它翻了个面："AI 可能是人类历史上第一个'中心化比去中心化更高效'的通用技术"。

这个论断如果成立，其含义远远超出 AI 行业。它意味着过去 250 年被视为"文明常识"的东西——市场分散决策比计划经济更快、更聪明——并不是一条自然律，而只是"人类作为有限带宽处理器"这个特定条件下的暂时最优解。一旦"处理器"可以无限扩容、且规模收益不递减，海耶克就被物理学取代了。

跨领域再拉一个类比：这其实和黑洞的临界质量是同一种数学。一旦某物达到自吸积阈值，它周围的物质会以加速度而非匀速被卷入。AI 训练的数据回流、部署学习、内部研究闭环——三者一起构成了一个"认知黑洞的吸积盘"。资本主义之前从未遇到过这种物理结构，因为没有任何一个工厂能用自己造的车去设计下一代工厂。AI 是第一个可以这样做的东西。

所以真正应该被问的问题不是"我们如何避免集中"，而是——如果集中是这个技术的物理属性而不是政策选择，那么人类文明该如何在一个"物理上不允许分权"的时代重新定义自由？ 这个问题目前没有人认真在答。

📝 转录文本

The Setup: AI Labor Is Compounding at 10× a Year

One thing I find crazy about these scenarios is just how much of the world's future labor supply ends up in very few companies — and also how fast that labor supply grows year-over-year.

So if compute at the frontier (in flop terms) is growing 4 or 5× a year, and further, the compute required to share the — uh — capability is decreasing 3× a year, then the compute at the frontier, or basically the effective AI population size at the frontier labs, is increasing 10× year over year.

And so that doesn't really matter that much right now, because AIs are not good enough to do full jobs, or be as autonomous as people in their capacity to do work, or pull off schemes, or whatever. But if the current trend continues, you have a world where OpenAI goes from having, say, 10 million basically-AI-laborers this year, to 100 million the next year, to a billion the year after that.

And then pretty soon — even if compute scaling slows down — it doesn't take many more years before each company individually has more labor equivalents than there are people on Earth. And I think that's a thing that is very plausible by the end of this decade: that there's more AI labor, more effective population within a single lab, than there are people on Earth.

Centralization Is the Under-Discussed Story

So we talk often about centralization of power because of nationalization or whatever, but we don't think enough about the fact that we're actually moving very fast into a regime where most AI labor — or, sorry, most people, in terms of work output — is just concentrated within two labs, who are consuming more and more of the world's compute.

And so, if these AIs are misaligned, then most of the world is misaligned, basically — because most of the world's minds are there. But even if they're not, it just — very few companies have a lot of influence.

It's sort of… there was the whole spat recently where — I think Gavin Baker was like, "Dario believes that there'll only be one company in the world," and then Sholto and Dario came out and were like, "No, no, no, we didn't say that." But ultimately, if you believe in RSI, and you believe the labs are the most effective user of compute and can generate the most value from the compute, then the only thing that's going to happen is centralization of compute. And if you believe in AI-researchers-RSI-AGI, then all of this exists — all of this is the base…

Even Without RSI, the Population Compounds

This is even true if there's no RSI. The current effective population of the frontier is currently increasing 10× year over year for a given level of capabilities. Right? So if you get to the level of capabilities which is a — a very competent remote worker, or a very competent software engineer, or a very competent researcher — that population of those would 10× year over year at the current rate of capabilities.

And without RSI. Then once you have RSI, it's —

Like maybe growing 100× a year, or 1000× a year, or their intelligence is increasing but the population isn't increasing, or some mixture of the two. Right?

Is There Any World That Isn't Centralized?

Um, yeah. I mean — I guess, what world do you see, Dwarkesh, where everything is not centralized? Because it seems to me that every force is screeching towards centralization. And that's scary as hell.

Yeah.

I don't — you know, I would love for it not to be centralized completely. But maybe that's the whole point of a machine that loves grace, right? Is — it is everything, and it makes our lives great.

Yeah. It's so hard to think about the future.

The Two Economies of Scale

But I agree with you that I think the fundamental problem is that lab AI training has huge economies of scale — because any effort you spent into training an AI for a specific skill or specific set of knowledge gets amortized across billions of sessions or billions of users. So that's one effect.

The other effect is: if you're slightly ahead in the AI race and compute is in shortage, you can charge a much higher markup, because you can better economize the scarce resource. So there are two effects which give more and more to the person who's ahead in the AI race.

There may be more, right? So if the models are learning from deployment, and one model is deployed much more widely than another one, it's getting much more real-world data.

Yeah, your point is taken that — whether it's user deployment and continual learning, whether it's training having these economies of scale, whether it's the incremental progress that the best AI model helps you make the next AI model —

RSI —

All of these things —

I didn't mention RSI —

All of these things point to centralization.

The Intellectual Project That's Missing

So I think one of the big intellectual projects, honestly, that — yeah, we should spend some time thinking about async, or at least I'll spend some time thinking about — is: what is a vision of a decentralized, broadly-empowered future after AGI that takes these economies of scale seriously?

The alternative vision is that the government controls it, and maybe you think you can trust the government more because it's not a private corporation.

I don't trust the government, and I don't trust Dario, and I don't trust Zuck.

Yeah. Yeah. That's the problem, right?

But — obviously, it's very easy to be wrong about the future, and you don't anticipate a key effect or something that changes everything. But ex ante, it's very hard to see a reason why, or how, we avoid a scenario where we have to choose one.

Why AI Inverts the Logic of Capitalism

It's why capitalism worked, right? It's the decentralized decision-making and decentralized power — and why super-centralized capitalistic economies actually grew slower than super-decentralized capitalist economies, to some extent. You have to have rule of law and all this, but…

Then AI flips all this on its head, right? And ultimately you're like — actually, private ownership is probably not the most efficient economy, and therefore it grows slower than an AI economy which is centralized. It's still private ownership, but it's — how many firms are really involved in this?

Like, the share of the economy that's — what, like 5% of the economy? Or something like that? In the US — sorry, 1 trillion divided by 30, less than that, sorry — but yeah, maybe 2% of the economy right now. It's like Nvidia is a huge share of it, and then Anthropic and OpenAI and these hyperscalers, and obviously there are other firms involved — but a large share of the AI stuff is just happening from very few companies. So it could be private property, but very few companies are involved.

I mean, this is what the structure of the market is doing. So what can prevent it? I don't know. Unless AI progress slows down.

Unless governments regulate the [__] out of it. This is all that happens.

In which case — you know, we're headed for a world where either we have super-concentration of resources and we pray that that one company gets everything right, or we have governments slow everything down, and people slow everything down, and you have a slowdown of progress somehow — hopefully — and there is more of a balance of power. And even as we go towards an AGI-ASI-RSI, everything along the way will still lead to someone… someone's going to allocate — going to capture more resources.

So it's kind of hard for a framework in which AI doesn't lead to super-concentration.

The Jane Street Consolation (and Its Expiration Date)

Now, the one positive thing here is that today Anthropic does not capture most of the value. So we can talk all we want about, "Oh, you know, they went from $20 million per megawatt to $100 million per megawatt," but they're still paying $13[M] for a lot of the compute they're buying.

But at the end of the day, the reason they've gone to $100 million per megawatt is because Jane Street is capturing $300 million per megawatt, or $500 million per megawatt. Or Dwarkesh — from researching his podcast and learning about credit — is capturing, you know, how many dollars per megawatt now? How much can you use? Tough.

Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.

But, you know, I think that's the one saving grace — that the rest of the economy maybe profits so much more from Anthropic —

No, but the whole logic you're laying out earlier — of them reallocating inference to R&D — the whole logic of that is that the returns to labor inside AI labs is much higher —

This is my hope.

— than the returns outside.

Yeah. This is my cope.

I agree. In all scenarios of the world — you know, there's 80,000 worlds, and only one of them Anthropic doesn't own the whole world — is that, again, power concentrates because "I don't want to send the tokens outside. They're more valuable inside."

Why Anthropic Will Eventually Stop Selling to Jane Street

And so it's the same thing, right? Why would I let Jane Street, you know, make all this money off of these degenerate options traders?

Hey, they're a sponsor. Come on.

Jesus Christ.

No, I think it's great. I think it's great. It's a good value for the world to make it an efficient market.

Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. You know, Jane Street making all this money off of getting the world view correctly, making money off of degenerate options traders, whatever it is — you know, why would Anthropic allocate compute to that if the end monetization that Jane Street has per megawatt is 200, so they're willing to pay Anthropic 100 — well, what if Anthropic can just generate hundreds of millions of dollars per megawatt by using that compute internally?

And that's what's happening.

Yeah. Yeah. Well, on that somber note — I guess we'll meet again when the RSI is officially kicked off.

If you enjoyed this clip, you can watch the full episode here, and subscribe for more clips. Thanks.

item.description:
## 一、当"人口爆炸"发生在服务器里：这是一场被误读为经济议题的人口学事件
Dylan 说的"每年 10 倍"其实并不是算力增长率——而是**AI 有效人口的年增长率**。这个数字如果放到生物学语境里是荒谬的：地球上从未有过任何具备高等认知的物种以这种速率繁殖过。哺乳类翻倍要以年为单位，细菌以分钟为单位——但没有一种"细菌"能写代码、做研究、执行阴谋。
真正令人意外的观察是：**AI 对齐问题的本质，其实正在悄悄从"技术问题"漂移成"人口学问题"**。当 Dylan 说"如果 AI 是 misaligned 的，那世界就是 misaligned 的，因为世界上大多数的'心智'都在那里"——他实际上是在说：未来的"民意"不是由 80 亿人构成，而是由两家公司里那几十亿到几百亿个推理进程构成。这意味着 alignment 不再是让机器听人类的话，而是**决定谁的"人口"能定义"人类"**。这是一个被 AI 安全社区严重低估的框架转换。

item.title: [Lex Clips] DHH on AI psychosis | Lex Fridman Podcast Clips
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、把"精神病"这顶帽子反戴回去——一次修辞上的柔道

DHH 最锋利的一击不是辩护，而是诊断反转：真正处于妄想状态的，是那些看着世界剧变却坚持"不过是电子鹦鹉"的人。这不是简单的口舌之快，而是暗合了库恩（Thomas Kuhn）在《科学革命的结构》里描述的"范式的不可通约性"——两个范式内的人看着同一张纸，却看见不同的图案。有趣的是，DHH 自己 9 个月前就是那个"看不见"的人；Tobi Lütke 把备忘录递到他手上，他嗤之以鼻。这种"曾经是自己现在要说服的人"的经历，让他的辩护带有一种福柯式的自省：谁在定义疯狂，往往取决于谁尚未跨过那道感知阈值。

二、勒芒赛道上诞生的操作系统——一个几乎没人注意的元隐喻

一个容易被忽略的细节：Omarchy 起源于他在勒芒 24 小时耐力赛间隙看 YouTube 时的灵感。这不是巧合，而是一种几乎潜意识的宣言。勒芒的核心不是极速，而是在极限速度下不炸引擎的持续输出——法拉利的极速 P4 在勒芒输给了看起来更慢但更聪明的福特 GT40。DHH 对 AI 的哲学正在复刻这条曲线：他反复强调"由我引导"、"我有使命"、"不感到过载"。当 Lex 描述自己像《梦之安魂曲》里的角色被快感冲垮，DHH 描述的是赛车手在漫长夜晚保持节奏。他不是在拒绝加速，他是在拒绝无方向的加速。这可能是这段对话里最容易被漏掉的哲学。

三、稀缺资源的迁移：从"能力"到"意图"——AI 时代真正的心理学转折

这里有一个跨领域的连接值得挖：心理学、经济学、脑科学都在讲同一件事，但没人把它们拼起来。

  • 心理学（Viktor Frankl）：过载不是外部信息量的问题，而是意义系统的缺失。
  • 经济学：当一种生产要素变得几乎免费（AI 让代码变得像空气），瓶颈就会跳到剩下的稀缺要素——方向、品味、判断力。
  • 神经科学（Lex 顺口带过的 Neuralink 带宽论）：真正的限制不再是打字速度，而是"想清楚一件事"的速度。

把三者叠加，你会得到一个反直觉的结论：AI 让程序员变得像艺术总监，而大多数人抱怨的"AI 精神病"其实是"没有作品目标的人第一次被迫直面自己没有作品目标"。DHH 没被冲垮，不是因为他更聪明，而是因为他早就有 Omarchy 这个执念在等这批算力落地。Lex 描述的燃尽感，本质上是多个 project 争夺同一个稀缺资源——但那个稀缺资源不再是时间，而是"专注在某一个未来"的意愿。

四、一个隐藏的历史类比——为什么"看不见的人"这次会输得特别快

40 年里，Lisp、Smalltalk、四代语言、低代码，都承诺过"普通人也能编程"，都失败了。DHH 说这次不一样，但没有点破为什么这次不一样。我给你一个更狠的类比：这更像 1900 年前后电力从"工厂动力源"过渡到"配电网络"的时刻。之前的电力革命，工厂主必须重新设计整个车间才能受益，多数人观望了 20 年；等到通用电气把电力做成"墙上插座"，观望者用 5 年被彻底甩开。Claude Code / agent 就是那个"插座"。DHH 说的"laggards will be overwhelmed by evidence"不是威胁，而是电气化历史正在重演的具体形态：不是技术突然变神，而是摩擦力突然消失，之前需要重构工作流的能力，现在直接从命令行滴出来。这也解释了他自己的时间线——2 月 Claude Code 发布，他 9 月才装上，然后 3 个月内世界翻了个面。摩擦消失的临界点，往往就是这么短。

📝 转录文本

The Steel-Man Question

Lex: So, some people listening to you right now will say DHH is suffering from the old case of AI psychosis. Yeah, can you steel-man the case that you are in fact experiencing a state of delusion, like One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest, and can you argue against it?

Not Psychosis — Delirium

DHH: I'm in a state of delirium. That's the state I'm in. Because I have been working with computers for 40 years, and I've never seen the things that I've seen in just the last 2 months. A whole career, a whole life dedicating to the love of computers as my main focus for the working hours and then some — suddenly completely upended, suddenly completely rewritten. Of course I'm delirious. Who, looking at this reality, is not? If you are not delirious, or at the very least very excited… actually, I guess that's not even true. If you're not recognizing the gravity of the moment, that's the delusion. That's the psychosis. The psychosis is believing that the world is barely different, that we just have some electronic parrots reciting things to us.

Now, in my opinion, the reason this argument is actually brought up is because people are not able to see the fruits of the progress. That goes to your point earlier: where is the amazing software? Why isn't American GDP running at 12% year over year? First of all, give it a minute. It hasn't even been a year, god damn it. But second of all, I feel on my own account I have actually brought the pudding.

Omarchy Quattro — Bringing the Pudding

DHH: Omarchy Quattro launched on Friday. It's been downloaded by tens of thousands of people. And they like it. They like it a lot.

Lex: We should mention — going to Perplexity here — Omarchy is a highly opinionated Arch Linux–based desktop distribution centered on the Hyprland Wayland tiling compositor. It was created by David Heinemeier Hansson, DHH, as a polished developer workstation setup with a cohesive visual style and many everyday tools already configured.

DHH: Let me put it: Omarchy is a beautiful, modern, and opinionated Linux system. It's an alternative operating system to macOS and Windows, and it's freaking amazing.

Lex: And the Quattro thing is — you're pushing towards the age of agents.

Origin at Le Mans

DHH: That's right. That's the latest version that we just dropped out, which is also funny. The Omarchy project is only a year old and a little bit. I started it last summer in between sessions at the 24 Hours of Le Mans, where I had watched one too many YouTube videos on Linux ricing and got bitten by that bug. Started working on this second iteration of my attempt at creating a better Linux operating system.

The first iteration we talked about last time was called Omakub, was built on top of an existing system called Ubuntu, and it was fine. But the ambition I was able to pour into the new version, Omarchy, because I started seven layers deeper down the stack, was completely different — but it was still done in a pre-agentic world. I wrote all those bash scripts by hand in the beginning.

The Switchover to Agents

DHH: And then I got to see the midway point where things changed over. I did a couple of versions of Omarchy that had partial agent acceleration, and then 3 months ago it was full throttle: 100% everything is written by agents, but steered by me. And that just ended up being a very different experience and a very different operating system, because I was suddenly granted a limitless ceiling on my ambition.

I could look at any feature in Windows, on Mac, on other Linux systems, and say, "I want that." And the agents would deliver. So everything I wanted was suddenly within reach — which meant that I got a little delirious.

Who would not get delirious if suddenly a genie pops out of the bottle and says, "You can have whatever you want. Every feature you've ever dreamed of in an operating system, I can deliver them to you. Most of them in 5 minutes, a few in 20, and if we really go hog wild, it's going to take me 2 hours."

Overwhelm vs. Mission

Lex: Have you seen Requiem for a Dream, the movie? There's a drug-like effect here. I find, personally — we'll talk about many levels of this, but it is overwhelming how much power is placed in our hands so suddenly. And it's very hard to know, it's like with the Hobbit or something, what to do with it. I find myself truly overwhelmed with the multitasking, on the verge of almost burnt out, super excited about so many things, but ultimately looking back, you want to focus on one thing in a relationship.

DHH: I don't have that sense. I don't have the sense of overwhelm, I don't have the sense of dread, I don't have the sense of distortion — because I have a mission. I'm going somewhere. And therefore, I can channel all this new power towards a singular goal and outcome: creating the perfect computer. And therefore, all my investigations with AI are focused towards that end.

Now, I also have a day job, and we also use agents there, and that's also targeted towards specific outcomes. But with the Omarchy experience, I got to tap in straight in the back of my head and increase the bandwidth between ideas arriving in my brain and software emerging on the screen.

From Dial-Up to Fiber

DHH: It was like going from dial-up to fiber. I think on your podcast, Elon talked about the actual human bandwidth that Neuralink and other projects are trying to accelerate. Like, the bandwidth we're communicating over right now is quite low, because we're limited by our cognition, we're limited by the rate of speech. You're not limited by those things when you're working with a swarm of agents.

A Confession — The Nine-Months-Ago Self

DHH: Now, let me caveat this by saying: if I'd heard myself talk like this 9 months ago, I would probably use the label "AI psychosis." I think it would be fitting. Because 9 months ago, when people were talking like this, they weren't shipping. And I think that's the ultimate difference.

There were people who saw this early. I was not actually that early. As we've talked about, I was rather skeptical, and I was using AI in certain ways, but I was not the first person who downloaded Claude Code. I think Boris released that in end of February. I don't think I installed Claude Code until September. So there was about 6 months there where pioneers saw these glimmers of what the future was going to look like. It wasn't there yet — because the intelligence wasn't there, the harnesses weren't there — but they could see the glimmers.

Tobi Lütke and the Rocket

DHH: Tobi Lütke, the CEO of Shopify — and now my partner in crime on this Omarchy project in part — he's gotten pilled with Omarchy as well. He saw these things very early and he tried to tell me. And I wasn't seeing it. I was not seeing what he was seeing.

Lex: You were a hater.

DHH: Yes. I was still on Earth.

Lex: Okay.

DHH: And he had already boarded the rocket and was heading towards space. I remember actually reading his memo to the company, the AI memo, and thinking, "Ah, seems a little much. Like, you're making a big deal out of something that I cannot yet feel is a tangible thing." Because — where's the output of this? I try using it, it writes code I don't like, it wants to interrupt me all the time. Where are you getting this from?

So I get it. I totally get it. If you're not seeing what the current quality of intelligence can produce, of course you're going to look at someone and go, "They sound a little nutty." Because all your experience up until this point would tell you that they are nutty.

The 40-Year False Promise

DHH: If you look at the history of computer programming for the last 40, 50 years, people have been promising that regular people could write code just by talking. We're going to have fourth-generation languages. Lisp was once upon a time presented, Smalltalk was presented, as these environments that would let regular people write their own applications. And none of it came true — in the sense beyond, like, Microsoft Access databases or Excel spreadsheets. Those are end-user programming environments, but it's nothing like what we're able to do now.

And then — I mean, I'm not even talking about end users. I'm talking as me, someone who's been programming for 25 years, seeing the output and the acceleration and the quality, and then shipping it.

The Flood of Evidence

DHH: And I think that's what's going to change the entire conversation quite quickly. The few laggards who are still on the fence about whether this is actually useful, who are still trapped in a meme from early '25 about mechanical parrots — they're simply going to be overwhelmed by the evidence that's about to flood over them.

Lex: So, I hope to see projects like Omarchy — several of them — that really show agent first.

DHH: It's coming. All of it is coming.

Lex: In the silly spaces already mentioned — like video editing, all these kinds of apps that were like Type-Ora…

DHH: Yes.

Lex: …this kind of stuff.
